descriptors.title: Fundamental movement skills
descriptors.description: practise fundamental movement skills in minor game and play situations
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students bring informal movement experience from play and daily life — walking, running, throwing, catching — but without structured FMS practice.
descriptors.endpoint: Students practise locomotor, object-manipulation and balance skills in minor game and play situations, combining them with increasing control and purpose.

nodes.label: Locomotor skills in play
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply different locomotor skills (walking, running, jumping, hopping, skipping) to move purposefully from one point to another in a play context.
criteria: Applies at least two different locomotor skills during a game or play activity
Moves with basic control, including stopping and changing direction when needed
nodes.hinge_reason: Locomotor control underpins safe participation in all subsequent FMS combinations. Students who cannot move purposefully between points struggle with every minor game context in this standard and in the Y1-2 band.

width.minimum: Move between two points using at least two different locomotor skills in a simple game or activity.
width.typical: Apply a range of locomotor skills (at least four) in minor games and imaginative play; demonstrate basic control of starting, stopping and changing direction.
wider: Apply locomotor skills in natural and outdoor environments, adapting movement to uneven terrain or open space
Combine locomotor sequences (e.g. run–jump–hop) in response to game signals or teacher cues
Explore locomotor skills used in First Nations Australian games such as running-based chasing games

modes.reason: Foundation students need repeated practice across varied play contexts before locomotor patterns become reliable. Precision of starting, stopping and direction changes should be emphasised before combining with object manipulation.
Vary the play contexts (chasing games, imaginative play, natural environments) to build transferable locomotor control across settings.

nodes.label: Object manipulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can send, control and receive objects (rolling, throwing, catching, kicking) in different ways and at different levels.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one sending skill and one receiving skill with a manipulable object
Attempts to adjust body position to send or receive the object at different heights or distances
nodes.hinge_reason: Object manipulation skill is a prerequisite for most minor game and sports contexts in Y1-2. Students with very limited manipulation experience cannot access game structures that form the basis of later FMS progression.

width.minimum: Practise at least one sending skill (throw or kick) and one receiving skill (catch or stop) using a ball or similar object.
width.typical: Practise a range of object manipulation skills — throwing, catching, rolling, kicking — in minor games; send and receive objects at different heights and distances.
wider: Explore sending and receiving objects using non-standard equipment (scarves, beanbags, balloons) to isolate tracking and timing
Practise water confidence skills such as floating with a buoyancy aid and receiving objects in/near water
Combine object manipulation with locomotion in simple game structures (e.g. carry-and-pass relay)

modes.reason: Fine and gross motor patterns for throwing and catching require repeated, low-pressure practice. Use varied equipment sizes and distances to build consistency before applying in game contexts.
Different equipment types (balloon, beanbag, ball) and environments (pool, outdoor) broaden manipulation experience and reveal transfer gaps.

nodes.label: Weight transfer and balance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can transfer weight from one body part to another with control, and demonstrate basic balance in still and moving positions.
criteria: Transfers weight from one body part to another in a practised sequence
Holds a balance position on at least one body base with brief stillness

width.minimum: Demonstrate one weight-transfer sequence (e.g. roll, cartwheel attempt, or step-and-balance) with basic control.
width.typical: Practise a range of weight-transfer movements — rolling, rocking, stepping patterns, simple gymnastic sequences; hold balance positions on different body bases.
wider: Explore weight transfer and balance on natural surfaces and equipment (logs, slopes, uneven ground)
Combine balance sequences with locomotion in movement stories or creative play contexts
Explore fine motor combining tasks: threading, stacking or building activities that develop hand-coordination alongside gross motor balance

modes.reason: Weight transfer and balance require body awareness that develops through repeated exploratory practice — not from a single lesson. Low-stakes, playful contexts are most effective at Foundation.

nodes.label: FMS in minor games
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine locomotor, manipulation and balance skills in minor game and play situations with purpose and enjoyment.
criteria: Participates in a minor game that requires combining two or more movement skills
Applies fundamental movement skills with intent — moves in response to game demands, not randomly

width.minimum: Participate in at least one minor game that requires combining two or more FMS (e.g. running and catching, or skipping and kicking).
width.typical: Participate in a range of minor games that combine locomotor, object-manipulation and balance skills; apply skills with increasing control and adapt to game demands.
wider: Apply FMS in First Nations Australian game contexts, comparing game structures with other minor games experienced
Apply FMS skills in natural and outdoor environments with varying terrain and conditions
Participate in games combining multiple skill types simultaneously (e.g. run, dodge, send) in progressively more complex play structures

modes.reason: This node is the integration point — locomotor, manipulation and balance skills are combined in game contexts. Teacher investment here is in facilitating game structures that demand skill combination, not isolated skill repetition.

descriptors.title: Moving body and manipulating objects
descriptors.description: experiment with different ways of moving their body safely and manipulating objects and space
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students bring informal movement experience and basic spatial awareness from daily life. No prior structured experimentation with movement choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment with different ways of moving their body safely and manipulating objects and space, making judgements about effectiveness and demonstrating spatial awareness.

nodes.label: Suggest and test movement choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can suggest different ways to move or use equipment and test them, making simple judgements about which are most effective.
criteria: Attempts at least two different approaches to a movement task or equipment use
Makes a simple statement about which approach worked better or which they preferred
nodes.hinge_reason: The capacity to deliberately experiment with movement — rather than simply move habitually — is the cognitive foundation of this standard. Students who only replicate demonstrated movements cannot access the investigative intent of this descriptor or the Y1-2 equivalent which demands conclusions about effectiveness.

width.minimum: Suggest at least one alternative way to move or use equipment in a play context and test it.
width.typical: Suggest and test multiple movement approaches across different play situations; make and share simple judgements about which approaches work best and which they prefer.
wider: Suggest and test movement choices in outdoor and natural settings, adapting to different terrain
Experiment with non-standard equipment or everyday objects in movement tasks
Compare movement strategies with peers, discussing differences in effectiveness

modes.reason: Scaffold the experiment cycle explicitly: 'Try this way. Try another way. Which worked better? Why?' Simple verbal or gestural reflection is sufficient at Foundation — the thinking process is what matters.
Varied play equipment and environments give students more raw material for genuine experimentation rather than replicating teacher demonstrations.

nodes.label: Persistence and resilience in movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can persist with movement challenges, demonstrating resilience when a movement or task is difficult.
criteria: Attempts a challenging movement task more than once without giving up
Shows or describes a self-regulation strategy when movement is difficult (e.g. trying again, pausing)

width.minimum: Attempt a challenging movement task at least twice, persisting through difficulty.
width.typical: Demonstrate persistence across a range of movement challenges; describe or show what they do when a movement is hard (try again, modify approach).
wider: Reflect on how persistence felt — linking emotional experience to physical challenge
Observe and discuss a peer's persistence, connecting to fair play and encouragement
Engage with movement challenges in outdoor settings where uncertainty and variability are higher

modes.reason: Persistence is cultivated through repeated low-stakes challenge, not through a single difficult task. Design movement circuits with graduated difficulty and celebrate effort explicitly.

nodes.label: Safety in shared movement spaces
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate spatial awareness when moving around and through environments, and participate in games with awareness of personal safety.
criteria: Moves through a shared space without colliding with others or equipment
Follows a safety rule in a game context and can name it when asked

width.minimum: Move through a shared play space with awareness of others, avoiding collisions; follow basic game safety rules.
width.typical: Demonstrate spatial awareness in indoor and outdoor environments; participate in games that require awareness of boundaries, rules and safe use of equipment; describe a safety rule in a game context.
wider: Navigate outdoor and natural environments with varying spatial demands (open fields, obstacle courses, natural features)
Identify and explain safety considerations for a specific equipment type used in games
Design a simple safety rule for a class game and explain its purpose

modes.reason: Safety awareness is context-dependent — students who understand indoor gym safety may not transfer it automatically to outdoor or water environments. Vary settings to build genuine awareness.

descriptors.title: Physical activity benefits
descriptors.description: participate in a range of activities in natural and outdoor settings and explore the benefits of being physically active
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students have informal experience being physically active. No prior structured exploration of the benefits of physical activity or outdoor settings.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in a range of activities in natural and outdoor settings and explore what it feels like to be physically active and why it is beneficial.

nodes.label: Participating in outdoor and natural settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore ways to be active and participate safely in outdoor or natural settings.
criteria: Participates in a physical activity in an outdoor or natural setting
Identifies at least one way to stay safe while being active outdoors

width.minimum: Participate in at least one physical activity in an outdoor or natural setting.
width.typical: Participate in a range of physical activities in outdoor and natural settings; identify safety strategies for outdoor play including risk awareness.
wider: Participate in activities in a variety of natural environments — grassed areas, bush, beach or similar — adapting movement to the setting
Explore First Nations Australian games traditionally played in outdoor settings and discuss how the setting shapes the game
Identify and practise considered risk strategies for outdoor play (testing footing, staying within boundaries)

modes.reason: Outdoor and natural settings are varied — safety, movement demands and environmental features differ. Participate across multiple settings rather than a single outdoor session.

nodes.label: Exploring benefits of physical activity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss opportunities to be active and make simple connections between physical activity and how it makes them feel.
criteria: Names at least one feeling associated with physical activity
Identifies at least one place or opportunity to be physically active outside of school

width.minimum: Describe one way physical activity makes them feel (e.g. energetic, happy, tired) and identify one opportunity to be active at home or in their community.
width.typical: Discuss a range of feelings associated with physical activity; identify multiple opportunities to be active in and around home, school and community contexts.
wider: Connect physical activity opportunities to specific locations or community resources (parks, sporting clubs, community spaces)
Explore how family or cultural practices shape opportunities to be physically active
Discuss how being active in nature might feel different from being active indoors

modes.reason: Foundation students benefit from scaffolded discussion prompts to articulate connections between physical activity and wellbeing. Feeling-response prompts before, during and after activity support this reflection.

descriptors.title: Fair play rules
descriptors.description: follow rules to promote fair play in a range of physical activities
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students bring informal social experience of turn-taking and sharing from play and home contexts. No prior structured engagement with game rules or fair play.
descriptors.endpoint: Students follow rules in a range of physical activities and can identify what fair and unfair play looks like.

nodes.label: Fair and unfair play
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe actions that would constitute fair and unfair play in minor games.
criteria: Names at least one example of fair play and one example of unfair play in a game context
Gives a simple reason why fair play is important (e.g. so everyone can enjoy the game)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify fair and unfair play lack the conceptual foundation to follow rules purposefully (next node) — they comply mechanically at best. The Y1-2 equivalent (co-constructing rules) requires this conceptual base.

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of fair play and one example of unfair play in a game they have participated in.
width.typical: Identify and describe fair and unfair play actions across a range of minor game contexts; explain why fair play matters to participants.
wider: Explore fair play examples from First Nations Australian games and compare with other game contexts
Discuss scenarios where intent (accidental vs deliberate) affects judgements about fairness
Connect fair play to feelings — how unfair play makes participants feel

modes.reason: Use game stoppages and brief scenario discussions to make fair/unfair distinctions explicit. Foundation students need the concepts named and exemplified concretely before they can apply them.
Varied game contexts — chasing games, target games, cooperative games — reveal that fair play principles are consistent across different rule structures.

nodes.label: Following rules in games
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate how to play fairly in a range of minor games and play situations, following rules relating to safety, boundaries and equipment use.
criteria: Follows the safety, boundary and equipment rules of a minor game during participation
Demonstrates fair play behaviour (e.g. takes turns, respects boundaries, accepts outcomes)

width.minimum: Follow the rules of one minor game, including safety, boundary and equipment rules, with teacher support.
width.typical: Demonstrate fair play across a range of minor games; follow safety, boundary and equipment rules consistently; discuss rules when prompted.
wider: Participate in games with varying rule complexity, applying fair play in each
Practise a First Nations Australian game with its specific rules and discuss how the rules promote fair participation
Lead a brief rule explanation for a peer before beginning a game

modes.reason: Foundation students need repeated practice following rules across multiple game contexts to internalise fair play as a habit, not just a concept. Consistent, low-stakes practice across diverse games builds rule-following disposition.

descriptors.title: Who they are and their world
descriptors.description: investigate who they are and the people in their world
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students bring lived experience of family, community and personal identity. No prior structured curriculum investigation of identity and belonging.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate who they are and the people in their world, making connections between identity, belonging and community.

nodes.label: Personal identity and belonging
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make personal connections between their identity and their sense of belonging — who they are, where they come from, the people in their lives.
criteria: Shares at least one aspect of who they are or where they come from
Makes a connection between something about themselves and a feeling of belonging to a group or community
nodes.hinge_reason: A secure sense of personal identity is the conceptual foundation for investigating others and differences (next node). Students who cannot articulate aspects of their own identity cannot meaningfully compare or connect with others' identities and family structures.

width.minimum: Share something about who they are — including at least one aspect of family, culture or personal interest — and connect this to a story or text about identity and belonging.
width.typical: Explore personal identity through stories, discussion and creative expression; make connections between personal qualities, family background and belonging in class and community contexts.
wider: Explore identity and belonging stories from First Nations Australian contexts, discussing similarities and differences with their own experience
Investigate cultural practices from different cultures, including cultures of Asia, that are important to families and communities
Explore how belonging to groups (family, class, community) shapes identity and personal connections

modes.reason: Identity is expressed through multiple lenses — family, culture, physical strengths, community. Varied expression modes (drawing, story, movement, talk) allow all students to access this concept from their own starting point.

nodes.label: Families and communities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different family structures and explore similarities and differences across communities and cultures.
criteria: Identifies at least two different types of family structures
Describes one similarity or difference between families in different communities or cultures

width.minimum: Identify their own family structure and at least one other type of family structure that is different from their own.
width.typical: Identify and discuss a range of family structures; explore similarities and differences in families across First Nations Australian communities and other cultures; recognise the right to belong and contribute.
wider: Compare family structures and community roles across First Nations Australian communities with students' own experience
Investigate how families from different cultural backgrounds, including cultures of Asia, organise themselves and their practices
Explore community contributions — how each person, including themselves, contributes to a group

modes.reason: Family diversity is the content here — restrict to generalising across types. Use texts, images and discussion rather than requiring personal disclosure from students about their own family.

nodes.label: Strengths and contribution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify personal strengths and recognise how they contribute to group success and a sense of belonging.
criteria: Names at least one personal strength
Describes one way their strength has helped them or others in a shared activity

width.minimum: Identify at least one personal strength and describe one way they have helped themselves or others in a physical or group activity.
width.typical: Identify and discuss personal strengths in physical and social contexts; connect strengths to contributions in group situations; recognise that everyone has a right to belong and contribute.
wider: Explore how different strengths contribute to team success in varied physical activity contexts
Connect the idea of contribution to belonging — what it feels like to be valued in a group
Investigate how First Nations Australian communities recognise and value different strengths and roles

modes.reason: This node integrates personal identity (N1) and community belonging (N2) — strengths connect who you are with how you contribute. Design activities that surface both simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Personal and social skills
descriptors.description: practise personal and social skills to interact respectfully with others
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students bring social experience from home and prior care/education settings. No prior structured curriculum practice of respectful interaction skills.
descriptors.endpoint: Students practise personal and social skills to interact respectfully with others, including cooperating, collaborating and responding to challenging social situations.

nodes.label: Inclusive and exclusive behaviour
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify behaviours that may be disrespectful or cause harm during play, and discuss how excluded characters or peers could be included.
criteria: Identifies at least one disrespectful or hurtful behaviour in a play or story context
Suggests a more inclusive action the character or peer could have taken
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify disrespectful or excluding behaviour cannot apply respectful interaction skills (next node) meaningfully. This conceptual understanding of what counts as respectful vs disrespectful is the foundation for practising the skills.

width.minimum: Identify at least one behaviour that is disrespectful or hurtful in a play or story context, and suggest how someone could have acted more inclusively.
width.typical: Explore stories and play scenarios involving exclusion; discuss why exclusion occurs, how it feels, and what more inclusive behaviour looks like; identify disrespectful behaviours in their own play contexts.
wider: Explore characters from stories across different cultural contexts who navigate inclusion and exclusion
Discuss exclusion and inclusion in First Nations Australian community contexts using relevant stories or examples
Connect inclusion behaviours to fair play — how respectful social interaction and fair play reinforce each other

modes.reason: Use story-based scenarios and game stoppages to make inclusion/exclusion visible and nameable. Foundation students benefit from explicit naming of the concepts before practising them.
Varied story and cultural contexts broaden understanding of what respect and inclusion look like across different settings.

nodes.label: Cooperating and collaborating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can cooperate, collaborate and negotiate with others in physical activities to achieve agreed outcomes.
criteria: Takes turns and shares equipment with at least one other person in a shared activity
Makes a simple shared decision with a partner or group during a play activity

width.minimum: Work with at least one other person in a shared play activity, taking turns and making a simple shared decision.
width.typical: Cooperate and collaborate in a range of physical activities; negotiate roles, share equipment and reach agreed outcomes; explain their own reasoning and actions in challenging social situations.
wider: Collaborate in team-based physical activities requiring role differentiation (e.g. one sends, one receives, one retrieves)
Practise negotiation in contexts where students must agree on rules or equipment use before a game begins
Reflect on a challenging collaboration and identify what helped the group succeed

modes.reason: Collaboration skills develop through repeated, structured practice. Foundation students need scaffolded social scripts and low-stakes activities before negotiation becomes genuinely collaborative.

descriptors.title: Express emotions
descriptors.description: express and describe emotions they experience
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students have intuitive emotional experience but limited vocabulary and structured practice for identifying and expressing emotions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students express and describe emotions they experience using appropriate language and actions, and make connections between feelings, body reactions and body language.

nodes.label: Naming emotions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and name a range of emotions — happy, sad, excited, tired, angry, scared, confused — and describe what they look like in others and themselves.
criteria: Names at least four emotions correctly when shown or described a scenario
Describes at least one observable indicator (expression, posture, voice) for two different emotions
nodes.hinge_reason: Emotion vocabulary is prerequisite for expressing and communicating feelings (next node). Students with limited emotion vocabulary cannot access appropriate language or actions for communicating their feelings in different situations.

width.minimum: Name at least four emotions and describe what they look like (facial expression, body language) in a character, image or peer.
width.typical: Identify and describe a range of emotions (at least six) in stories, images and peers; connect emotion names with observable indicators (expression, posture, voice); recall emotional responses to their own experiences.
wider: Explore how emotions are expressed differently across cultures — using stories or examples from First Nations Australian or Asian cultural contexts
Investigate emotion expression in physical activity contexts — e.g. how winning, losing or taking risks feels
Represent a range of emotions through movement, drawing or creative expression

modes.reason: Emotion vocabulary is genuinely a repertoire — more named emotions means more precise communication. Accumulate the range systematically through stories, imagery and physical activity reflection.
Emotions in varied contexts — stories, movement, cultural settings — broaden recognition beyond the classroom's dominant emotional register.

nodes.label: Communicating emotions appropriately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use appropriate language and actions to communicate their feelings in different situations, and connect feelings to body reactions and body language.
criteria: Uses appropriate language or gesture to communicate a feeling in at least one situation
Makes a simple connection between a feeling and a body reaction or body language signal

width.minimum: Use words or gestures to communicate one feeling in a social or play context in a way that is appropriate for the situation.
width.typical: Practise and refine appropriate emotional communication in a range of situations; make connections between feelings, body reactions (heart racing, stomach butterflies) and visible body language; share emotional responses to experiences in a variety of ways.
wider: Explore and practise communicating emotions in challenging situations — adventures, risks or emergencies in stories
Connect body reactions during physical activity (breathlessness, energy) to emotional states
Discuss how expressing emotions helps social connection and conflict resolution

modes.reason: Appropriate emotional communication is a practised skill — Foundation students need repeated, safe opportunities to try emotion vocabulary and receive affirming feedback before it becomes reliable.

descriptors.title: Seek, give or deny permission
descriptors.description: explore how to seek, give or deny permission respectfully when sharing possessions or personal space
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students have informal experience of asking and being asked to share. No prior structured curriculum exploration of consent, rights and respectful negotiation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore and practise how to seek, give or deny permission respectfully when sharing possessions or personal space, recognising their right to say no.

nodes.label: The importance of asking permission
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why asking for permission matters when sharing possessions or personal space, and identify situations where permission is needed.
criteria: Identifies at least one situation where asking permission is required
Gives a simple reason why asking permission is important for respecting others
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding why permission matters, practising how to ask becomes mechanical compliance. The Y1-2 equivalent (practising strategies) requires this conceptual foundation. Body autonomy connections are foundational to protective behaviours work in AC9HPFP05.

width.minimum: Identify at least one situation where they would need to ask permission before sharing or accessing something, and give a reason why asking is important.
width.typical: Explore multiple situations requiring permission — sharing possessions, personal space, and activity roles; explain why asking matters for respect and rights; recognise the right to say no as part of respecting others.
wider: Explore permission and consent in play contexts across different cultural settings, including First Nations Australian negotiation practices in games
Discuss digital contexts where permission is needed — e.g. taking or sharing a photo of someone
Connect body autonomy to permission — explaining that our bodies belong to us and others must ask before touching

modes.reason: The concept of rights — including the right to say no — requires explicit, teacher-led discussion. Scenario-based exploration (what would you do if... ?) is more effective than rule-telling.
Permission situations vary: possessions, personal space, digital contexts, bodily autonomy. Varied context discussion prevents students from associating permission only with object-sharing.

nodes.label: Practising seeking, giving and denying permission
nodes.checkpoint: Students can practise and refine how to ask for permission and how to give or deny permission respectfully, including respecting someone's right to say no.
criteria: Uses respectful language or gesture to ask permission in a play or sharing context
Accepts a yes or no response to a permission request without acting disrespectfully

width.minimum: Practise asking permission in at least one play or sharing context using respectful language, and demonstrate accepting a yes or no response.
width.typical: Practise and refine seeking, giving and denying permission across play and imaginative situations; demonstrate respect for different responses including 'no'; negotiate roles through imaginative and shared play while maintaining awareness of rights.
wider: Practise permission-seeking in physical activity contexts involving personal space (e.g. partner games, dance, contact activities)
Use role-play to rehearse scenarios where permission is denied and explore how to respond respectfully
Discuss and practise digital scenarios involving permission (e.g. asking before taking a photo)

modes.reason: Permission-seeking and denial is a practised social skill. Foundation students need repeated, structured role-play and play experiences before respectful language and acceptance of 'no' become habitual.

descriptors.title: Protective behaviours and help-seeking
descriptors.description: demonstrate protective behaviours, name body parts and rehearse help-seeking strategies that help keep them safe
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students have some awareness of trusted adults from home and care settings. No prior structured curriculum work on protective behaviours, anatomical naming or assertive help-seeking.
descriptors.endpoint: Students demonstrate protective behaviours, name body parts correctly, and rehearse help-seeking strategies including identifying trusted adults and assertive strategies for unsafe situations.

nodes.label: Naming body parts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name body parts using correct anatomical language, and understand that all people have the right to bodily autonomy.
criteria: Names major body parts including private body parts using correct anatomical terms
States that their body belongs to them and that others must ask before touching
nodes.hinge_reason: Correct anatomical language is prerequisite for describing unsafe situations clearly to trusted adults. Students who cannot name body parts accurately cannot effectively communicate when protective behaviours have been violated.

width.minimum: Name at least the major external body parts including private body parts using correct anatomical terms.
width.typical: Name a full range of body parts using correct anatomical language; discuss why using correct names is important; articulate that all people have the right to bodily autonomy — the right to make choices about what others ask them to do with their bodies.
wider: Explore body-naming in different health and safety contexts — swimming, first aid — where correct naming matters
Discuss the difference between public and private body parts and why privacy rules exist
Connect anatomical naming to protective behaviours — being able to describe accurately when something has happened

modes.reason: Anatomical naming requires straightforward, repeated, normalised practice to overcome social awkwardness. Matter-of-fact lesson delivery and consistent correct language are the key teaching moves.

nodes.label: Trusted adults and support networks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a support network of trusted adults they can go to if they feel unsafe, uncomfortable or scared.
criteria: Names at least two trusted adults who could help them if they felt unsafe
Describes at least one situation that would require them to go to a trusted adult
nodes.hinge_reason: Knowing who to go to is prerequisite for all help-seeking strategies (next node). Without a concrete trusted adult support network, help-seeking strategies are abstract and unusable. This is one of the highest-stakes cascade risks in the Foundation band.

width.minimum: Name at least two trusted adults they could go to for help if they felt unsafe.
width.typical: Identify a support network of trusted adults including family, school and community figures; explain what makes someone a trusted adult; distinguish between comfortable and uncomfortable situations that need trusted adult support.
wider: Discuss what makes an adult trustworthy and how to judge who is safe to go to
Explore trusted adult networks in different community contexts, including in First Nations Australian family and community structures
Identify trusted online spaces and digital tools, and discuss when to seek help from a trusted adult if feeling unsafe online

modes.reason: Trusted adult networks vary by context — at school, at home, in community, online. Discuss each context so students know who their trusted adults are across settings, not only at school.

nodes.label: Protective behaviours and assertive help-seeking
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore and demonstrate protective behaviours and assertive strategies for seeking help when they or others feel unsafe or uncomfortable.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one assertive protective behaviour (saying no, moving away, telling a trusted adult)
Rehearses a help-seeking response in a scenario involving an unsafe or uncomfortable situation

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least one assertive strategy for seeking help in an unsafe situation (e.g. saying 'no', moving away, telling a trusted adult).
width.typical: Explore and demonstrate a range of protective behaviours and assertive help-seeking strategies; practise responses to unsafe or uncomfortable scenarios; rehearse help-seeking with trusted adults.
wider: Rehearse help-seeking in varied scenarios — physical, emotional and online unsafe situations
Practise assertive strategies with different trusted adults in different contexts
Explore how to help a friend who is unsafe, extending help-seeking beyond self-protection

modes.reason: Protective behaviours and help-seeking require rehearsal — not just knowledge. Foundation students need repeated, low-stakes role-play scenarios where they practise the actual words and actions of help-seeking.

descriptors.title: Health symbols and messages
descriptors.description: identify health symbols, messages and strategies in their community that support their health and safety
descriptors.knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students have informal exposure to health symbols in the environment (road signs, food packaging) but without structured curriculum identification or explanation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify health symbols, messages and community strategies that support their health and safety, and explain what these symbols and strategies mean.

nodes.label: Health and safety symbols
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify health and safety symbols in their environment and explain what they mean.
criteria: Identifies at least two health or safety symbols correctly
Explains the safety message of each identified symbol
nodes.hinge_reason: Symbol recognition and meaning is the conceptual foundation for understanding community health strategies (next node). Students who cannot read health symbols cannot apply or follow the safety strategies those symbols signal.

width.minimum: Identify at least two health or safety symbols (e.g. a danger symbol on a household substance, a pedestrian crossing sign) and explain what each means.
width.typical: Identify and explain a range of health and safety symbols — household substance danger symbols, food labelling symbols, road safety symbols, water safety symbols — and describe the safety messages they communicate.
wider: Investigate symbols on food packaging that indicate healthier choices, including reading food labels
Explore how different types of advertising influence food choices and discuss how to evaluate health messages critically
Compare health symbols across different community contexts — home, school, road, water

modes.reason: Health symbol knowledge is genuinely a repertoire — each symbol is a discrete piece of community health literacy. Accumulate symbols across contexts systematically using real examples from the environment.
Symbols vary by environment — road, food, water, household. Cross-context exposure builds a broader health literacy foundation.

nodes.label: Community health and safety strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and follow community strategies that keep children safe, including safety procedures at specific community environments.
criteria: Identifies at least one community safety strategy and names the environment it applies to
Describes what the safety strategy requires them to do in that environment

width.minimum: Identify at least one community strategy that keeps children safe (e.g. pedestrian crossing, swimming pool rules) and describe what it requires them to do.
width.typical: Identify and explain a range of community safety strategies — pedestrian crossings, traffic controllers, pool and beach safety procedures, road environment rules; follow safety symbols and procedures in relevant environments.
wider: Investigate the purpose behind different safety strategies — why we have pool rules, road rules, school crossing procedures
Explore safety strategies in natural and outdoor environments, including water safety in different contexts
Connect community safety strategies to personal responsibility — what their role is in following and promoting safety

modes.reason: Community safety strategies differ by environment — road, water, home, outdoor. Students who understand pool rules may not automatically transfer reasoning to road contexts. Vary the environments.

descriptors.title: Fundamental movement in varied situations
descriptors.description: practise fundamental movement skills and apply them in a variety of movement situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students have practised fundamental movement skills in minor game and play situations (AC9HPFM01). They have experimented with different ways of moving their body safely and manipulating objects and space (AC9HPFM02).
descriptors.endpoint: Students practise fundamental movement skills and apply them in a variety of movement situations.

nodes.label: Locomotor and non-locomotor movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform locomotor movements using different body parts to travel in different directions, and perform non-locomotor balances.
criteria: Performs at least two locomotor movements using different body parts in at least two directions
Holds a balance and can name one thing that helps them stay stable
nodes.hinge_reason: Locomotor and balance competence underpins all subsequent application tasks. Students who cannot reliably execute a core movement pattern in isolation will not be able to select and implement skills in game situations (Node 2) or control objects while moving (Node 3).

width.minimum: Perform at least two locomotor movements (e.g. run, jump) in two directions; hold a balance and describe what helps maintain a stable position.
width.typical: Demonstrate a range of locomotor movements using different body parts across multiple directions and levels; perform and describe balances including what contributes to stability.
wider: Practise gliding forward and backward in the water using arm and kicking movements, comparing water movement to land-based locomotion
Sequence locomotor movements into a short movement phrase, varying direction, speed and level
Explore First Nations Australian movement games that use specific locomotor patterns

modes.reason: Fluency in basic locomotor patterns and balance needs repetition across varied settings before application becomes possible. Focus practice on one or two movement forms across multiple activities rather than sampling many forms once.
Vary the surfaces, spaces and directions used so students experience the movement in different physical environments, reducing reliance on a single learned setting.

nodes.label: Selecting and applying movement skills in games
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and implement different movement skills to be successful in a range of games.
criteria: In a game situation, selects a movement skill appropriate to what the game requires
Can describe why they used a particular movement in at least one game
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to select movement skills purposefully — not just perform them in isolation — is the core transfer move of this descriptor. Thin treatment here leaves students able to perform skills in drills but unable to apply them in context, which undermines all subsequent movement application across the band.

width.minimum: In at least one minor game, select an appropriate movement skill and use it purposefully to participate successfully.
width.typical: Across a range of minor games, select and implement movement skills appropriate to the game context; describe why they chose a particular movement.
wider: Invent a new game using known movement skills and reflect on whether the movement choices made the game interesting and challenging
Participate in children's games from First Nations Australian cultures and identify which movement skills are used
Modify a familiar game to require a different movement skill and evaluate whether the change improves the game

modes.reason: Make the selection process explicit: before and after games, ask students why they chose a particular movement. Brief verbal or visual prompts help students articulate skill choice rather than just performing habitually.
Vary game types (chasing, fielding, net, target) so students practise selection across different movement demands rather than optimising for one game context.

nodes.label: Controlling objects with equipment and body parts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform fundamental movement skills involving controlling objects with equipment and different parts of the body.
criteria: Uses at least one piece of equipment to send or receive a moving object
Attempts object control using a non-dominant body part in a movement activity

width.minimum: Use at least one piece of equipment to control a moving object; attempt control using a non-dominant body part.
width.typical: Use a range of equipment types and body parts to send, receive and retain objects in movement contexts; practise across both dominant and non-dominant body parts.
wider: Use different types of equipment to create an original movement challenge and evaluate how difficult object control was
Compare controlling objects in water versus on land, noting how the medium changes the challenge
Explore equipment from different cultural contexts, noting similarities and differences in how objects are controlled

modes.reason: Object control requires repetition with feedback — students benefit from focused practice on one control pattern before switching equipment or body parts.
Varying equipment types (bats, racquets, hands, feet) and object types (balls of different sizes, beanbags) broadens the range of control experiences without increasing conceptual demand.

nodes.label: Applying skills across varied movement situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can practise fundamental movement skills and apply them purposefully across a variety of movement situations, including games, sequences, and object control contexts.
criteria: Demonstrates a fundamental movement skill in at least two different movement situations
Makes a purposeful movement choice and can describe it in at least one situation

width.minimum: Demonstrate the same fundamental movement skill across at least two different movement situations (e.g. a game and a sequence or object control task).
width.typical: Apply a range of fundamental movement skills across varied movement situations — games, sequences, and individual and partner object control tasks — making purposeful choices about which skill to use.
wider: Design a short movement sequence that incorporates locomotor, balance and object control elements and perform it for a partner
Participate in a range of movement situations including one in an outdoor or natural setting, comparing how skills transfer
Reflect on which movement situations they find most and least enjoyable and explain how that affects how well they apply skills

modes.reason: This node draws together locomotor movement, skill selection, and object control into the descriptor's full demand — purposeful application across varied situations. Provide tasks that require students to draw on all three prior nodes simultaneously rather than practising each in isolation.

descriptors.title: Moving and manipulating objects
descriptors.description: investigate different ways of moving their body, and manipulating objects and space, and draw conclusions about their effectiveness
descriptors.knowledge: Students have experimented with different ways of moving their body safely and manipulating objects and space (AC9HPFM02). They can practise fundamental movement skills in varied situations (AC9HP2M01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate different ways of moving their body, and manipulating objects and space, and draw conclusions about their effectiveness.

nodes.label: Movement variation — speed, direction, level
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate changes in speed, direction and level as they use locomotor and non-locomotor skills.
criteria: Demonstrates a deliberate change in at least two movement variables (speed, direction, or level)
Can describe what they changed and how it felt different
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to deliberately vary movement parameters (speed, direction, level) is foundational to the investigative intent of this descriptor. Students who cannot vary their movement purposefully will not be able to compare effectiveness or draw meaningful conclusions (Node 3).

width.minimum: In a movement task, deliberately change at least two of: speed, direction, or level, and describe what changed.
width.typical: Demonstrate intentional changes in speed, direction and level across locomotor and non-locomotor movement sequences; describe how each change affects movement.
wider: Use stimuli such as music, rhythm or words to drive changes in speed and level, and compare which stimuli produce the greatest movement variation
Participate in movement activities that require safe navigation of different outdoor spaces, comparing which movement patterns are most efficient
Create a short movement sequence that deliberately uses all three variables (speed, direction, level) and reflect on which combinations felt most effective

modes.reason: Students need repeated opportunities to practise deliberate variation — first one variable at a time, then in combination. Rushing to comparison before variation is controlled produces weak conclusions.

nodes.label: Investigating object and space manipulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use different types of equipment and explore different ways of manipulating objects and space to solve a movement challenge or create a game.
criteria: Uses at least two types of equipment in a movement challenge or game context
Describes how the equipment affected what they could do

width.minimum: Use at least two types of equipment to attempt a movement challenge; describe how using different equipment changed what they could do.
width.typical: Use a range of equipment to create an original game or solve a movement challenge; compare how different equipment choices affected the movement possibilities and game outcomes.
wider: Invent a new game based on rules and equipment from a familiar game and evaluate whether the rules and equipment provide an interesting and challenging game
Use stimuli such as equipment, rhythm and music to create a simple playground game and assess which game they enjoy most
Compare moving around different outdoor spaces and identify which types of movement are most appropriate for safe and efficient travel through each space

modes.reason: Students need experience with a range of equipment types before they can genuinely compare effectiveness. Build a catalogue of equipment-movement combinations first, then move to evaluation.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions about movement effectiveness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate different movement approaches and draw conclusions about which are most effective for a given purpose.
criteria: Identifies which of two movement approaches was more effective for a given purpose
Gives at least one reason for their conclusion linked to what they observed or experienced
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to draw conclusions about effectiveness — not just describe what was done — is the descriptor's primary inquiry demand. Thin treatment here leaves students able to perform movement tasks but unable to evaluate them, which is the prerequisite capability for the investigative movement standards in Years 3–4.

width.minimum: After trying at least two movement approaches (different equipment, speed, space use or game rules), identify which was more effective and give one reason.
width.typical: Across multiple movement investigations, compare different approaches and draw conclusions about effectiveness against a defined purpose or set of criteria; explain reasoning.
wider: Evaluate a self-created game against a set of criteria (e.g. inclusive, challenging, enjoyable) and propose changes
Compare movement approaches across indoor and outdoor settings and draw conclusions about which settings favour which movement types
Use peer feedback to evaluate the effectiveness of a movement approach and revise conclusions based on additional evidence

modes.reason: Provide a simple evaluative scaffold (e.g. 'I tried __ and __; __ was more effective because __') to make the conclusion-drawing move explicit. Without structure, young students often describe what happened rather than evaluating it.

Conclusions drawn about only one movement context are thin. Vary the contexts (games, sequences, outdoor settings) so students practise drawing conclusions across different types of movement investigations.

descriptors.title: Physical activity enjoyment
descriptors.description: participate in a range of physical activities in natural and outdoor settings, and investigate factors and settings that make physical activity enjoyable
descriptors.knowledge: Students have participated in activities in natural and outdoor settings and explored the benefits of being physically active (AC9HPFM03).
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in physical activities in natural and outdoor settings and investigate factors and settings that make physical activity enjoyable.

nodes.label: Features of natural and outdoor settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise physical features of natural and outdoor settings and describe how those features relate to physical activity.
criteria: Identifies at least one physical feature of an outdoor or natural setting
Describes how that feature affects physical activity in that space
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding what makes a setting suitable for physical activity is the conceptual foundation for the investigation in Node 2. Students who only 'participate' without noticing environmental features cannot meaningfully investigate what makes activity enjoyable in different settings.

width.minimum: In at least one outdoor or natural setting, identify one or two physical features and describe how they affect physical activity in that space.
width.typical: Across a range of natural and outdoor settings, identify key physical features and describe how those features enable or constrain different types of physical activity.
wider: Compare physical activity in an indoor setting to the same or similar activity in an outdoor or natural setting, noting how features of the environment change what's possible
Explore a natural setting (e.g. bushland, beach, park) and identify movement possibilities that do not exist in built spaces
Investigate how First Nations Australians' connections to country relate to physical activity in natural settings

modes.reason: Provide a simple observation prompt (e.g. 'I notice __ in this space; this makes __ possible/difficult') to shift students from passive participation to active noticing of environmental features.

nodes.label: Investigating factors that make activity enjoyable
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in a range of physical activities and identify factors that make them enjoyable.
criteria: Participates in at least two different physical activities
Identifies at least one factor that made an activity enjoyable or less enjoyable

width.minimum: Participate in at least two different physical activities and identify at least one factor that made each enjoyable or less enjoyable.
width.typical: Participate in a range of minor games and physical activities, including in outdoor settings; identify and compare the factors that make each enjoyable and explain which factors matter most to them.
wider: Participate in children's games from First Nations Australian cultures (such as Keentan played by the Kalkadoon People) and compare what makes these games enjoyable with other games they know
Investigate which factors of enjoyment are shared with classmates and which are personal preferences, and discuss what this means for planning class activities
Explore physical activities unique to outdoor or natural settings and identify what features of those settings contribute to enjoyment

modes.reason: The investigation of enjoyment factors is enriched by a wider range of activity types. Students who have only participated in one type of activity have limited data for comparison.

nodes.label: Comparing indoor and outdoor activity settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the characteristics and benefits of physical activities that take place in outdoor settings with those that take place inside.
criteria: Identifies at least one characteristic difference between indoor and outdoor activity settings
Names at least one benefit of physical activity in each setting

width.minimum: Describe one difference between participating in a physical activity indoors versus outdoors; identify at least one benefit of each setting.
width.typical: Compare characteristics and benefits of physical activities across indoor and outdoor settings; explain personal preferences and link them to specific features of each setting.
wider: Investigate a physical activity that can only happen outdoors and reflect on what makes it uniquely enjoyable
Survey classmates about their preferred settings and analyse what patterns emerge, relating findings to different environmental features
Explore how seasonal changes to outdoor settings affect which activities are available and how enjoyable they are

modes.reason: This node brings together environmental feature recognition (Node 1) and enjoyment factor investigation (Node 2) into the descriptor's comparative intent. Use tasks that require students to explicitly connect setting features to enjoyment factors rather than treating them as separate observations.

descriptors.title: Co-construct fair play rules
descriptors.description: co-construct and apply rules to promote fair play in a range of physical activities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have followed rules to promote fair play in a range of physical activities (AC9HPFM04). They have practised turn-taking and basic inclusion in game contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students co-construct and apply rules to promote fair play in a range of physical activities.

nodes.label: Purpose of rules in fair play
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how rules contribute to fair play and apply them in group activities.
criteria: Applies at least one rule correctly in a group physical activity
Explains why that rule makes the activity fairer
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding why rules exist — not just what they are — is the prerequisite for co-constructing new rules (Node 2). Students who can only follow rules without understanding their purpose cannot meaningfully participate in rule construction.

width.minimum: In a physical activity, apply a rule and explain why that rule makes the activity fairer.
width.typical: Across a range of physical activities, apply rules and explain how specific rules contribute to fair play; identify what would change if a rule were removed.
wider: Compare rules across two different activities and identify which rules serve the same fair-play purpose in different forms
Investigate examples of unfair play and identify which rule was absent or broken, and how adding or restoring the rule would help
Discuss rules from a First Nations Australian game and compare the fair-play principles they embody with rules from familiar games

modes.reason: Ask students to explain the 'why' behind a rule, not just state it. A prompt like 'This rule is fair because...' makes the reasoning explicit and surfaces whether students understand the principle or just recall the procedure.

nodes.label: Co-constructing and modifying rules
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in co-constructing or modifying rules that make a physical activity fairer or more inclusive.
criteria: Contributes at least one suggestion during a group rule-making discussion
Applies a co-constructed or modified rule in a physical activity

width.minimum: With others, suggest or agree to at least one change to a game rule that makes the activity fairer; apply the changed rule.
width.typical: Participate in discussions to co-construct or modify rules for a range of physical activities; explain how proposed changes improve fairness or inclusion for all learners.
wider: Design a set of rules for a new game from scratch that ensures all players have equitable opportunities to participate
Discuss how a rule change might affect different players differently (e.g. players with different abilities or skill levels) and refine the rule to address this
Compare self-constructed rules with official game rules and identify similarities and differences in the fairness principles each reflects

modes.reason: Co-construction of rules is richer when students have encountered it across multiple activity types. Vary the activity context (chasing games, target games, partner activities) so students practise the co-construction process in different movement settings.

nodes.label: Turn-taking, sharing and inclusive participation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate turn-taking and sharing of equipment when participating in play and minor games, and connect these behaviours to fair play.
criteria: Demonstrates turn-taking or equipment sharing in a group physical activity
Explains how this behaviour supports fair play in the activity

width.minimum: In a group activity, demonstrate turn-taking or equipment sharing and explain how this contributes to fair play.
width.typical: Consistently demonstrate turn-taking and equipment sharing across a range of minor games and play contexts; link specific behaviours to the fair-play rules in place.
wider: Identify a situation where turn-taking or sharing broke down and propose a rule change or behaviour strategy that would prevent it
Reflect on how including everyone affects the quality of the game for all participants
Observe a game (live or recorded) and identify examples of fair and unfair sharing or turn-taking, linking them to the rules in place

modes.reason: Turn-taking and sharing are the behavioural application of the fair-play principles established in Nodes 1 and 2. Use activities that require students to manage both rule application and social behaviour simultaneously — not just practise each in isolation.

descriptors.title: Collaborative participation
descriptors.description: apply strategies to work collaboratively when participating in physical activities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have followed rules to promote fair play (AC9HPFM04) and have experienced cooperative interaction in basic game contexts. There is no direct Foundation predecessor for collaborative strategy use — this is a new demand at this band.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply strategies to work collaboratively in physical activities.

nodes.label: Working cooperatively with a partner
nodes.checkpoint: Students can work cooperatively with a partner when practising new movement skills.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one cooperative behaviour (e.g. waiting turn, encouraging partner) during a paired movement activity
Can name what they did to cooperate with their partner
nodes.hinge_reason: Partner cooperation is the building block for group collaboration. Students who cannot sustain cooperative behaviour in a paired context will not be able to apply inclusion strategies or adapt games for group participation (Nodes 2 and 3).

width.minimum: In a paired activity, cooperate with a partner to practise a movement skill; demonstrate at least one cooperative behaviour (e.g. waiting, encouraging, sharing feedback).
width.typical: Across several partner activities, consistently demonstrate cooperative behaviours including turn-taking, encouragement and mutual practice; describe what cooperation looks like in movement contexts.
wider: Compare how practising with a partner differs from practising alone, and reflect on which produces better skill development and why
Work with a partner from a different cultural background or with different physical abilities and reflect on how to adjust cooperative strategies
Design a partner skill-practice routine and evaluate how well the cooperative strategies used supported both partners' learning

modes.reason: Cooperative behaviour in movement contexts requires deliberate, repeated practice — students need regular paired tasks with explicit attention to the cooperative dimension, not just movement skill practice.

nodes.label: Describing and demonstrating inclusion in physical activities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and demonstrate how to include others in physical activities.
criteria: Describes at least one way to include another person in a physical activity
Demonstrates an inclusion behaviour in a group movement context

width.minimum: Describe at least one way to include another person in a physical activity; demonstrate this in a group context.
width.typical: Identify and demonstrate multiple strategies for including others in physical activities; explain why inclusion matters for everyone's participation.
wider: Identify a physical activity where a classmate is having difficulty participating and propose a specific inclusion strategy
Compare how the same inclusion strategy works across different activity types (e.g. a running game vs a ball game) and adjust if needed
Discuss how using different languages or non-verbal communication can support inclusion for students who speak different languages

modes.reason: Inclusion strategies need to be practised across different activity structures — what works in a partner drill may not work in a team game. Vary the social and movement context so students develop a range of applicable strategies.

nodes.label: Adapting games for collaborative inclusion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can propose and trial how a game can be changed so that everyone can be included.
criteria: Proposes at least one game modification intended to improve inclusion
Trials the change and describes whether it achieved its purpose

width.minimum: Suggest at least one change to a game that would allow more participants to be included; trial the change and comment on whether it worked.
width.typical: Propose, trial and evaluate game modifications designed to improve inclusion; explain why specific changes support collaborative participation for all.
wider: Design a version of a familiar game with modifications that address multiple potential barriers to inclusion (skill level, physical ability, language)
Compare two different modifications to the same game and evaluate which better supports collaborative participation for all students
Reflect on a game modification that did not work as intended and propose a revised approach

modes.reason: This node integrates partner cooperation (Node 1) and inclusion strategies (Node 2) into the collaborative game-modification demand of the descriptor. Use tasks where students must draw on both — cooperating with others to design and trial a more inclusive activity.

descriptors.title: Personal qualities and identities
descriptors.description: describe their personal qualities and those of others, and explain how they contribute to developing identities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have investigated who they are and the people in their world (AC9HPFP01). They can name people in their life and explore basic features of themselves and their communities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe personal qualities and explain how they contribute to developing identities.

nodes.label: Identifying personal qualities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe their own personal qualities and those of others.
criteria: Names and describes at least two of their own personal qualities
Identifies at least one personal quality in another person
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to name and describe personal qualities is the necessary foundation for explaining how those qualities shape identity (Node 2). Students who can only vaguely characterise themselves or others cannot make the explanatory move the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Name and describe at least two of their own personal qualities and identify at least one quality in another person.
width.typical: Describe a range of personal qualities in themselves and others, including qualities that contribute to positive relationships and activities; connect qualities observed in others to their own experience.
wider: Describe personal qualities of characters in stories and compare them to their own qualities
Explore how different communities and cultural groups may describe and value personal qualities differently
Identify personal qualities that help in physical activities and explain how those qualities contribute to a positive experience for everyone

modes.reason: Students need a working vocabulary of personal quality descriptors before they can meaningfully explain identity. Build a shared class vocabulary of qualities through stories, physical activities and discussion before moving to explanatory tasks.

nodes.label: Explaining how qualities contribute to identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how personal qualities contribute to developing identities.
criteria: Explains how at least one personal quality contributes to their own or another person's identity
Links a specific quality to a specific aspect of identity (e.g. how they are seen, how they feel about themselves)
nodes.hinge_reason: The explanatory move — 'how qualities contribute to identity' — is the descriptor's primary demand and the conceptual foundation for examining group and community identity in Years 3–4. Thin treatment here (staying at description) means students carry forward only a surface understanding of identity.

width.minimum: Explain how at least one personal quality contributes to their own identity or the identity of someone they know.
width.typical: Explain how multiple personal qualities contribute to individual identities; discuss how different qualities shape how a person is known and how they see themselves.
wider: Explore how belonging to First Nations Australian cultural groups contributes to identities and how cultural practices shape personal qualities
Examine examples from Australians of Asian heritage that recognise how family and friends contribute to identities
Describe personal achievements and explain how succeeding (or struggling) in physical activities influenced their personal identity

modes.reason: Provide a simple causal scaffold: 'I am [quality] and this shapes my identity because...'. Without this structure, students tend to list qualities rather than explain their contribution.

Exploring identity through cultural belonging, achievement in physical activities, and stories provides genuinely different angles on how qualities shape identity — not just the same explanation in different words.

nodes.label: Group and community belonging and identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how personal and cultural identities are influenced by the groups and communities to which they belong.
criteria: Identifies at least one group or community they belong to
Describes how membership of that group influences their identity or qualities

width.minimum: Identify at least one group or community they belong to and describe how membership influences their identity or personal qualities.
width.typical: Explain how belonging to different groups and communities — including cultural, family and school communities — shapes personal and cultural identities; describe how this is seen in themselves and others.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian cultural group membership shapes personal identity and contributes to community belonging
Compare how identity is expressed in different cultural communities represented in the class and identify shared qualities
Explore how participating in physical activities as part of a team or group shapes identity and personal qualities over time

modes.reason: This node integrates personal quality description (Node 1) and individual identity explanation (Node 2) into the broader social and cultural dimension of identity. Tasks should connect who students are to the communities they belong to, not treat group identity as a separate concept.

descriptors.title: Respectful relationships
descriptors.description: identify and explore skills and strategies to develop respectful relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students have practised personal and social skills to interact respectfully with others (AC9HPFP02). They can demonstrate basic respectful interaction in familiar contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and explore skills and strategies to develop respectful relationships.

nodes.label: Recognising respectful and disrespectful behaviours
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify behaviours that demonstrate respect and those that may cause hurt, harm or disrespect to others.
criteria: Identifies at least one behaviour that shows respect
Identifies at least one behaviour that may cause hurt or disrespect to others
nodes.hinge_reason: Students need a clear conceptual anchor for respectful versus disrespectful behaviour before they can identify or practise strategies to build respect (Node 2). Without this, strategy exploration is superficial — students know what to do but not why.

width.minimum: Identify at least one behaviour that demonstrates respect and at least one that causes disrespect or hurt, in a familiar context.
width.typical: Identify a range of respectful and disrespectful behaviours across different contexts (stories, physical activities, everyday interactions); distinguish verbal, non-verbal and physical forms of both.
wider: Examine characters in texts who demonstrate respect for different types of families and carers, including those of different cultures, abilities or compositions
Identify and describe verbal and physical forms of bullying and explain how they affect others
Explore what respect looks like for First Nations Australians and how to acknowledge difference using appropriate language

modes.reason: Use stories, role play or movement scenarios to prompt students to name specific behaviours and classify them. Concrete examples from familiar contexts are more effective than abstract definitions at this year band.

nodes.label: Skills and strategies for respectful relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explore skills and strategies to develop respectful relationships.
criteria: Names at least one skill or strategy for showing respect in a relationship
Describes how that skill or strategy contributes to a respectful relationship

width.minimum: Identify at least one skill or strategy used to show respect in a relationship context and describe how it works.
width.typical: Identify and explore a range of skills and strategies for showing respect in relationships — including appropriate language, body language, inclusion, and encouragement — across different social and movement contexts.
wider: Demonstrate appropriate verbal and non-verbal language (including gestures) when encouraging and including others in physical activities
Explore strategies for showing respect to First Nations Australians and discussing difference using appropriate language
Compare how strategies for showing respect might look different in physical activity contexts versus classroom or social contexts

modes.reason: Students benefit from building a repertoire of specific respect strategies across contexts — not just knowing that 'respect is important' but having named, practisable moves they can call on.

descriptors.title: Emotional responses
descriptors.description: identify how different situations influence emotional responses
descriptors.knowledge: Students have expressed and described emotions they experience (AC9HPFP03). They can name basic emotions and connect them to personal experiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify how different situations influence emotional responses.

nodes.label: Recognising emotional cues in self and others
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise emotions in themselves and others by reading words, facial expressions and body language.
criteria: Identifies an emotion in a person or character in a given scenario
Names at least one cue (word, expression, or body language) that supports the identification
nodes.hinge_reason: Reading emotional cues is the prerequisite for understanding how situations trigger emotional responses (Node 2). Students who cannot reliably read cues in others will not be able to identify situational triggers or understand their impact on others.

width.minimum: In at least one scenario (real or imaginative), identify an emotion a person or character might be feeling and give one reason based on their words, expression or body language.
width.typical: Across a range of scenarios and contexts, predict and identify emotions in self and others using verbal and non-verbal cues; describe what evidence (words, expression, body language) supports the prediction.
wider: Use role play and imaginative play to identify how someone might feel, think and act during an emergency or unexpected situation
Compare how emotions are expressed differently across cultural contexts and discuss why this matters for respectful interaction
Observe a physical activity scenario and identify the emotions of multiple participants, explaining what cues led to each identification

modes.reason: Provide explicit prompts that direct students to evidence: 'I can tell they feel __ because I can see/hear __'. This prevents students from simply guessing emotions without attending to the situational or interpersonal cues.

nodes.label: Situations that trigger emotional responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific situations that may trigger strong emotional responses in themselves and others, and recognise the impact those responses can have on others.
criteria: Identifies at least one situation that triggers a strong emotional response
Describes how that emotional response could affect the person experiencing it or those around them

width.minimum: Identify at least one situation that typically triggers a strong emotion; describe what the emotional response might look like and how it could affect others.
width.typical: Identify a range of situations that trigger strong emotional responses; explain how the same situation might produce different responses in different people and how those responses affect others.
wider: Explore self-regulation strategies to manage emotional responses in situations that trigger strong feelings
Recognise own emotions in a range of situations and describe ways to manage how they are expressed
Identify how someone might feel, think and act in an emergency through role play — connecting situational triggers to response patterns

modes.reason: Emotional trigger situations vary widely. Students benefit from exploring triggers across physical activity, social, and imaginative contexts so the concept of 'situations influencing responses' is not over-indexed to one context type.

nodes.label: Managing emotional expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise their own emotions and describe ways to manage how they express emotions in different situations.
criteria: Names at least one strategy for managing how they express a strong emotion
