Can connect the strategy to a specific type of situation where it would be useful

width.minimum: Describe at least one strategy they can use to manage how they express a strong emotion in a given situation.
width.typical: Describe and demonstrate a range of self-regulation strategies for managing emotional responses across different types of situations; explain why managing emotional expression matters for themselves and others.
wider: Practise self-regulation strategies in a simulated situation (e.g. a physical activity where frustration is likely) and reflect on how well the strategy worked
Explore how cultural context affects how emotions are expressed and what self-regulation strategies are appropriate
Compare strategies for managing emotions across different types of situations (physical activity, social conflict, unexpected events)

modes.reason: This node connects emotional recognition (Node 1) and situational trigger understanding (Node 2) with the self-regulatory response that is implicit in the descriptor's 'influence' framing. Tasks should require students to both identify the trigger and select a management strategy — not treat recognition and regulation as separate skills.

descriptors.title: Seek, give or deny permission
descriptors.description: practise strategies they can use when they need to seek, give or deny permission respectfully
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how to seek, give or deny permission respectfully when sharing possessions or personal space (AC9HPFP04).
descriptors.endpoint: Students practise strategies for seeking, giving or denying permission respectfully.

nodes.label: Seeking, giving and refusing consent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can practise strategies for giving or refusing consent, including verbal and non-verbal approaches.
criteria: Uses at least one verbal strategy to give or refuse consent in a practised scenario
Uses at least one non-verbal cue or gesture to communicate consent or refusal
nodes.hinge_reason: Practising assertive verbal and non-verbal permission strategies is the foundational capability of this descriptor. Students who lack a practised, embodied set of responses cannot apply them confidently in real situations — which is the safety concern underpinning this standard.

width.minimum: In a practised scenario, use at least one verbal strategy (e.g. saying yes or no assertively) and one non-verbal cue or gesture to give or refuse consent.
width.typical: Practise a range of strategies for seeking, giving and denying permission — including assertive verbal responses, body cues, and gestures — across a variety of situations.
wider: Practise saying no to inappropriate touching and other boundary violations using assertive language and non-verbal cues
Explore situations where non-verbal cues alone may not be sufficient and discuss when verbal communication is essential
Compare how permission strategies are used in different contexts (sharing equipment, physical contact, personal space) and identify which strategies are most effective in each

modes.reason: These strategies must be rehearsed until automatic — not just understood conceptually. Regular role-play practice across varied scenarios builds the fluency required for confident real-world application.

nodes.label: Fair and respectful interaction regardless of difference
nodes.checkpoint: Students can practise ways to interact with others in a fair and respectful way in play and other activities, regardless of differences in gender, abilities, race or personality.
criteria: Demonstrates a fair and respectful interaction with a peer who is different from themselves
Can describe what they did to interact respectfully

width.minimum: In a play or activity context, demonstrate at least one fair and respectful interaction with a person who is different from themselves; describe what they did.
width.typical: Practise fair and respectful interaction across a range of play and activity contexts involving diverse peers; explain how respecting difference contributes to the activity being positive for everyone.
wider: Compare how the same respectful interaction strategy works with peers of different abilities, genders, or backgrounds
Explore scenarios where differences in personality or preferences create friction in activities, and practise strategies for managing these respectfully
Discuss how respecting difference in physical activities connects to the fair-play principles students have explored in movement contexts

modes.reason: Respectful interaction across different types of difference requires practice in varied contexts. Explicitly vary peer configurations (different abilities, genders, personalities) in activity tasks so students practise the full range of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Protective behaviours and help-seeking
descriptors.description: identify and demonstrate protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies they can use to help them and others stay safe
descriptors.knowledge: Students have demonstrated protective behaviours, named body parts and rehearsed help-seeking strategies that help keep them safe (AC9HPFP05).
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and demonstrate protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies to help them and others stay safe.

nodes.label: Body reactions to safe and unsafe situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the body's reaction to safe and unsafe situations and compare the different emotional responses.
criteria: Describes at least one body reaction that signals a safe situation and one that signals an unsafe situation
Identifies these reactions as signals to consider a protective response
nodes.hinge_reason: Recognising bodily and emotional signals as safety indicators is the conceptual anchor for all protective and help-seeking action. Students who do not understand the signal cannot reliably trigger the protective response in real situations.

width.minimum: Describe how their body feels in a safe situation versus an unsafe or uncomfortable situation; identify this as a signal to act.
width.typical: Identify the body's physical and emotional reactions to a range of safe and unsafe situations; explain how these reactions can help them recognise when they need to use protective behaviours.
wider: Explore how characters in texts experience safe and unsafe situations and compare their emotional responses to the student's own experience
Identify body reactions in emergency scenarios through role play and describe what these signals mean
Compare how the same situation might feel different to different people, and discuss what this means for recognising when others may need help

modes.reason: Use explicit language scaffolds to connect body signals to meaning: 'When I feel __ in my body, it might mean __'. This prevents the concept staying at the level of emotion labelling rather than signal interpretation.

nodes.label: Help-seeking strategies and safe networks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and rehearse strategies they can use when requiring assistance, including trusted adults, safe places and problem-solving with friends.
criteria: Names at least one trusted adult and one safe place they could access for help
Describes at least one strategy for asking for help in a situation

width.minimum: Name at least one trusted adult and one safe place they could go to for help; describe one strategy for asking for help.
width.typical: Identify a network of trusted people and safe places; practise strategies for seeking help including asking an adult, reading signs, recognising safe locations, and problem-solving with friends.
wider: Recognise photos and locations of safe places in the school and local community and explain why these are safe
Explore how to seek help in different scenarios — at school, at home, and in public — and compare which strategies are most appropriate in each context
Discuss the importance of seeking help when a problem is too big to solve alone, and practise how to communicate the nature of the problem to a trusted adult

modes.reason: Students need a practical repertoire of help-seeking strategies and a named network of trusted people. Build this explicitly — not all students have clear networks or know how to activate them.

nodes.label: Protective behaviours including digital safety
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and rehearse protective behaviours, including strategies for safe use of digital tools.
criteria: Identifies at least one protective behaviour for a physical safety situation
Identifies at least one protective behaviour for safe digital tool use

width.minimum: Identify at least one protective behaviour for a physical safety context and one for digital tool use; practise or describe each.
width.typical: Identify and rehearse a range of protective behaviours across physical and digital contexts; explain how these behaviours help them and others stay safe.
wider: Propose strategies for healthy and manageable use of digital tools at school and home and explain how these protect wellbeing
Explore how to respond to uncomfortable or unsafe situations in digital spaces and compare these strategies to responses in physical situations
Role-play using protective behaviours in a range of scenarios drawn from stories, everyday life and online contexts

modes.reason: This node connects body-signal awareness (Node 1) and help-seeking strategies (Node 2) into the full protective behaviour repertoire, extended to digital contexts. Tasks should require students to identify a signal, select a protective behaviour and identify a help-seeking path — not treat each as a separate skill.

descriptors.title: Health messages in community
descriptors.description: investigate a range of health messages and practices in their community and discuss their purposes
descriptors.knowledge: Students have identified health symbols, messages and strategies in their community that support their health and safety (AC9HPFP06).
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate health messages and practices in their community and discuss their purposes.

nodes.label: Health symbols, labels and community messages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify health symbols, medicine packaging and community health messages and understand the safety purposes they serve.
criteria: Identifies at least two health symbols or labels
Explains the safety purpose or required action communicated by each
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that health symbols and messages communicate safety-relevant actions is prerequisite to investigating broader community health practices and purposes (Node 2). Without this anchor, students treat health messages as decorative rather than purposive.

width.minimum: Identify at least two health symbols or labels (e.g. poison labels, medicine packaging) and explain the safety action each communicates.
width.typical: Identify a range of health symbols, medicine labels, and community health messages; explain the safety purpose of each and what action it requires.
wider: Investigate how foods are marketed and promoted to children through advertisements in online spaces, supermarket placement and packaging, and discuss the health messages these convey
Compare health messages in different community contexts (school, supermarket, online) and identify whether they promote similar or different health behaviours
Explore how digital tools and screen-based products communicate health messages and discuss whether these are reliable

modes.reason: Require students to decode the message: 'This symbol/label tells me __ because __'. The reasoning step prevents stopping at label identification without understanding the safety purpose.

nodes.label: Food, health and community practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how eating a variety of fresh foods and community health practices influence health and wellbeing.
criteria: Describes how eating a variety of fresh foods can influence health and wellbeing
Identifies at least one community health practice and explains its purpose

width.minimum: Using a reference such as the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating, describe how eating a variety of fresh foods can influence health and wellbeing.
width.typical: Investigate how food choices and a range of community health practices influence health and wellbeing; discuss the purpose of these practices and why they matter.
wider: Explore sustainable practices students can implement in the classroom to improve health and wellbeing, such as composting food waste, creating an edible garden, or reducing single-use plastics
Investigate how foods are marketed to children and discuss how marketing influences food choice and health messages
Compare a food or health practice from a First Nations Australian or Asian Australian community with a familiar practice and discuss similarities and differences in health purpose

modes.reason: Community health practices vary widely — food, digital use, sustainability, medicine safety. Investigating across multiple practice types gives students a genuinely broader picture of what 'community health' encompasses.

nodes.label: Digital health rules and practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create rules and apply them to implement healthy and manageable practices with their use of digital tools.
criteria: Describes at least one rule for healthy digital tool use
Explains how that rule supports health or wellbeing

width.minimum: Describe at least one rule for healthy digital tool use at school or home and explain its health purpose.
width.typical: Create and apply rules for healthy digital tool use; explain how these rules support health and wellbeing and discuss challenges to following them.
wider: Compare self-created digital use rules with recommendations from health organisations and evaluate whether the rules are consistent
Investigate how too much or unmanaged screen time can affect health and wellbeing, and propose specific rules to address the risks identified
Explore how digital rules at school might differ from those at home and discuss why context matters for health practice

modes.reason: This node connects health message literacy (Node 1) and community health practice understanding (Node 2) to the active health-practice demand of the descriptor. Tasks should require students to apply health knowledge to create and justify their own rules — not just identify what others recommend.

descriptors.title: Refine movement skills
descriptors.description: refine and apply fundamental movement skills in new movement situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students have practised fundamental movement skills and applied them in a variety of movement situations (AC9HP2M01). They can apply skills across locomotor and object control domains in familiar contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students refine and apply fundamental movement skills in new and varied movement situations.

nodes.label: Combining locomotor and object control skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform activities that combine locomotor and object control skills to complete a movement task or challenge.
criteria: Identifies the locomotor and object control components in a given movement task.
Performs a combined-skill movement task, demonstrating coordination between the two skill types.
Completes the movement task or challenge with at least partial success.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot integrate locomotor and object control skills in combination, they cannot access the refinement and adaptation work in subsequent nodes — all applied movement tasks in this band require combined-skill execution.

width.minimum: Combine at least one locomotor skill with one object control skill to complete a set movement task.
width.typical: Perform a range of activities that combine locomotor and object control skills across different movement tasks and challenges, including games contexts.
wider: Design and perform their own combined-skill movement challenge, explaining the locomotor and object control components involved.
Compare how the combination of locomotor and object control skills differs across two distinct movement contexts (e.g. a field game vs a court game).

modes.reason: Students who can execute skills in isolation but not in combination need structured practice that gradually introduces dual demands — locomotor task first, then add the object control component.

nodes.label: Propelling objects towards targets
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore and practise different techniques to propel objects towards a range of targets.
criteria: Demonstrates at least two different techniques for propelling an object.
Adjusts their technique when the target changes (e.g. closer vs further, larger vs smaller).
Describes what they changed in their technique and why.

width.minimum: Practise at least two different techniques for propelling an object towards a stationary target.
width.typical: Explore and compare multiple propelling techniques across varied objects and target types (distance, accuracy, height), identifying what makes each technique effective.
wider: Investigate how adjusting force, angle or body position changes the outcome when propelling objects towards targets of different sizes and distances.
Apply propelling techniques in a game or challenge context where target type changes across rounds, and reflect on which techniques were most effective.

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of propelling techniques across different objects and target configurations — depth in one technique is less useful than breadth across contexts.

nodes.label: Weight transference in movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform fundamental movement skills that demonstrate weight transference in different physical activities.
criteria: Identifies at least one point in a movement activity where weight is transferred.
Performs a movement that involves deliberate weight transference.
Describes how transferring weight supports the movement outcome.

width.minimum: Perform a movement activity that involves transferring body weight (e.g. a roll, step pattern or balance transition), identifying where weight transfer occurs.
width.typical: Demonstrate weight transference across a range of physical activities — gymnastics, dance, games — and explain how weight transfer contributes to the movement.
wider: Explore how weight transference principles apply across culturally diverse movement forms such as martial arts, traditional dance, or First Nations Australian movement practices.
Design a short movement sequence that deliberately highlights weight transference at three different points, and coach a peer using appropriate vocabulary.

modes.reason: Students often perform weight transference implicitly without conceptual awareness of it. Scaffolding the language and identification of weight transfer — 'where does the weight go, when, and why' — develops the awareness needed to apply it deliberately.

nodes.label: Coordinated swimming strokes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can coordinate kicking with arm movements to move their body through the water using different types of strokes.
criteria: Coordinates kicking and arm movements in at least one swimming stroke.
Sustains the stroke across a short distance without stopping.
Identifies whether their kick and arm timing felt coordinated and what they would adjust.

width.minimum: Coordinate kicking and arm movements to sustain one swimming stroke across at least a short distance.
width.typical: Demonstrate coordination across two or more swimming strokes, sustaining rhythm and timing between kick and arm action across varied distances.
wider: Explore how the coordination demands differ between freestyle and breaststroke — or between any two strokes with different timing patterns — and explain what makes each challenging.
Apply coordinated stroke technique in a minor water-based activity or challenge, adjusting technique in response to feedback.

modes.reason: Swimming stroke coordination requires timing precision between two independent movement chains (kick and arms). Students need repeated practice to build automaticity before they can apply skill in varied water contexts.

nodes.label: Movement sequences — jumping, landing and balancing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform and connect movement sequences incorporating different jumping, landing and balancing techniques.
criteria: Performs a movement sequence that includes a jump, landing and balance with controlled transitions.
Maintains balance and control at the connection points between elements.
Describes the sequence they performed and at least one aspect they would refine.
nodes.hinge_reason: Sequencing and connecting movements is the integration demand that spans the whole standard. Students who cannot connect skill components into a sequence will be unable to demonstrate the 'new movement situations' requirement at the progression endpoint, and this limitation cascades into AC9HP6M01 where more complex combined sequences are expected.

width.minimum: Perform a movement sequence that connects at least a jump, a landing and a balance, with controlled transitions.
width.typical: Create and perform a sequence that incorporates multiple jumping, landing and balancing techniques with controlled connections and smooth transitions.
wider: Choreograph and perform a movement sequence for an audience (class or small group), incorporating transitions that are deliberate and match a chosen theme or musical structure.
Compare how jumping, landing and balancing techniques feature in gymnastics, dance and outdoor/adventure activities — identifying similarities and differences in technique demands.

modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate previously practised individual skills (jump, land, balance) into a connected sequence. Teacher investment should focus on the transitions — the linking moments — rather than re-teaching individual skills.
Students who achieve the minimum sequence benefit from performing in different movement contexts (gymnastics, dance, outdoor) to build transferability of the sequencing capability.

descriptors.title: Movement strategies
descriptors.description: apply and adapt movement strategies to achieve movement outcomes
descriptors.knowledge: Students have investigated different ways of moving and manipulating objects and space and drawn conclusions about their effectiveness (AC9HP2M02). They can experiment with movement but have not yet applied structured strategies to game contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply and adapt movement strategies to achieve movement outcomes across a range of activity types.

nodes.label: Planning strategies in minor and small-sided games
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and perform strategies to be successful in minor and small-sided games.
criteria: Describes a strategy they will use before participating in a game.
Performs the game using the planned strategy.
Reflects on whether the strategy achieved the intended outcome.
nodes.hinge_reason: Planning a strategy — even a simple one — is the prerequisite cognitive move for all subsequent adaptation work. Students who act purely reactively without planning cannot access the evaluation and adaptation demands in the next nodes.

width.minimum: Plan and perform a simple movement strategy in one minor or small-sided game (e.g. a tag game, target game or net/court game) and reflect on whether it achieved the intended outcome.
width.typical: Plan and perform strategies in a range of minor and small-sided game types, reflecting on what worked and adjusting approach across games.
wider: Compare strategies across two different game categories (e.g. tag game vs target game) and explain why the same strategy does or does not transfer.
Lead a small group in planning and trialling a strategy, gathering peer feedback on its effectiveness.

modes.reason: Students need a scaffold for thinking before and after a strategy attempt: what are we trying to achieve, what will we do, what happened. Brief structured reflection (e.g. a verbal debrief format) is more useful at this stage than extended written analysis.

nodes.label: Adapting strategies to create scoring opportunities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate how movement strategies can be adapted to create scoring opportunities across different game categories.
criteria: Identifies a scoring opportunity in a game and names a strategy to exploit it.
Adapts their movement strategy in response to a change in the game (e.g. opponent movement, rule change, new target).
Explains what they changed in their strategy and the reason for the change.

width.minimum: Demonstrate one adapted strategy in a game context where scoring is involved, explaining what was changed and why.
width.typical: Demonstrate adapted strategies across invasion, target, net/court, and striking/fielding game contexts, identifying how each game's rules and structure require different adaptations.
wider: Design a new rule or constraint variation for a known game and trial it, explaining how the change shifts the strategy space for players.
Investigate how professional or community teams adapt game strategies in response to opposition — using video or direct observation — and apply one observed adaptation to their own game.

modes.reason: Strategy adaptation is highly context-dependent — what works in an invasion game fails in a target game. Students need exposure across game categories to build genuine strategic flexibility rather than context-specific habits.

nodes.label: Centre of gravity and stability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate their centre of gravity to enhance stability and explain how centre of gravity and base of support influence stability.
criteria: Demonstrates a balance that requires adjusting centre of gravity.
Identifies their base of support in the balance and explains how changing it affects stability.
Uses the terms 'centre of gravity' and 'base of support' correctly in a short explanation.

width.minimum: Perform a balance activity that requires manipulating centre of gravity; explain in simple terms how centre of gravity affects stability.
width.typical: Perform and explain centre of gravity and base of support relationships across a range of balance activities; apply this understanding deliberately when attempting unfamiliar balances.
wider: Investigate how martial arts, gymnastics, or dance practitioners deliberately use centre of gravity manipulation as a movement strategy and demonstrate one application.
Design a balance challenge for a peer that deliberately varies the base of support and centre of gravity demands, and coach them using the relevant language.

modes.reason: The conceptual link between centre of gravity, base of support and stability is not intuitive. Students benefit from structured vocabulary scaffolding — label-then-demonstrate rather than demonstrate-then-label — to anchor the understanding to their physical experience.

nodes.label: Evaluating game tactics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the outcome of a game tactic that has been adapted to improve scoring options using set criteria.
criteria: Uses provided criteria to assess whether an adapted tactic achieved its intended effect.
Identifies at least one strength and one limitation of the tactic.
Proposes a specific change to the tactic based on their evaluation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluation using criteria is the capability move that connects strategy use to learning — without it, students simply repeat tactics rather than developing strategic thinking. This evaluation habit is directly required in AC9HP6M02 and underpins the more sophisticated tactical analysis expected at Y5-6.

width.minimum: Use a provided set of criteria to evaluate one adapted game tactic, identifying whether it improved scoring options and one change they would make.
width.typical: Evaluate adapted game tactics across two or more game types using criteria, identifying strengths and areas for improvement and connecting evaluation to future strategy decisions.
wider: Develop their own evaluation criteria for assessing a game tactic, trial the criteria with peers, and refine the criteria based on what they found most useful.
Compare tactic evaluations across two game sessions to track whether strategic decision-making improved over time and explain what evidence supports this.

modes.reason: Criteria-based evaluation is a new metacognitive layer for this age group. Providing a structured debrief format (what did we try, what happened, what would we change) and gradually releasing criteria construction to students builds the evaluation capability systematically.

descriptors.title: Movement concepts
descriptors.description: demonstrate how movement concepts related to effort, space, time, objects and people can be applied when performing movement sequences
descriptors.knowledge: Students have investigated different ways of moving their body and manipulating objects and space (AC9HP2M02). They have explored movement in an experimental way but have not yet applied named movement concepts deliberately in sequences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students demonstrate how movement concepts related to effort, space, time, objects and people can be applied when performing movement sequences.

nodes.label: Effort concepts — acceleration, deceleration, direction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate acceleration, deceleration and changing direction of movement in minor games and rhythmic or expressive activities.
criteria: Demonstrates deliberate acceleration, deceleration or direction change in a movement activity.
Labels at least two effort concepts when observing or performing movement.
Explains how changing effort helped them achieve a movement outcome.
nodes.hinge_reason: Effort concepts (especially acceleration/deceleration and direction change) are the foundation for strategic movement in games contexts. Students who cannot execute deliberate effort changes cannot meaningfully demonstrate space and time concepts in node 2, because spatial manipulation depends on timed effort shifts.

width.minimum: Demonstrate acceleration, deceleration and direction change in at least one minor game or movement activity, and label each when prompted.
width.typical: Demonstrate and name effort concepts across minor games and rhythmic/expressive activities; explain how varying effort achieves different movement outcomes.
wider: Explore how acceleration and deceleration are used strategically in a chosen sport (e.g. to evade an opponent or close a gap) and demonstrate an application.
Compose a short expressive movement phrase in which effort changes (fast/slow, strong/light) are the deliberate communication tool.

modes.reason: Students often experience effort changes without naming them. Explicit labelling practice — calling out 'accelerate', 'decelerate', 'change direction' during activity — builds the conceptual vocabulary needed for deliberate application.

nodes.label: Space concepts — levels, pathways, flow
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss and demonstrate different levels, movement pathways and use of space and flow in movement sequences.
criteria: Demonstrates at least two different spatial elements (level, pathway or use of space) in a movement sequence.
Describes the spatial choices made and explains why those choices were made.
Identifies where flow (smooth vs sudden transitions) occurs in their sequence.

width.minimum: Perform a movement sequence that uses at least two different levels or pathways, and describe the spatial choices made.
width.typical: Design and perform a movement sequence that deliberately uses levels, pathways, space and flow as compositional tools; discuss the effect of spatial choices on the sequence.
wider: Analyse how different dance forms or gymnastic styles use levels and pathways as expressive elements and incorporate one observed spatial pattern into their own sequence.
Create a movement map (diagram or annotated sketch) showing the levels and pathways in their sequence, then modify the sequence and update the map.

modes.reason: Spatial concepts apply differently in dance, gymnastics, and games contexts. Experiencing the same concepts across contexts builds richer and more flexible spatial understanding.

nodes.label: Body awareness — symmetry, shapes, angles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use their body to demonstrate symmetry, shapes and angles when performing movement skills, balances or sequences.
criteria: Names and demonstrates at least three different body shapes.
Identifies whether a movement or balance is symmetrical or asymmetrical.
Uses the term 'angle' correctly when describing a body position.

width.minimum: Perform at least one movement or balance that demonstrates a named body shape (e.g. tuck, straddle, straight, star) and identify the symmetry or angle involved.
width.typical: Perform a range of movements and balances that demonstrate symmetrical and asymmetrical shapes, different angles and contrasting body shapes; describe the body awareness used in each.
wider: Explore how body shape concepts connect to geometric concepts (lines of symmetry, angles as degrees) and demonstrate a sequence where body shapes are described using mathematical language.
Investigate how specific performance styles (e.g. classical ballet, gymnastics, First Nations Australian dance) use body shape as a primary expressive or technical element.

modes.reason: Students need to build a vocabulary of named body shapes and positions (tuck, pike, straddle, straight, wide, narrow) to access more complex composition and performance tasks. Accumulating a repertoire of demonstrated shapes is the primary investment here.

nodes.label: Manipulating space in games contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore different ways of manipulating space to receive passes, maintain possession, or increase or decrease scoring opportunities in games.
criteria: Identifies a spatial opportunity or problem in a game and names a strategy to address it.
Demonstrates deliberate space manipulation (creating or closing space) in a game.
Explains how their spatial movement affected a scoring or possession outcome.
nodes.hinge_reason: Spatial manipulation in games is the integrative application that demonstrates the full movement concepts standard. Without this applied understanding, the concepts of effort, space, time, objects and people remain disconnected from the games literacy demanded at Y5-6 (AC9HP6M03).

width.minimum: Demonstrate one spatial strategy in a game (e.g. moving to create space, closing space defensively) and explain what they were trying to achieve.
width.typical: Demonstrate spatial manipulation strategies across at least two game categories (invasion, net/court, striking/fielding or target games); explain how space manipulation connects to the scoring or possession outcome.
wider: Analyse a game play (observed or played) to identify how both teams are using space manipulation — mapping movements and explaining the spatial battle.
Design a small-sided game modification that forces a particular type of space manipulation (e.g. a constraint that limits defending space) and explain its intended effect.

modes.reason: This node draws together effort (when to move), space (where to move), time (how quickly) and people (relative to teammates and opponents). Teacher investment should focus on helping students connect these concepts rather than treating each separately.
Spatial manipulation works differently across game categories. Students who have only experienced invasion game space concepts may have limited transfer to target or net/court contexts.

descriptors.title: Regular physical activity and health
descriptors.description: participate in physical activities to explore how their body feels and describe how regular physical activity helps the body stay healthy and well
descriptors.knowledge: Students have participated in a range of physical activities in natural and outdoor settings and explored the benefits of being physically active at a general level (AC9HPFM03). They can identify enjoyment as a reason for activity but have not yet explored specific physiological or wellbeing effects.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in physical activities and describe how regular physical activity helps the body stay healthy and well.

nodes.label: Body awareness before, during and after activity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in physical activity circuits and explore how their body feels before, during and after participation.
criteria: Describes at least two physical sensations experienced during a physical activity.
Distinguishes between how their body felt before and during activity.
Identifies at least one specific body system that was affected (e.g. heart, lungs, muscles).
nodes.hinge_reason: Noticing and naming body responses is the perceptual foundation for the health knowledge in node 2. Students who cannot connect physical sensation to language cannot meaningfully describe or reason about how physical activity affects health.

width.minimum: Participate in a physical activity circuit and describe at least two physical sensations they notice before, during and after the activity.
width.typical: Participate in varied activity circuits and systematically notice and record body responses across all three phases (before, during, after), identifying patterns across activities.
wider: Compare how the body responds across activities of different intensity (e.g. walking vs sprinting vs sustained game play) and explain why the responses differ.
Explore how Indigenous Australian communities describe and understand the body's response to physical exertion in traditional activities.

modes.reason: Body awareness vocabulary (heart rate, breathing, temperature, muscle feel) needs to be explicitly taught and repeatedly practised. Students benefit from a consistent check-in format used across multiple activities to build familiarity with noticing and naming.

nodes.label: Warm-up and preparation for activity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform warm-up and stretching routines and understand how to prepare the body for being active.
criteria: Performs a warm-up routine with at least three distinct components.
Explains what at least two components of the warm-up do for the body.
Identifies the difference between warming up and cooling down.

width.minimum: Perform a warm-up routine and explain why warming up prepares the body for physical activity.
width.typical: Perform warm-up and cool-down routines in different activity contexts, explaining how each component prepares or recovers specific parts of the body.
wider: Lead a warm-up routine designed for a specific physical activity, explaining the purpose of each component to peers.
Investigate how warm-up practices differ across sporting codes (e.g. swimming vs team sports vs gymnastics) and explain why the differences exist.

modes.reason: Students often perform warm-ups as a compliance routine without understanding the purpose. A simple cause-effect scaffold — 'we do X because it does Y to the body' — builds the functional understanding needed to link warm-up behaviour to health outcomes.

nodes.label: Regular activity and health benefits
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how regular physical activity influences sleep quality, concentration and overall wellbeing.
criteria: Names at least two health benefits of regular physical activity.
Explains how at least one benefit connects to a specific body function (e.g. 'activity improves sleep because it helps the body feel tired in a healthy way').
Identifies one change they could make to be more regularly active and explains the expected benefit.

width.minimum: Describe at least two health benefits of regular physical activity, including at least one beyond physical fitness (e.g. sleep, concentration).
width.typical: Describe how regular physical activity influences multiple dimensions of health and wellbeing, including sleep, concentration, mood and physical health, using examples from their own participation experiences.
wider: Investigate the Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for Children and Young People and compare their own activity patterns against the recommendations, identifying gaps and proposing changes.
Research and present how regular physical activity is linked to mental health and wellbeing, drawing on one real-world example (e.g. a community sport program or physical activity initiative).

modes.reason: Health benefit understanding deepens when students connect it to a range of activity types and personal contexts, not just formal sport. Exploring benefits through classroom activity, outdoor adventure, sport and incidental movement builds a more holistic understanding.

descriptors.title: Outdoor physical activity
descriptors.description: participate in physical activities in natural and outdoor settings to examine factors that can influence their own and others' participation
descriptors.knowledge: Students have participated in physical activities in natural and outdoor settings and investigated factors that make physical activity enjoyable (AC9HP2M03). They can identify enjoyment factors but have not yet examined broader participation influences including community, cultural and social factors.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in outdoor physical activities and examine factors that influence their own and others' participation.

nodes.label: Participating in natural settings and reflecting on enjoyment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in physical activities in natural settings and reflect on enjoyable components and how to encourage others.
criteria: Participates in a physical activity in a natural setting.
Identifies at least two components of the experience they found enjoyable.
Suggests one specific way to encourage someone else to participate.

width.minimum: Participate in a physical activity in a natural setting and identify at least two components they found enjoyable and one way they could encourage a peer or family member to participate.
width.typical: Participate in varied outdoor settings, systematically reflecting on enjoyment components and generating multiple strategies to encourage others' participation.
wider: Explore First Nations Australians' connection to special places and how these places are linked to physical activities — inviting a community member or using respectful resources to inform understanding.
Design a plan to encourage family or community members to participate in a specific natural setting activity, addressing barriers they might face.

modes.reason: Enjoyment factors vary significantly across natural settings (bushland, water, open spaces, urban parks). Broader setting experience builds more nuanced understanding of what drives participation.

nodes.label: Home-based and everyday physical activity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore physical activities they can do at home using everyday items, and identify ways to be more active at home.
criteria: Identifies at least two physical activities that can be done at home using everyday items.
Explains what makes each activity accessible (no special equipment, small space, etc.).
Proposes one way to increase their physical activity level at home.

width.minimum: Identify and demonstrate at least one physical activity that can be done at home using everyday items, and explain why this is accessible.
width.typical: Explore a range of home-based physical activity options using everyday items, comparing their appeal and accessibility, and proposing a realistic home activity plan.
wider: Research how different households (urban, rural, small space, large space) might have different everyday item resources for activity, and propose adaptations to suit different contexts.
Create an 'activity at home' guide for a younger student, presenting accessible options with household equipment.

modes.reason: Students benefit from building a broad repertoire of accessible home activity options — the richer this repertoire, the more likely they are to identify options that work for their specific home context.

nodes.label: Community connections through physical activity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine how physical activity connects people to their community and explore community participation factors.
criteria: Identifies at least one way physical activity connects individuals to community.
Names at least two factors that can influence whether people participate in physical activity.
Explains how one identified factor specifically affected their own or someone else's participation.

width.minimum: Identify at least one way physical activity connects people to community members, and describe one factor that influences whether people in their community participate.
width.typical: Examine multiple ways physical activity builds community connections, and discuss a range of factors (social, cultural, environmental, logistical) that influence community participation in physical activity.
wider: Research a specific community physical activity program or event and examine how it was designed to be inclusive and accessible to different community members.
Explore how community sport and recreation look different across urban, regional and remote contexts in Australia — including the role of physical activity in First Nations community life.

modes.reason: Students need a multi-factor analysis scaffold to move beyond 'people like it' explanations of participation. A simple factors framework (social, environmental, access, cultural) helps them categorise and examine participation influences systematically.

descriptors.title: Physical activity recommendations
descriptors.description: explore recommendations about physical activity and sedentary behaviours, and discuss strategies to achieve the recommendations
descriptors.knowledge: Students have participated in physical activities and described how regular activity supports health and wellbeing (AC9HP4M04, same band). They have a working understanding of health benefits but have not yet engaged with formal guidelines or sedentary behaviour recommendations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore physical activity and sedentary behaviour recommendations and discuss strategies to achieve them.

nodes.label: Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore physical activity and screen-usage time recommendations in the Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for Children and Young People.
criteria: States the key physical activity recommendation (minutes per day) for their age group.
Identifies what is meant by 'sedentary behaviour' in the guidelines.
Explains one connection between the guidelines and a health benefit they have studied.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the guidelines is the prerequisite for all strategy-setting work in node 2. Students who do not understand what the recommendations are cannot meaningfully propose strategies to achieve them.

width.minimum: Identify the key physical activity and screen time recommendations in the Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines and describe in general terms what they mean for daily life.
width.typical: Explore the Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines in detail, examining the physical activity, sedentary and sleep components and connecting each to the health benefits discussed in AC9HP4M04.
wider: Compare the 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for different age groups (children vs teenagers vs adults) and explain how and why recommendations change across life stages.
Investigate how the 24-Hour Movement Guidelines were developed — who made them, what evidence was used — and discuss what it means for a guideline to be evidence-based.

modes.reason: Guidelines contain specific numbers and categories (daily minutes, screen limits, sleep hours) that require direct teaching and structured unpacking before students can engage with them critically. A guided reading and annotation activity is more effective than discovery.

nodes.label: Benefits of regular activity — sleep, concentration, wellbeing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine the benefits of regular physical activity including the influence on sleep, concentration and wellbeing.
criteria: Describes at least two specific benefits of regular physical activity.
Links at least one benefit to sleep, concentration or emotional wellbeing.
Uses an example from their own life to illustrate a benefit.

width.minimum: Describe how regular physical activity specifically benefits sleep, concentration or general wellbeing — with at least one example from their own experience.
width.typical: Examine and discuss the multiple health and wellbeing benefits of regular physical activity, including physical, mental and social dimensions, connecting these to the 24-Hour Movement Guidelines.
wider: Investigate how a specific community or school program uses physical activity to support wellbeing, and evaluate its design against the recommendations.
Explore research or case studies showing how physical activity interventions have supported concentration or mental health outcomes in children.

modes.reason: The benefits of activity are best understood when students connect them to varied personal and community examples — not just general statements. Moving from abstract benefit to specific contextual example is the key teaching move.

nodes.label: Strategies to meet recommendations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can propose realistic strategies to incorporate physical activity and reduce sedentary time to meet the 24-Hour Movement Guidelines.
criteria: Proposes at least two specific strategies to meet physical activity recommendations.
Explains how each strategy would increase activity or reduce sedentary time.
Identifies one realistic barrier to the strategy and suggests how it could be overcome.

width.minimum: Propose at least two specific strategies to increase physical activity or reduce sedentary time in their own daily routine.
width.typical: Propose and discuss a range of strategies to meet physical activity recommendations across school, home and community contexts; evaluate the feasibility of each strategy.
wider: Develop and trial a one-week 'active plan' for their own life, tracking whether they met the recommendations and reflecting on what worked and what was difficult.

Design an activity plan for a peer or family member who faces a specific barrier to meeting the guidelines (e.g. limited outdoor space, long screen time habits) and explain how the plan addresses the barrier.

modes.reason: Students need a broad repertoire of strategy options — at school, at home, in community settings, using different activity types — so they can select strategies that fit their specific circumstances. A narrow strategy set limits real-world application.

descriptors.title: Creative movement design
descriptors.description: apply creative thinking when designing movement sequences and solving movement problems
descriptors.knowledge: Students have co-constructed and applied rules to promote fair play (AC9HP2M04) and applied strategies to work collaboratively in physical activities (AC9HP2M05). They have experience working with others in movement contexts but have not yet applied creative thinking explicitly to design and problem-solving in movement.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply creative thinking when designing movement sequences and solving movement problems.

nodes.label: Transferring movement skills to solve challenges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can transfer and apply fundamental movement skills to solve movement challenges in different contexts.
criteria: Identifies a movement skill they know and describes a new context where it could be applied.
Demonstrates the skill in the new context.
Explains what made the transfer work or what they needed to adjust.
nodes.hinge_reason: Skill transfer is the cognitive basis of creative movement thinking — students who can only apply skills in the context they learned them cannot engage in the design and problem-solving that the rest of this standard demands.

width.minimum: Apply at least one movement skill from a familiar context to solve a movement challenge in an unfamiliar context, and explain the transfer.
width.typical: Transfer movement skills across a range of contexts (field, net/court, outdoor, gymnastics) to solve varied movement challenges, explaining the rationale for each transfer.
wider: Design a movement challenge for peers that requires them to transfer a named skill to a new context, and evaluate whether the transfer was successful.
Investigate how athletes transfer movement skills across different sports (e.g. a gymnast's body control applied to water polo) and explore examples from their own experience.

modes.reason: Transfer requires students to see the structural similarity between contexts ('what's the same about this problem and one I've solved before?'). A think-aloud or 'what do I already know about this?' prompt scaffold helps surface the prior knowledge needed for transfer.

nodes.label: Using prior knowledge in outdoor and novel activity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw on prior knowledge from other physical activity experiences to solve challenges faced when participating in outdoor activities.
criteria: Names at least one prior physical activity experience that gave them useful knowledge for a new challenge.
Applies that knowledge in a new outdoor activity context.
Explains what they drew on and whether it was useful.

width.minimum: Identify and use knowledge from one prior physical activity experience to address a challenge in an outdoor activity setting.
width.typical: Systematically draw on prior movement knowledge to approach outdoor activity challenges, reflecting on which prior experiences were most useful and why.
wider: Document prior movement knowledge in a 'skills I can use' record and actively reference it when approaching a new outdoor challenge.
Explore how Indigenous Australian communities pass on physical skills and knowledge through traditional outdoor activities — and discuss what this suggests about learning from experience.

modes.reason: Students who have a broader physical activity repertoire have more prior knowledge to draw on. Widening experience across activity types — particularly outdoor and adventure contexts — directly increases the resource pool for creative problem-solving.

nodes.label: Collaborative problem-solving in movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop questions and trial answers collaboratively to solve movement challenges.
criteria: Works with others to generate at least one solution to a movement challenge.
Trials the solution and observes what happens.
Reflects on whether the solution worked and suggests one adjustment for next time.

width.minimum: Work with a partner or small group to develop and trial at least one solution to a movement challenge (e.g. a partner balance or game tactic), and reflect on whether it worked.
width.typical: Collaboratively design and trial multiple solutions to varied movement challenges across partner, small group and team contexts; reflect on the process of group problem-solving and what made it effective.
wider: Lead a small group through a structured problem-solving process for a movement challenge, using a plan-try-reflect cycle, and evaluate the group's creative thinking.
Compare how different groups solved the same movement challenge, examining the variety of solutions generated and what this reveals about creative thinking in movement.

modes.reason: Collaborative problem-solving integrates creative thinking with teamwork and movement skills. The teaching focus should be on the problem-solving process (question → trial → reflect) as much as on the movement outcome.

Movement problem types vary substantially — partner balance challenges, game tactics, obstacle courses and outdoor activities each have distinct problem structures. Exposure across types builds more versatile creative problem-solving capability.

descriptors.title: Rules and fair play
descriptors.description: apply rules and scoring systems to promote fair play when participating or designing physical activities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have co-constructed and applied rules to promote fair play in a range of physical activities (AC9HP2M04). They can co-create and apply rules but have not yet engaged with officiating roles, scoring systems, or the rules and games of First Nations Australians.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply rules and scoring systems to promote fair play in physical activities they participate in or design.

nodes.label: Collaborating to design rules for fair play
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collaborate to decide rules for a new game that promote fair play and inclusion of all learners.
criteria: Creates at least two rules for a physical activity.
Explains how each rule promotes fairness or inclusion.
Adjusts at least one rule after trialling the activity.

width.minimum: Collaborate with others to create at least two rules for a physical activity that address fairness or inclusion, and explain the purpose of each rule.
width.typical: Collaboratively design a rule set for a new or modified game that explicitly addresses fair play and inclusion; trial the rules and adjust based on what happens during play.
wider: Design a rule set for a game that makes it equitable for players with different physical abilities, and explain how each rule addresses a specific inclusion challenge.
Explore rules and scoring systems used in traditional games of First Nations Australians and compare them with those used in modern games, examining how each system promotes fair play.

modes.reason: Rule design for different game types (active/tag, target, invasion, net/court) raises different fairness challenges. Exposure to designing rules across contexts builds richer understanding of what 'fair' means in different movement settings.

nodes.label: Fair decision-making and applying rules
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe processes of decision-making that ensure fairness in games and contribute to fair decision-making by applying rules appropriately.
criteria: Applies at least one rule correctly during a physical activity.
Describes what fair decision-making looks like in a game context.
Resolves a rule-based situation by explaining their decision and its basis.
nodes.hinge_reason: Fair application of rules is the operational counterpart to rule design. Students who cannot apply rules consistently and fairly cannot meaningfully take on officiating roles (node 3) and will undermine the group's fair play outcomes — cascading into AC9HP6M07 where more complex fair play contexts are expected.

width.minimum: Apply the rules of a physical activity fairly during participation, making at least one decision that requires rule interpretation.
width.typical: Apply rules fairly across a range of physical activity contexts; describe what fair decision-making requires (consistency, knowing the rules, impartiality) and demonstrate these during play.
wider: Examine a case where a rule was disputed or applied inconsistently in a game, and analyse what would have made the decision fairer.
Discuss how referees or officials are trained to make fair decisions in sport, and identify the skills and knowledge required for the officiating role.

modes.reason: Rule application requires students to interpret rather than just recall rules. Scenarios with ambiguous or contested situations — debriefed using a structured 'what does the rule say, what happened, what would be fair' format — build the interpretive reasoning required.

nodes.label: Officiating in physical activities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret and apply rules fairly when in an officiating role in physical activities.
criteria: Takes on an officiating role and makes at least two rule-based decisions.
Explains the reasoning for at least one decision when asked.
Reflects on one aspect of officiating they found challenging and what they would do differently.

width.minimum: Take on an officiating role in a physical activity and apply the rules to make at least two decisions during the activity.
width.typical: Officiate in a physical activity across multiple rounds or contexts, making multiple rule-based decisions and explaining reasoning for disputed calls.
wider: Compare the officiating demands across two different game types and explain what makes each challenging for an official.
Design and trial a peer feedback process for officiating quality — what does good officiating look like and how would you assess it?

modes.reason: Officiating requires simultaneously understanding rules, observing action, and making timely decisions under social pressure. This is the highest-demand integration of the standard and works best when students have practised both rule design and fair application first.

descriptors.title: Group roles and teamwork
descriptors.description: perform a range of roles in respectful ways to achieve successful outcomes in group or team movement activities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have applied strategies to work collaboratively when participating in physical activities (AC9HP2M05). They have experience collaborating but have not yet taken on differentiated roles within teams or considered how role performance affects group outcomes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students perform a range of roles respectfully to achieve successful outcomes in group or team movement activities.

nodes.label: Cooperative skills in movement tasks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use cooperative skills to complete a movement task, such as a partner balance, passing strategy or team strategy.
criteria: Demonstrates at least two cooperative skills during a partner or group movement task.
Names the cooperative skills they used.
Identifies how their cooperative behaviour contributed to the group's success.

width.minimum: Use cooperative skills (e.g. communication, support, listening) to complete one partner or group movement task.
width.typical: Apply cooperative skills across varied partner and group movement tasks, identifying which cooperative skills were most important in each context and why.
wider: Compare the cooperative skill demands across different task types (partner balance vs team game vs performance task) and explain how the demands shift.
Observe and analyse how a team in a game or performance successfully uses cooperative skills, then apply one specific observation to their own group work.

modes.reason: Cooperative skills (communication, encouragement, turn-taking, supporting others) need to be named, practised and accumulated as a repertoire. Students who only have 'be nice' as a cooperative strategy have limited capacity to adapt to different group contexts.

nodes.label: Maintaining possession — passing and listening
nodes.checkpoint: Students can work cooperatively with team members to maintain possession in a game by passing to other players and listening to teammates.
criteria: Passes to a teammate to maintain possession in a game.
Communicates with at least one teammate during a movement activity (e.g. calling for the ball, giving direction).
Reflects on how passing and communication helped or hindered possession maintenance.

width.minimum: Demonstrate passing and listening to teammates as strategies for maintaining possession in a small-sided game.
width.typical: Apply possession-maintenance strategies (passing, communication, positioning) across a range of small-sided games, reflecting on which strategies were most effective in different game contexts.
wider: Analyse possession statistics from a game session (who passed to whom, when possession was lost) and use the data to propose a modified strategy.
Explore how possession-maintenance strategies differ across game types (e.g. basketball vs soccer vs touch football) and explain what changes and what stays the same.

modes.reason: Passing and communication during game play require simultaneous execution under pressure. Repeated practice in low-pressure, small-sided formats builds automaticity before students can apply these skills reliably in team contexts.

nodes.label: Modifying activities for inclusion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can modify physical activities to ensure that everyone is included, such as changing equipment, rules or playing space.
criteria: Identifies at least one barrier to inclusion in a physical activity for a specific player.
Proposes a specific modification (equipment, rule or space change) to address the barrier.
Trials the modification and reflects on whether it improved inclusion.
nodes.hinge_reason: Inclusion through modification is the integrative outcome of this standard — it requires applying cooperative skills (node 1), game understanding (node 2) and perspective-taking simultaneously. Students who cannot modify for inclusion have not yet demonstrated the full capability demand of this standard, and this directly cascades into AC9HP6M09 which requires more complex and independent teamwork with diverse groups.

width.minimum: Propose and implement at least one modification to a physical activity that makes it more inclusive for a specific player or group.
width.typical: Identify inclusion barriers in a range of physical activities and propose and trial multiple modifications (equipment, rules, playing space) to address them; reflect on the effectiveness of each modification.
wider: Research how disability sport has adapted mainstream game rules and equipment to enable participation, and apply one adaptive principle to a class activity.
Design a fully modified version of a known game that is accessible to players with a specific additional need, trialling and refining the design based on peer feedback.

modes.reason: Modification for inclusion requires students to hold multiple perspectives simultaneously (their own experience, another's need, the game's purpose) and make adjustments that serve all. Structured perspective-taking activities (role swap, scenario analysis) support this integrative thinking.

Inclusion barriers look different across movement contexts — game space, equipment type, physical demand, communication style. Wider students who explore modifications across varied activity types develop more nuanced and transferable inclusion thinking.

descriptors.title: Resilience and identities
descriptors.description: investigate how success, challenge, setbacks and failure strengthen resilience and identities in a range of contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have described their personal qualities and those of others, and explained how they contribute to developing identities (AC9HP2P01). They understand personal qualities but have not yet examined how experiences of success, setback and failure shape identity and resilience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how success, challenge, setbacks and failure strengthen resilience and identities in a range of contexts.

nodes.label: Stories of challenge and success
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how characters or people overcome challenge and adversity and achieve success in different ways.
criteria: Identifies a challenge or setback a person faced in a story or real example.
Explains how the person's response to the challenge affected their resilience or identity.
Describes what 'resilience' means using language connected to a real example.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that challenge and setback contribute to rather than undermine identity is the core conceptual shift of this standard. Without it, students' work on resilience strategies (node 2) has no conceptual grounding — they treat resilience as a technique rather than an outcome of how one relates to difficulty.

width.minimum: Analyse at least one story or example of a person overcoming a challenge, identifying what the challenge was, how they responded, and what the outcome was for their identity or resilience.
width.typical: Examine multiple stories and examples (from texts, sport, community, peers) of overcoming challenge; identify patterns in how people respond to adversity and what builds resilience.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' pride in cultural background strengthens identity and resilience — exploring stories of First Nations athletes, leaders or community members.
Explore how responses to success, challenge, setbacks and failure are shaped by cultural beliefs and values — comparing examples from different cultural contexts.

modes.reason: Students often conflate success with positive identity development and failure with negative — the key insight that challenge and failure are also identity-strengthening requires explicit discussion and counterexample. Text-based case analysis with guided questions builds this reasoning.

First Nations Australian perspectives on resilience and identity, and cross-cultural comparisons of responses to adversity, offer substantively different frameworks for understanding how identity is built — not just additional examples. Exploring these contexts enriches the conceptual understanding meaningfully.

nodes.label: Unity through shared adversity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how overcoming challenge or adversity together can unite a group of diverse people.
criteria: Describes an example of people overcoming a challenge together.
Explains how shared challenge contributed to group connection or unity.
Identifies what was different about the group after experiencing the challenge together.

width.minimum: Describe at least one example (real or from a text) where people worked through a challenge together and explain how this strengthened the group.
width.typical: Examine multiple examples of shared adversity building group connection across diverse communities; discuss what makes shared challenge a unifying experience.
wider: Explore a community event or initiative where diverse groups came together in response to a shared challenge (e.g. a natural disaster, community project) and analyse how the experience affected group identity.
Investigate the role of shared physical challenge (e.g. team sport, expedition, community sport programs) in building group resilience and identity.

modes.reason: The concept that shared adversity builds diverse communities is best explored across multiple group contexts — classroom, sport team, community, cultural group — rather than through a single case study.

nodes.label: Physical activity and identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise how success, challenge, failure and enjoyment of physical activities influence identities.
criteria: Describes a specific physical activity experience involving success, challenge or failure.
Explains how the experience affected their confidence or sense of self.
Connects the experience to the idea of resilience or identity development.

width.minimum: Describe how one experience of success, challenge or failure in a physical activity affected how they felt about themselves.
width.typical: Reflect on a range of physical activity experiences (success, struggle, failure, enjoyment) and explain how each influenced their developing sense of identity and confidence.
wider: Design a journal or reflective record of physical activity experiences that tracks identity and confidence changes over a unit, identifying patterns in what builds and what challenges their sense of self.
Compare how different students in the class connect physical activity to identity — exploring why the same experience (e.g. team sport) can have very different identity effects for different people.

modes.reason: This node integrates the abstract understanding of challenge and resilience from node 1 with students' direct lived experience of physical activity. The teaching focus should bridge the two — helping students see their own PE experiences as identity-relevant.

descriptors.title: Coping with changes and transitions
descriptors.description: plan, rehearse and reflect on strategies to cope with the different changes and transitions they experience, such as the changes associated with puberty
descriptors.knowledge: Students have described personal qualities and explained how they contribute to developing identities (AC9HP2P01). They have some awareness of personal change but have not yet planned, rehearsed or reflected on coping strategies in a structured way, including for puberty.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, rehearse and reflect on strategies to cope with the changes and transitions they experience, including those associated with puberty.

nodes.label: Changes and transitions — physical, social, emotional
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss physical, social and emotional changes that occur as people get older and explore how these changes affect thinking and feeling.
criteria: Names at least two types of changes people experience as they grow older.
Classifies a given change as physical, social or emotional.
Describes how one type of change might affect a person's feelings or sense of self.
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying and understanding the types of changes is prerequisite to selecting and applying relevant coping strategies. Students who conflate physical changes with emotional ones, or cannot name the change type they are experiencing, will select poorly matched coping strategies.

width.minimum: Identify at least two types of changes (physical, social or emotional) that people experience as they grow older, and describe how one of these might affect how a person feels about themselves.
width.typical: Discuss physical, social and emotional changes across multiple transitions (e.g. primary to secondary school, puberty, family changes); explore how these changes interact and affect wellbeing.
wider: Explore the nature of family support networks in First Nations Australian communities and discuss how a wide range of family and community members support young people through changes and transitions.
Investigate how different cultures mark or celebrate the transition from childhood — examining what is valued and what support is provided.

modes.reason: Distinguishing physical, social and emotional changes requires a classification scaffold. A sorting activity (type of change → physical/social/emotional) followed by guided discussion of interactions between types builds the vocabulary and conceptual clarity needed for strategy planning.

nodes.label: Sources of support for puberty and change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify people or sources of information they can access when they have questions about puberty-related changes.
criteria: Names at least two people or sources of information they could turn to with questions about change or puberty.
Identifies at least one feature that makes a source of information trustworthy.
Distinguishes between a helpful and an unhelpful source of support or information.

width.minimum: Identify at least two trusted people or reliable sources of information they could access for support or information about puberty.
width.typical: Identify a range of trusted people, organisations and information sources relevant to puberty and other changes; evaluate what makes a source trustworthy.
wider: Compare how young people in different contexts (urban/rural, cultural backgrounds, family structures) have access to different types of support, and discuss what this means for who young people turn to.
Design a simple 'where to go for help' resource for a younger student — identifying trusted people and reliable information sources with brief explanations of what each provides.

modes.reason: Students benefit from knowing a wide range of support options — trusted adults, peers, school resources, health professionals, reputable online resources — so they can identify accessible options for their specific situation. A single 'ask a parent' strategy is insufficient.

nodes.label: Practising and reflecting on coping strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can practise and refine coping strategies for dealing with challenges and changes, and evaluate the effectiveness of different responses.
criteria: Practises at least one coping strategy in a scenario or real context.
Describes whether the strategy was helpful and why.
Identifies a different strategy they could try if the first one did not work.

width.minimum: Practise at least one coping strategy (e.g. positive self-talk, problem-solving, mindfulness, seeking help) and reflect on whether it was useful for a specific challenge or change.
width.typical: Practise a range of coping strategies across different challenge and change scenarios; compare strategies and reflect on which were most useful and why.
wider: Analyse a text or scenario where a character experiences and reacts to change — evaluate the effectiveness of the character's response and identify alternative strategies they could have used.
Develop a personal 'coping toolkit' that documents strategies that work for them across different types of challenges, with reflection on what each strategy is best suited for.

modes.reason: Strategy selection requires integrating understanding of the change type (node 1) with knowledge of available supports (node 2) and the specific strategy itself. The teaching focus should be on the match between situation type and strategy selection.

Different change and challenge contexts (school transitions, friendship changes, puberty, family change) benefit from different coping strategy emphases. Practising across contexts builds more flexible and transferable coping capability.

descriptors.title: Stereotypes and choices
descriptors.description: describe how choices and actions can be influenced by stereotypes
descriptors.knowledge: Students have described their personal qualities and those of others, and explained how they contribute to developing identities (AC9HP2P01). They have a basic understanding of personal qualities but have not yet examined how external stereotypes influence choices and actions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe how choices and actions can be influenced by stereotypes.

nodes.label: Stereotypes in texts and media
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify gender stereotypes in texts and media and discuss the messages they portray and how they can influence choices and actions.
criteria: Identifies at least one stereotype in a text or media example.
Describes the message the stereotype sends about a particular group.
Explains how that message could influence a person's choices or actions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Recognising a stereotype as a message about expected behaviour is the prerequisite conceptual move. Students who cannot identify a stereotype as such cannot describe how it influences choices — they will describe the influence without identifying its source.

width.minimum: Identify at least one stereotype in a text or media example and describe the message it sends about what is expected of a particular group.
width.typical: Explore a range of texts and media examples; identify stereotypes about gender and other characteristics; discuss the messages portrayed and how they could influence a person's choices or actions.
wider: Analyse how stereotypes in media targeting children (advertisements, games, toys, clothing) send messages about what is 'for' which gender, and investigate how these messages may limit choices.
Compare stereotyping in media across two different time periods or cultural contexts, examining how portrayals have changed or remained similar.
