modes.reason: Students need a working definition of 'stereotype' and practice identifying examples before they can analyse influence. A define-identify-analyse sequence with concrete media examples is more effective than abstract discussion of the concept.

nodes.label: Unfair treatment and human rights
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that unfair or unequal treatment based on gender, abilities or other differences is wrong and against human rights.
criteria: Describes what unfair treatment looks like in a familiar context.
Explains why treating people unequally based on stereotypes is wrong.
Uses the term 'human rights' correctly in their explanation.

width.minimum: Describe what unfair or unequal treatment means in a school or community context, and connect it to the idea that all people deserve to be treated fairly.
width.typical: Discuss how stereotypes can lead to unfair treatment of people based on gender, abilities or other characteristics; connect this to the concept of human rights and equal treatment.
wider: Investigate a specific human rights principle (e.g. the right to education, the right to be treated without discrimination) and examine how stereotypes can threaten this right.
Explore examples from history or current events where unfair treatment based on stereotypes was challenged, and discuss what changed as a result.

modes.reason: Connecting stereotype-based treatment to human rights requires an explicit conceptual bridge. Students need to understand that rights are not just about rules — they are about the equal worth of people — before the 'unfair' judgement has moral grounding.

nodes.label: Fair and equitable roles and responsibilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe ways to make roles and responsibilities at home, at school and in communities fair, equitable and inclusive.
criteria: Identifies at least one context where roles or responsibilities are affected by stereotypes.
Proposes a specific change that would make the distribution fairer.
Practises or demonstrates a way to challenge a stereotyped expectation.

width.minimum: Identify at least one situation where roles or responsibilities are distributed unequally based on stereotypes, and suggest a more equitable approach.
width.typical: Describe how stereotypes influence role and responsibility distribution across home, school and community contexts; identify specific actions that promote fairness and equity in each.
wider: Design an audit of roles and responsibilities in a familiar context (e.g. classroom tasks, household jobs) to identify where stereotyping is influencing distribution, and propose a fairer system.
Explore how stereotyped expectations about gender roles in physical activity limit participation for some students and discuss what schools and communities can do to address this.

modes.reason: Stereotyped role distribution looks different at home, school and community levels. Students who only explore one context have limited understanding of how pervasive and varied the influence of stereotypes can be.

descriptors.title: Personal and social skills in relationships
descriptors.description: select, use and refine personal and social skills to establish, manage and strengthen relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students have identified and explored skills and strategies to develop respectful relationships (AC9HP2P02). They have practised basic social skills but have not yet selected, evaluated and refined specific skills in response to relationship challenges.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select, use and refine personal and social skills to establish, manage and strengthen relationships.

nodes.label: Perspective-taking and empathy in relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can predict and reflect on how other students might feel in challenging situations and discuss what they can do to support them.
criteria: Describes how another person might feel in a challenging situation.
Identifies at least one action they could take to support that person.
Explains their reasoning — why they think the person feels that way.
nodes.hinge_reason: Perspective-taking is the foundational social skill required before students can meaningfully select, use or refine relationship skills. Without the ability to consider another's experience, skills like empathy, encouragement and conflict resolution remain surface-level behaviours rather than responsive actions.

width.minimum: Predict how at least one person might feel in a described challenging situation, and suggest one action they could take to support that person.
width.typical: Engage in perspective-taking across a range of challenging scenarios; discuss the range of possible emotional responses and identify specific support actions for each.
wider: Explore how demonstrating respect and empathy for First Nations Australians builds positive relationships — examining specific community or cultural contexts and what respectful engagement looks like.
Investigate how characters in texts from diverse cultural backgrounds demonstrate respect and empathy, comparing the strategies used across different relationship contexts.

modes.reason: Perspective-taking requires students to step out of their own viewpoint — a deliberate cognitive skill. Role-play, scenario analysis and guided questions ('what might this person be thinking?', 'what do they need?') scaffold this reasoning.

nodes.label: Respect and diversity in relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore strategies for demonstrating respect for difference and diversity in individuals and communities.
criteria: Names at least two strategies for showing respect for diversity.
Describes how each strategy supports positive relationships.
Demonstrates at least one strategy in a class or group activity.

width.minimum: Identify and describe at least one strategy a person used to demonstrate respect for difference or diversity in a text or real example.
width.typical: Explore a range of strategies for respecting difference and diversity across personal, school and community relationship contexts; discuss what makes each strategy effective.
wider: Research and participate in games from different cultural heritages, reflecting on what the games reveal about cultural values and how engagement shows respect for diversity.
Design a class event or activity that celebrates cultural diversity, identifying specific relationship skills that make multicultural engagement respectful and enriching.

modes.reason: Students benefit from building a repertoire of named, specific strategies for respecting diversity — not just the general instruction to 'be respectful'. Named strategies (active listening, asking questions, acknowledging difference) can be practised and transferred.

nodes.label: Challenging bullying
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that bullying takes many forms including online and can propose strategies to challenge bullying in and out of school.
criteria: Identifies at least two forms of bullying, including at least one online form.
Proposes a specific strategy a bystander could use to respond to bullying.
Explains why their proposed strategy would be effective in the given scenario.

width.minimum: Identify at least two forms of bullying (including online) and propose at least one strategy a bystander or target could use to address it.
width.typical: Recognise bullying across varied online and offline contexts; propose and evaluate a range of bystander and help-seeking strategies for different bullying scenarios.
wider: Examine the difference between bystander, upstander and target roles in bullying situations, and practise upstander strategies in role-play scenarios.
Investigate what safe and effective bystander actions look like in online contexts — comparing strategies that are useful offline with those needed for cyberbullying.

modes.reason: Challenging bullying integrates perspective-taking (node 1), respect for others (node 2) and strategy selection into a high-stakes social context. The teaching focus should be on practice through scenario work — not just knowledge of what bullying is.
Bullying strategies that work face-to-face often look different online. Students who practise strategies across both contexts develop more versatile and realistic capability.

descriptors.title: Diversity and inclusion
descriptors.description: describe how valuing diversity influences wellbeing and identify actions that promote inclusion in their communities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored skills and strategies to develop respectful relationships (AC9HP2P02) and investigated emotional responses (AC9HP2P03). They have practised respectful interaction but have not yet made explicit connections between valuing diversity and wellbeing outcomes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe how valuing diversity influences wellbeing and identify actions that promote inclusion in their communities.

nodes.label: Cultural diversity — sharing and celebrating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and celebrate the cultural diversity of their class and community.
criteria: Describes at least one aspect of a cultural background different from their own.
Identifies something they learned from engaging with that cultural perspective.
Explains why cultural diversity is valued in their community.

width.minimum: Identify and describe at least one cultural practice, game or tradition from their own or a classmate's cultural background.
width.typical: Explore and share cultural practices, stories and games from multiple cultural backgrounds; reflect on what learning about different cultures adds to the class community.
wider: Explore the diversity of backgrounds, experiences, beliefs and practices of Asian cultures, examining similarities and differences and connecting this to Australian cultural diversity.
Recognise the important role of cultural narratives in First Nations Australian communities — exploring how stories describe diversity and share beliefs and practices.

modes.reason: Cultural diversity understanding requires genuine exposure to multiple cultures — not just general awareness that diversity exists. Participation in games, sharing of stories and personal accounts from within the class community grounds the concept in lived experience.

nodes.label: Diversity, wellbeing and inclusion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how valuing diversity influences the wellbeing of individuals and communities.
criteria: Describes at least one specific connection between valuing diversity and wellbeing.
Explains what 'belonging' means and how it relates to inclusion.
Identifies a consequence for wellbeing when diversity is not valued.
nodes.hinge_reason: The causal connection between valuing diversity and wellbeing is the conceptual core of this standard. Students who describe 'being kind' without the wellbeing link cannot meaningfully identify actions that promote inclusion — their proposed actions will lack rationale.

width.minimum: Describe at least one way that valuing diversity benefits the wellbeing of individuals or a community.
width.typical: Describe multiple connections between valuing diversity and wellbeing, including social, emotional and community dimensions; discuss what happens when diversity is not valued.
wider: Investigate a real community initiative designed to promote inclusion and cultural diversity — examining how it was designed, who it reached, and what wellbeing benefits it aimed to create.
Explore research or statistics on the relationship between inclusion, belonging and mental health in school communities.

modes.reason: Students need to build the explicit causal chain: diversity valued → belonging felt → wellbeing improved. A structured discussion or scenario analysis that makes this chain visible — rather than leaving it implicit — is the key teaching move.

nodes.label: Safe bystander actions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and practise safe bystander actions when they notice unfair or disrespectful behaviour towards others.
criteria: Identifies at least one safe bystander action in a given scenario.
Explains why the action is safe for the bystander as well as the person affected.
Practises the action in a role-play or simulation.

width.minimum: Identify at least one safe bystander action they could take when they see unfair or disrespectful behaviour.
width.typical: Describe and practise a range of safe bystander actions across different scenarios (exclusion, disrespect, physical or verbal); evaluate which actions are safe and effective.
wider: Role-play bystander scenarios across different settings (classroom, playground, online) and debrief on the challenges of acting as an upstander and what makes it easier or harder.
Research the concept of 'bystander effect' at an age-appropriate level and discuss how understanding this effect changes their approach to acting when they witness unfair behaviour.

modes.reason: Safe bystander action integrates cultural understanding (node 1), wellbeing reasoning (node 2) and strategy selection into a high-stakes social moment. Scenario-based practice with structured reflection is the most effective preparation.

descriptors.title: Managing emotions
descriptors.description: explain how and why emotional responses can vary and practise strategies to manage their emotions
descriptors.knowledge: Students have identified how different situations influence emotional responses (AC9HP2P03). They can identify emotional responses to situations but have not yet explained why responses vary or practised structured strategies for managing emotions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how and why emotional responses can vary and practise strategies to manage their emotions.

nodes.label: Triggers, warning signs and emotional responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify possible triggers and warning signs to predict emotional responses.
criteria: Identifies at least one trigger for a strong emotional response in a scenario.
Describes at least one warning sign that the emotion is building.
Explains the connection between the trigger and the emotional response.
nodes.hinge_reason: Recognising triggers and warning signs is the prerequisite for deliberate emotion management. Students who cannot identify the signals that precede a strong emotional response cannot apply self-regulation strategies at the moment they are needed — they can only reflect after the fact.

width.minimum: Identify at least one trigger and one warning sign for a strong emotional response (e.g. frustration, anger, sadness) in a described scenario.
width.typical: Analyse multiple scenarios to identify triggers, warning signs and likely emotional responses; discuss how the same trigger can produce different responses in different people.
wider: Investigate how physical warning signs (heart racing, hands sweating, flushing) connect to emotional states, and explore how body awareness can help predict and manage emotional responses.
Explore how cultural backgrounds and family norms influence what triggers strong emotions and what is considered an appropriate response — using examples from different cultural contexts.

modes.reason: Students need a cause-effect scaffold for emotional analysis: trigger → warning sign → emotional response → consequence. Scenario analysis using a structured format (what happened, what did the person feel, what showed they were feeling that way, what did they do) builds this chain.

nodes.label: Responding helpfully in emergencies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how someone might respond in a helpful way during an emergency.
criteria: Describes a helpful response someone could have in an emergency.
Explains how managing their own emotions would help them respond effectively.
Identifies one specific thing they could do to stay calm in an emergency.

width.minimum: Describe at least one helpful response a person could have in an emergency situation — including managing their own emotional reaction to help effectively.
width.typical: Analyse a range of emergency scenarios and identify what helpful responses look like; discuss how managing one's own emotional state supports effective helping.
wider: Explore first aid or emergency response contexts where emotional regulation is critical for helpers — examining why staying calm is not just about the helper's comfort but about the quality of help provided.
Investigate how community members (e.g. emergency service workers, teachers) are trained to manage their emotional responses in order to respond helpfully.

modes.reason: Students need to see the functional connection between their own emotional state and their capacity to help others — this is not intuitive. A structured 'what happens to helping quality when the helper is panicking' analysis makes the link explicit.

nodes.label: Self-regulation strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can implement self-regulation strategies to manage the expression of emotional responses.
criteria: Practises at least one self-regulation strategy.
Identifies when in an emotional sequence the strategy should be applied.
Reflects on whether the strategy was effective and what they would do differently.

width.minimum: Practise at least one self-regulation strategy (e.g. deep breathing, counting, moving away) in a scenario or real context, and reflect on its effectiveness.
width.typical: Practise and compare a range of self-regulation strategies across different emotional scenarios; reflect on which strategies work best for them in different situations and explain why.
wider: Explore mindfulness-based self-regulation practices (e.g. guided breathing, body scan, visualisation) and practise at least one regularly over a period of time, tracking its effectiveness.
Investigate how athletes and performers use self-regulation strategies in high-pressure situations — applying one technique to a physical activity context.

modes.reason: Self-regulation in practice requires integrating trigger recognition (node 1) with deliberate strategy selection. Students who have practised both separately need opportunities to apply the full sequence — notice the trigger → apply the strategy — in scenario or real contexts.

No single self-regulation strategy works in all situations. Students benefit from practising multiple strategies (breathing, movement, self-talk, seeking support) and developing personal knowledge of what works for them.

descriptors.title: Consent strategies
descriptors.description: rehearse and refine strategies for seeking, giving and denying permission respectfully and describe situations when permission is required
descriptors.knowledge: Students have practised strategies for seeking, giving or denying permission respectfully (AC9HP2P04). They have practised basic consent strategies but have not yet rehearsed them in more complex contexts including online environments and situations involving personal safety.
descriptors.endpoint: Students rehearse and refine strategies for seeking, giving and denying permission respectfully, and describe situations when permission is required.

nodes.label: Practising consent strategies — giving and seeking
nodes.checkpoint: Students can practise and refine strategies for seeking and giving consent in different situations.
criteria: Demonstrates a strategy for asking for consent in a scenario.
Demonstrates a strategy for giving or denying consent clearly and respectfully.
Identifies a situation where seeking permission is required.
nodes.hinge_reason: Practised consent strategies are the operational foundation for all unsafe situation responses in node 2. Students who have not rehearsed clear consent language cannot access the more complex safety response skills that follow.

width.minimum: Practise at least one strategy for seeking consent and one for giving or denying consent in a described scenario.
width.typical: Rehearse and compare strategies for seeking, giving and denying consent across varied contexts (personal space, sharing photos, physical touch); evaluate which strategies are most clear and respectful.
wider: Explore how consent applies in digital contexts (e.g. photo sharing, tagging, personal information) and practise consent strategies appropriate for online interactions.
Investigate how consent is taught in different cultural contexts and discuss what is similar and different about the principles involved.

modes.reason: Consent strategy language needs to be rehearsed to automaticity — not just known conceptually. Role-play with explicit language scaffolding ('I'd like to..., is that okay?', 'I don't want that', 'Let me check first') is the most effective practice format.

nodes.label: Responding to unsafe situations and boundary violations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify actions they can take when they or others are unsafe — including online situations — and practise response strategies.
criteria: Identifies at least two actions they can take when someone acts without their consent.
Applies at least one response strategy appropriately in a scenario.
Identifies who they would go to for help in an unsafe situation.

width.minimum: Identify at least two actions they can take when something happens without their permission or consent, including at least one online scenario.
width.typical: Explore and practise a range of response strategies for different unsafe situations — online and offline — including saying no, leaving, reporting and seeking help; discuss which response is appropriate in each context.
wider: Analyse scenarios involving increasingly complex consent situations (e.g. someone posts an embarrassing photo online without permission, a trusted person crosses a boundary) and evaluate which response strategies apply.
Develop a personal safety plan that identifies trusted adults, response strategies and reporting options for different types of unsafe situations.

modes.reason: Responding to unsafe situations integrates consent understanding (node 1) with help-seeking skills (AC9HP4P08). Scenario-based practice that requires students to identify the situation type and select an appropriate response builds the integration needed.

Online and offline unsafe situations require different response strategies. Students who have only practised face-to-face responses are less prepared for the digital contexts where boundary violations are increasingly likely.

descriptors.title: Protective behaviours online and offline
descriptors.description: describe and apply protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies in a range of online and offline situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students have identified and demonstrated protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies to help themselves and others stay safe (AC9HP2P05). They can identify and demonstrate strategies in familiar contexts but have not yet applied them across the full range of online and offline situations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe and apply protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies in a range of online and offline situations.

nodes.label: Warning signs — physical, emotional and external
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe warning signs (physical, emotional and external) that help them know if they are safe or unsafe.
criteria: Names at least two warning signs from at least two different categories (physical, emotional, external).
Explains what each warning sign might indicate about a situation.
Describes what they would do after noticing a warning sign.
nodes.hinge_reason: Recognising warning signs is the precondition for all protective behaviour and help-seeking. Students who cannot identify that they are unsafe cannot access or apply the strategies in the subsequent nodes.

width.minimum: Identify at least two warning signs (across physical, emotional and/or external categories) that indicate an unsafe situation.
width.typical: Describe a range of physical, emotional and external warning signs across different unsafe situations; explain what makes each sign a reliable indicator of risk.
wider: Investigate how animals and humans use similar instinctive warning signals (physical responses like increased heart rate or hair standing up) as protective mechanisms, and connect this to the body's natural safety system.
Explore how cultural backgrounds influence what is recognised as an unsafe situation and what warning signs are prioritised — discussing how this affects protective behaviour.

modes.reason: Students need a classification system for warning signs (physical body responses, emotional feelings, external environmental signals) to organise their recognition and move from general unease to actionable assessment. Explicit categorisation practice with examples builds this.

nodes.label: Protective behaviours across situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine protective behaviours to stay safe in different situations, including near water or roads, in the park, online and when someone makes them feel uncomfortable.
criteria: Describes a protective behaviour relevant to at least two different contexts.
Explains how each behaviour reduces risk in that context.
Identifies one behaviour they already use and one they could strengthen.

width.minimum: Describe at least one protective behaviour relevant to at least two different contexts (e.g. near water, online).
width.typical: Describe and discuss protective behaviours across a full range of situations — water, roads, parks, online, personal safety — identifying what makes each behaviour protective and how it reduces risk.
wider: Indicate safe places and trusted people on a local map for their own neighbourhood, creating a personalised safety reference.
Examine protective behaviours used by characters in texts or media across varied situations, evaluating the effectiveness of each and identifying alternatives.

modes.reason: Protective behaviours look significantly different across contexts — water safety has different requirements from online safety, which differs again from personal space safety. Students need exposure across contexts to build situation-appropriate protective behaviour.

nodes.label: Help-seeking strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply help-seeking strategies to negotiate positive outcomes when challenging situations arise, including online contexts.
criteria: Identifies at least one help-seeking strategy for a specific challenging situation.
Explains how the strategy would help achieve a positive outcome.
Names at least one trusted adult or reporting option for online and offline unsafe situations.

width.minimum: Identify at least one help-seeking strategy for a challenging online or offline situation and explain how it would lead to a positive outcome.
width.typical: Identify and apply help-seeking strategies across varied challenging situations; discuss what makes each strategy appropriate in different contexts and how to access trusted support.
wider: Design a personal help-seeking plan that identifies trusted adults, contact options and reporting pathways for different types of unsafe situations — online and offline.
Practise navigating an online reporting or help-seeking process using a simulated or guided environment, building familiarity with digital help-seeking tools.

modes.reason: Help-seeking integrates warning sign recognition (node 1), situation-specific protective behaviour (node 2) and knowledge of trusted adults and reporting pathways. The integration — knowing when and how to seek help in a specific situation — is the operational skill.

descriptors.title: Health information and decisions
descriptors.description: interpret the nature and intention of health information and messages, and reflect on how they influence personal decisions and behaviours
descriptors.knowledge: Students have investigated health messages and practices in their community and discussed their purposes (AC9HP2P06). They can identify health messages and discuss purposes but have not yet interpreted the nature and intention of messages or reflected on how they influence decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret the nature and intention of health information and messages and reflect on how they influence personal decisions and behaviours.

nodes.label: Sources of health information and accuracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can access different sources of health information and examine the accuracy of those sources.
criteria: Identifies at least two different sources of health information.
Applies at least one criterion for evaluating source accuracy or trustworthiness.
Explains why one source is more or less reliable than another.
nodes.hinge_reason: Source evaluation is the prerequisite for interpreting health messages. Students who accept all sources uncritically cannot meaningfully interpret intention — they take messages at face value rather than as authored communications with specific purposes.

width.minimum: Identify at least two different sources of health information and examine one source to assess whether it appears accurate and trustworthy.
width.typical: Access and compare health information from multiple sources (brochures, websites, TV, advertisements, food labels); examine the accuracy and trustworthiness of each; identify markers of reliable health information.
wider: Investigate how advertising and commercial interests can bias health information — examining a food or health product advertisement and identifying what health claims are made and whether they are supported.
Compare health information about the same topic from two sources of different trustworthiness (e.g. a health authority website vs a social media post) and explain the difference.

modes.reason: Source evaluation requires explicit criteria (who made this, why, what evidence do they use, what do they want me to do). A simple trustworthiness checklist used repeatedly across different sources builds the evaluative habit.

nodes.label: Food and nutrition health messages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine health messages about food and nutrition from different sources and explore choices and behaviours conveyed.
criteria: Identifies a health message about food or nutrition from a specific source.
Describes the behaviour or choice the message promotes.
Discusses whether the message aligns with evidence-based nutrition advice.

width.minimum: Identify at least one health message about food or nutrition from a source, and describe the choice or behaviour it is encouraging.
width.typical: Examine food and nutrition health messages from multiple sources; compare the choices and behaviours promoted; discuss whether messages are aligned with evidence-based nutrition advice.
wider: Audit the health messages present in a school canteen menu, supermarket shelf display or breakfast cereal packaging — identifying what behaviours are being promoted and who benefits.
Investigate nutritional information on food labels from a range of products and discuss what information is present, what is emphasised and what might be misleading.

modes.reason: Nutrition messages appear in very different contexts (advertising, food labelling, health promotion, school canteen) that serve different interests and have different effects. Exposure across contexts builds richer critical literacy.

nodes.label: Influence of health messages on decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the level of influence health messages from different sources may have on their health decisions.
criteria: Identifies a health message that has influenced one of their health-related decisions.
Reflects on whether the message came from a trustworthy source.
Describes how they would evaluate a new health message before acting on it.

width.minimum: Reflect on one health decision they have made and identify at least one health message that influenced it.
width.typical: Investigate how health messages from different sources (peer, media, family, advertising) influence a range of personal health decisions; reflect on how to make informed decisions that critically weigh these influences.
wider: Develop a personal framework for evaluating health information before acting on it — identifying the questions they would ask and the sources they would trust.
Examine how a specific health campaign was designed to influence behaviour and evaluate its likely effectiveness for different audiences.

modes.reason: This node integrates source evaluation (node 1) and message interpretation (node 2) with personal decision-making. The teaching focus is the transfer from critical analysis of messages to students' own health decisions — bridging the two with personal reflection is essential.
Students need to move from 'this influenced me' to 'this influenced me, and here is whether that was appropriate'. A structured decision-making reflection format builds the metacognitive layer.

descriptors.title: Health and wellbeing behaviours
descriptors.description: investigate and apply behaviours that contribute to their own and others' health, safety, relationships and wellbeing
descriptors.knowledge: Students have investigated health messages and practices in their community and discussed their purposes (AC9HP2P06) and identified and demonstrated protective behaviours (AC9HP2P05). They understand health messages and basic safety behaviours but have not yet investigated or applied the full range of health behaviours across nutrition, physical activity, mental health and safety.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate and apply behaviours that contribute to their own and others' health, safety, relationships and wellbeing.

nodes.label: Safe storage of medications and substances
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how medications and other substances can be stored safely in the home and at school.
criteria: Identifies at least two rules for safely storing medications or substances.
Explains the reason for at least one rule.
Applies the rules to identify a safe storage scenario.

width.minimum: Identify at least two safety rules for storing medications or substances safely and explain why each rule matters.
width.typical: Investigate how different types of substances (medications, cleaning products, personal care items) require safe storage, and explain the safety rationale for each.
wider: Examine how household product labelling conveys safety storage information (e.g. 'keep out of reach of children', 'store below 25°C') and investigate what happens when storage instructions are not followed.
Explore how schools manage medication storage for students and discuss the safety procedures involved.

modes.reason: Safe storage rules are best understood when the risk-consequence logic is explicit: 'we store it this way because if we didn't, X could happen'. Connecting rules to consequences builds more durable health and safety understanding than rule-memorisation alone.

nodes.label: Nutrition and healthy eating patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore the benefits of eating patterns that reflect the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and investigate nutritional information about foods.
criteria: Names the main food groups in the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating.
Describes at least one health benefit associated with eating from each food group.
Reads basic nutritional information from a food label or database.

width.minimum: Identify the main food groups in the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and describe at least one benefit of eating a variety of foods from different groups.
width.typical: Explore how eating patterns aligned with the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating contribute to health; investigate nutritional information on food labels or in food databases; discuss choices and their health implications.
wider: Compare their own typical daily food intake against the Guide to Healthy Eating recommendations and identify areas of alignment and areas for change.
Investigate nutritional information from a range of foods and examine what information on food labels (ingredients, nutrients, serving sizes) is most useful for making healthy choices.

modes.reason: Nutrition understanding deepens when students connect the Guide to Healthy Eating to real food contexts — their own eating, school canteen offerings, food labelling, and cultural food practices. Broad context exposure makes the recommendations tangible.

nodes.label: Mental health, belonging and connection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss the importance of a sense of belonging and connection in promoting mental health and wellbeing.
criteria: Explains what 'belonging' and 'connection' mean in their own words.
Describes how belonging or connection affects a person's mental health.
Identifies one action they could take to strengthen belonging in their class or community.

width.minimum: Describe what belonging and connection mean and explain how they contribute to mental health and wellbeing.
width.typical: Discuss how belonging and connection in different contexts (family, school, community, sport) promote mental health; identify actions individuals and groups can take to strengthen connection.
wider: Investigate how physical activity participation contributes to social connection and belonging, and explore examples where sport or community activity has improved wellbeing.
Explore mindfulness and meditation practices as mental health strategies, practising at least one technique regularly and reflecting on its effects.

modes.reason: The link between belonging, connection and mental health is not intuitive for primary students — it requires explicit concept building. A concrete discussion of what it feels like to belong (and not to belong) grounds the abstract mental health relationship.

nodes.label: Sustainability and health behaviours
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate ways to change their behaviours to support both their own health and the sustainability of the Earth's systems.
criteria: Identifies at least one behaviour that benefits both their health and the environment.
Explains the health benefit and the environmental benefit of that behaviour.
Proposes one realistic change they could make to a current habit.

width.minimum: Identify at least one behaviour change that would benefit both their health and the environment (e.g. choosing sustainable, healthy foods; reducing food waste; active transport).
width.typical: Investigate multiple health behaviours that also support sustainability — food choices, waste reduction, active transport, school gardens — discussing how individual actions connect to broader environmental and community health.
wider: Design and implement a small sustainability and health project (e.g. a classroom composting system or school garden contribution) and reflect on its health, social and environmental benefits.
Investigate how community fruit and vegetable gardens support both health and sustainability — exploring examples from Australian communities including First Nations food practices.

modes.reason: This node connects personal health behaviours (nutrition, activity) with environmental responsibility — an integration that requires students to hold both domains simultaneously. Explicit 'dual-benefit' framing (good for me AND good for the environment) supports the integration.

descriptors.title: Adapt and modify movement skills
descriptors.description: adapt and modify movement skills across a variety of situations
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students refined and applied fundamental movement skills in new movement situations (AC9HP4M01) and applied and adapted movement strategies to achieve movement outcomes (AC9HP4M02). They can execute core locomotor, stability and object control skills and have begun adapting these to new contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students adapt and modify movement skills across a variety of situations, adjusting technique in response to changing movement demands.

nodes.label: Identifying when adaptation is needed
criteria: Can name the specific situational cue that requires a skill change (e.g. defender closing, surface change, transition between skills)
Can describe, verbally or in writing, what adaptation is needed before attempting it
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot read the situational cue will make adaptations based on habit rather than demand, making the next nodes — execution of the adaptation and evaluation of its effectiveness — meaningless. Phase collapse: every downstream node assumes perceptual-reading as a foundation.

width.minimum: Identify at least two situations in a familiar activity where a movement skill needs to be adapted and describe what needs to change.

modes.reason: Students practise naming the cue → response pairing explicitly before physical execution. Prompt: 'What changed in the situation? What does that mean you need to do differently?' Builds the perceptual habit.

nodes.label: Executing adaptations across locomotor and stability skills
criteria: Executes the adapted skill with recognisable technique (not just stopping and restarting)
Demonstrates at least one transition between two different movement skills in a continuous sequence
nodes.hinge_reason: Locomotor and stability adaptations are the physical foundation for object control adaptations in N3. Students who cannot adapt movement under their own body weight will not be able to coordinate object control adaptations alongside movement.

width.minimum: Perform at least two adapted locomotor or stability sequences in a movement situation, demonstrating a change in technique in response to a situational cue (e.g. dodge and feint, leaping to balancing).

modes.reason: Repetitive practice across multiple situations until transitions are smooth and automatic. Focus on precision of the transition moment — the point where one skill ends and another begins.

Vary the movement contexts systematically: evasion games (dodge/feint), gymnastics sequences (static to dynamic balances), outdoor traversal (uneven terrain). Each context demands a different adaptation logic, building genuine transfer rather than situation-specific habit.

nodes.label: Adapting object control skills
criteria: Applies a familiar object control skill in a new game or activity context
Adjusts the technique of the skill (force, angle, timing) to suit the new context's demands

width.minimum: Adapt at least one object control skill (kicking, striking or throwing) to a different game or activity than the one in which it was originally learned.

modes.reason: Expose students to the same base skill across distinct activity contexts: kicking in football vs kicking in a target game; throwing in cricket-based activities vs throwing in athletic games. Each shift in context surfaces a different adjustment requirement.

nodes.label: Adapting across integrated movement situations
criteria: Demonstrates adaptation of at least two skill types (e.g. locomotor + object control) within the same movement situation
Responds to changing conditions mid-activity without stopping to restart

width.minimum: Participate in a complex movement activity (game or sequence) that requires adapting at least two different skill types in response to changing conditions.

modes.reason: Complex game or sequence situations that require students to read and respond across multiple skill types simultaneously. This is the full descriptor demand — the integration of adapt and modify across a variety of situations.

descriptors.title: Transfer movement strategies
descriptors.description: transfer familiar movement strategies to different movement situations
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students applied and adapted movement strategies to achieve movement outcomes (AC9HP4M02). They have experience identifying strategies in familiar activities and can adapt skills at a technical level. They have not yet explicitly analysed why a strategy transfers or evaluated transfer effectiveness.
descriptors.endpoint: Students transfer familiar movement strategies to different movement situations and evaluate the effectiveness of the transfer.

nodes.label: Identifying transferable strategies
criteria: Can name a strategy (not just a skill) — e.g. 'press defence', 'zone defence', 'counterbalance', not just 'defend' or 'balance'
Can articulate why the strategy might transfer — the principle, not just the surface similarity
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate strategy with skill will attempt to transfer movements rather than principles — this leads to unsuccessful and confused transfer attempts. Downstream nodes require students to explain and evaluate transfer; both demand the strategy/skill distinction.

width.minimum: Name at least one movement strategy from a familiar activity and describe the underlying principle that might make it work in a different activity.

modes.reason: Explicit discussion: 'What is the strategy? What problem does it solve? Could the same problem appear in a different game?' Separating 'what I do' from 'why it works' is the conceptual move this node depends on.

nodes.label: Attempting and demonstrating transfer
criteria: Applies the strategy in the new context (not just names it) — the physical execution is visible
Can describe at least one adjustment made to the strategy to fit the new context

width.minimum: Apply at least one movement strategy from a familiar activity in a new activity or game context, with a description of how the strategy was modified to fit the new situation.

modes.reason: Provide transfer challenges across game categories (e.g. an invasion game strategy applied to a net game; a balance strategy from gymnastics applied to a natural terrain traversal). Each new context tests a different dimension of the strategy's transferability.

nodes.label: Evaluating transfer effectiveness
criteria: References a specific criterion (not just 'it worked' or 'it didn't work')
Proposes at least one concrete modification that would improve the transfer

width.minimum: Evaluate whether a transferred strategy was effective using at least one agreed criterion, and explain what modifications would improve its effectiveness.

modes.reason: Co-develop simple evaluation criteria with the class before trialling transfer. Return to criteria after practice to structure the evaluation. The criteria scaffold separates 'effective' from 'successful outcome' (a team can win without a transferred strategy being effective).
This node integrates the full descriptor demand: students have transferred a strategy and now judge it. The evaluation feeds back into further adaptation cycles.

descriptors.title: Movement concepts applied to outcomes
descriptors.description: investigate how different movement concepts related to effort, space, time, objects and people can be applied to improve movement outcomes
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students demonstrated how movement concepts related to effort, space, time, objects and people can be applied when performing movement sequences (AC9HP4M03). They can identify and apply individual movement concepts in structured sequences but have not systematically investigated how manipulating multiple concepts improves outcomes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how movement concepts related to effort, space, time, objects and people can be applied and combined to improve movement outcomes.

nodes.label: Isolating and manipulating individual concepts
criteria: Can identify which concept was manipulated (e.g. 'I changed the speed/force/direction')
Can describe the effect the change had on the movement outcome (e.g. more accurate, less controlled, harder for the receiver)
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot isolate a single concept and articulate its effect, the subsequent investigation of how multiple concepts interact to improve outcomes is inaccessible. The investigative logic of N2 and N3 depends on understanding single-variable effects first.

width.minimum: Modify one movement concept in a movement activity and observe and describe the effect on the movement outcome.

modes.reason: One-variable experiment design: 'Keep everything the same except X. What happened?' Builds the investigative habit of isolating variables before combining them.

nodes.label: Combining concepts to improve a specific outcome
criteria: Applies two identifiable concepts simultaneously (not sequentially)
Can explain how each concept contributed to the improved outcome

width.minimum: Apply at least two movement concepts together in a movement activity and describe how their combination improved the outcome.

modes.reason: Investigate combinations across different movement contexts: force+timing in a throwing/striking context; space+people in a game context; flow+levels in a sequence context. Different contexts surface different concept combinations as most productive.

nodes.label: Systematic investigation and improvement
criteria: Tests more than one approach before drawing conclusions
Bases the 'more effective' judgement on observed outcome rather than preference

width.minimum: Investigate and test at least two different concept combinations for a movement outcome, describe what was found, and explain which approach was more effective and why.

modes.reason: Students conduct a mini-investigation cycle: identify outcome goal → trial combinations → observe → refine. This is the full descriptor demand — 'investigate how concepts can be applied to improve outcomes' — not just demonstrate or apply.

descriptors.title: Body's reaction to physical activity intensity
descriptors.description: participate in physical activities to investigate the body's reaction to different levels of intensity
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students participated in physical activities to explore how their body feels and described how regular physical activity helps the body stay healthy (AC9HP4M04). They can describe subjective body sensations during activity but have not yet categorised intensity levels or measured physiological responses.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in physical activities of varying intensity and investigate the body's physiological and practical reactions, categorising activities by intensity level.

nodes.label: Identifying and categorising intensity levels
criteria: Can distinguish between at least two intensity categories using a measurable or observable body response
Uses evidence (measurement or observation) rather than subjective feeling alone to assign a category
nodes.hinge_reason: The category labels (low/moderate/high) are the conceptual scaffold for everything downstream — warm-up/cool-down design and goal-setting both require students to think in intensity terms. Students who only use subjective feeling cannot design or evaluate intensity-based routines.

width.minimum: Participate in activities of at least two different intensities; measure or observe at least one body response (e.g. breathing rate, heart rate) and use it to categorise each activity.

modes.reason: Structured data collection: record at least one measure at each intensity level. Discuss how body responses change with intensity. Build the low/moderate/high schema explicitly before applying it.

nodes.label: Connecting intensity to warm-up and cool-down
criteria: Explains the purpose of warm-up or cool-down in terms of intensity transition (not just 'to prevent injury' as a rehearsed phrase)
Can describe at least one specific feature of the routine that addresses the body's response

width.minimum: Participate in or evaluate a warm-up or cool-down routine and explain how it relates to managing the body's response to changing intensity levels.

modes.reason: Design warm-ups/cool-downs for different activity types. A warm-up before gymnastics differs from one before a running activity. The design task surfaces different intensity management thinking across contexts.

nodes.label: Designing personal activity for health and fitness goals
criteria: Names a specific goal (not just 'get fitter')
Justifies the intensity choices in the plan in terms of body response and goal

width.minimum: Describe or model a physical activity plan that uses intensity variation to support a named health or fitness goal.

modes.reason: This integrates investigation of body responses, intensity categories, and warm-up/cool-down knowledge into purposeful activity planning — the full descriptor demand.

descriptors.title: Physical activity in natural settings
descriptors.description: participate in physical activities that enhance health and wellbeing in natural and outdoor settings, and analyse the steps and resources needed to promote participation
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students participated in physical activities in natural and outdoor settings to examine factors that can influence their own and others' participation (AC9HP4M05). They can identify participation barriers and enablers at a descriptive level but have not yet analysed the steps and resources needed to actively promote participation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in physical activities in natural and outdoor settings and analyse the steps and resources needed to promote participation for themselves and others.

nodes.label: Connecting outdoor activity to health and wellbeing
criteria: Identifies the specific contribution of the outdoor/natural context (not just that activity is good for health)
Can reference at least one dimension of wellbeing (physical, mental, social, or connection to place)
nodes.hinge_reason: The promotion analysis in N2 depends on understanding why outdoor participation matters — students who cannot articulate the outdoor-specific benefit will produce generic 'exercise is good' promotion strategies that don't address access or connection to natural environments.

width.minimum: Participate in an outdoor physical activity and describe at least one way the natural or outdoor setting enhanced the health or wellbeing benefit beyond what an indoor activity would provide.

modes.reason: Compare: same physical activity indoors vs outdoors — what changes? Connects lived experience of the activity to the health/wellbeing concept and builds the outdoor-specific rationale needed for N2.

nodes.label: Analysing access and participation factors
criteria: Identifies both a barrier and an enabler (not just one type)
Proposes a concrete step or resource — not a vague 'we should encourage more people'

width.minimum: Identify at least two factors that influence access to or participation in an outdoor physical activity, and describe what steps or resources would help address one barrier.

modes.reason: Analyse participation factors for different natural settings and community contexts: a skate park, a bushwalking trail, a surf beach, a local park. The resource and step requirements differ across contexts, deepening analytical thinking.

nodes.label: Proposing promotion strategies
criteria: Strategy addresses a specific identified barrier (not a general appeal)
Includes both steps (what to do) and resources (what is needed)

width.minimum: Propose at least one strategy to increase participation in an outdoor physical activity, explaining the steps involved and the resources required.

modes.reason: Integrates health/wellbeing rationale and access analysis into a promotion proposal — the full descriptor demand of 'analyse the steps and resources needed to promote participation'.

descriptors.title: Strategies to increase activity and reduce sedentary behaviour
descriptors.description: propose and explain strategies to increase physical activity and reduce sedentary behaviour levels in their lives
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students explored recommendations about physical activity and sedentary behaviours and discussed strategies to achieve the recommendations (AC9HP4M06). They know that guidelines exist and can discuss strategies at a general level but have not yet proposed and explained strategies grounded in their own specific life contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students propose and explain strategies to increase physical activity and reduce sedentary behaviour in their own lives, with reference to health benefits and social and mental wellbeing.

nodes.label: Understanding the activity-sedentary balance
criteria: Correctly distinguishes physical activity from sedentary behaviour (e.g. light movement does not automatically mean 'active')
Connects sedentary behaviour specifically to a health consequence — not just 'it's bad for you'
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who lack the activity/sedentary distinction will propose strategies that address activity in isolation (do more exercise) without addressing sedentary reduction — the descriptor requires both. Strategies that only increase activity without reducing sedentary time may not achieve the health outcomes students are proposing.

width.minimum: Describe the difference between physical activity and sedentary behaviour, and explain at least one specific health or wellbeing consequence of each.

modes.reason: Case study or time-audit analysis: map a typical day and classify each block as active, sedentary, or light movement. This builds the conceptual distinction through their own lived experience rather than abstract definition.

nodes.label: Examining benefits across health dimensions
criteria: Names a social or mental wellbeing benefit specifically (not a physical health benefit reworded)
Connects the benefit to strategy design — e.g. 'because it also helps with social connection, we could design activities that involve others'

width.minimum: Describe at least one benefit of physical activity for mental or social wellbeing (not physical health) and explain how this benefit might influence strategy choices.

modes.reason: Research local physical activity options and their social/mental dimensions — community sport, lunchtime activities, active transport, nature-based activity. Each offers different social and mental wellbeing mechanisms.

nodes.label: Proposing and explaining personalised strategies
criteria: Strategies are specific to the student's life context, not generic ('go for a walk' alone is insufficient)
Includes at least one strategy addressing sedentary behaviour specifically (not just adding activity)
Explains why the strategy is realistic for them — acknowledges their actual constraints

width.minimum: Propose at least two strategies for their own life — one to increase physical activity and one to reduce sedentary behaviour — and explain why each is realistic and likely to be effective for them specifically.

modes.reason: Integrates the activity/sedentary distinction, multi-dimensional benefits, and personal context into proposed strategies. This is the full descriptor demand — propose and explain strategies in their own lives.

descriptors.title: Predict and test movement strategies
descriptors.description: predict and test the effectiveness of applying different skills and strategies in a range of movement situations
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students applied creative thinking when designing movement sequences and solving movement problems (AC9HP4M07). They have experience generating and trying movement solutions but have not yet explicitly predicted outcomes before testing or used agreed criteria to evaluate effectiveness.
descriptors.endpoint: Students predict and test the effectiveness of different skills and strategies across a range of movement situations, refining solutions based on systematic testing.

nodes.label: Forming a prediction before testing
criteria: Makes a prediction before (not after) the test
Prediction is based on a reason (prior experience, logic, observation) — not random
nodes.hinge_reason: Without pre-test prediction, the testing phase reduces to undirected trial-and-error. Prediction requires students to articulate their reasoning before physical testing — this is the cognitive load that distinguishes this descriptor from lower-band versions. Students who skip to testing cannot benefit from the comparison of predicted vs actual outcome.

width.minimum: Before testing a movement solution, make a prediction about its likely effectiveness and state the reason for the prediction.

modes.reason: Establish a predict-test-compare routine: students write or state their prediction and reason before any physical test. Debrief compares prediction to outcome explicitly. This habit must be formed before the criteria evaluation in N2.

nodes.label: Co-developing and applying evaluation criteria
criteria: Can name the criterion being applied (e.g. 'did it create space?', 'did it maintain balance?', 'was it completed within the time limit?')
Evaluates outcome against the criterion rather than personal preference

width.minimum: Use at least one agreed criterion to evaluate whether a tested movement solution was effective.

modes.reason: Apply criteria-based evaluation across different movement situation types: game/tactical situations, outdoor challenges, creative movement sequences. Different situations require different criteria — this variety builds evaluative flexibility.

nodes.label: Systematic testing and refining
criteria: Tests more than one solution before concluding
Refines the better solution (doesn't just stop at 'this one worked') or explains why it cannot be further improved

width.minimum: Test at least two different solutions for the same movement challenge, evaluate both against criteria, and explain which was more effective and why.

modes.reason: The full predict-test-refine cycle across a range of movement situations. Integrates prediction, criteria application and systematic refinement — the complete descriptor demand.

descriptors.title: Devise game modifications for fair play
descriptors.description: devise and test alternative rules and game modifications to support fair play and inclusive participation
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students applied rules and scoring systems to promote fair play when participating or designing physical activities (AC9HP4M08). They understand that rules exist to enable fair play and can apply existing rules. They have not yet devised their own rule modifications or tested them for inclusive effect.
descriptors.endpoint: Students devise and test alternative rules and game modifications, evaluating whether they support fair play and inclusive participation.

nodes.label: Recognising unfairness and exclusion
criteria: Identifies a game-structural cause (not just 'someone was mean') — a rule, scoring system, court size, team composition, or other structural feature
Distinguishes between unfairness (one side has a structural advantage) and exclusion (some participants are structurally unable to participate)
nodes.hinge_reason: Rule modification proposals that don't target the structural cause will be surface changes that don't address the identified problem. Students who cannot identify the structural cause cannot propose targeted modifications. All downstream nodes depend on this diagnosis.

width.minimum: Identify at least one game situation in which a rule or game condition creates unfairness or exclusion, and explain what feature of the game is causing the problem.

modes.reason: Analyse game situations through a structural lens: 'What is the rule or condition causing this? Would changing that rule fix it?' Separates diagnosis from remedy — both must be explicit before modification proposals are made.

nodes.label: Devising and proposing modifications
criteria: Modification is specific and implementable (not vague: 'make it fairer')
Explicitly links the modification back to the structural cause identified in N1

width.minimum: Propose at least one specific rule or game modification that addresses an identified fairness or inclusion problem, and explain how it targets the structural cause.

modes.reason: Apply game modification thinking across different game types and cultural contexts. Investigating games such as Inkanyi (cooperative, no winners) or Barambah gimbe provides structurally different models of inclusion that expand students' conception of what fair play can look like.

nodes.label: Testing and evaluating modifications
criteria: Tests the modification in practice (not just proposes it theoretically)
Evaluates against fairness or inclusion specifically — identifies whether the structural problem was reduced

width.minimum: Test at least one proposed modification in a game situation and evaluate whether it improved fairness or inclusion using a specific criterion.

modes.reason: Brings together structural diagnosis, targeted modification, and practical testing into the full devise-test cycle the descriptor requires.

descriptors.title: Positive group and team participation
descriptors.description: participate positively in groups and teams by contributing to group activities, encouraging others and negotiating roles and responsibilities
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students performed a range of roles in respectful ways to achieve successful outcomes in group or team movement activities (AC9HP4M09). They can take on assigned roles respectfully but have not yet explicitly practised negotiating roles or using specific verbal communication strategies (reflective listening, assertive communication) in group movement contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate positively in groups and teams, contributing to activities, encouraging others, and negotiating roles and responsibilities in movement situations.

nodes.label: Encouraging and supporting others
criteria: Behaviours are specific and observed (not self-reported only)
Can describe how the encouraging behaviour affected another person's participation or confidence

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two specific encouraging behaviours during a group movement activity and describe the effect on the group's participation.

modes.reason: Establish the base positive participation habit through repeated practice across different group activities. Encouragement needs to become automatic before negotiation skills (N2) can be practised in the same activity without cognitive overload.

nodes.label: Negotiating roles and responsibilities
criteria: Can name the communication strategy being used (assertive communication or reflective listening)
Can describe a situation where the strategy was used and what effect it had
nodes.hinge_reason: Negotiation is the most complex interpersonal demand in this descriptor and is a direct precursor to the conflict/disagreement resolution demanded in this and subsequent year bands. Students who cannot negotiate roles will default to avoidance or conflict, making positive group participation in complex tasks unsustainable.

width.minimum: Participate in a group activity where roles need to be negotiated; demonstrate at least one use of assertive communication or reflective listening during the negotiation.

modes.reason: Explicitly teach assertive communication and reflective listening as named strategies with examples. Role-play negotiation scenarios before applying in live activity situations — the language of the strategy matters for subsequent reflection.

Apply negotiation across different movement contexts: sport team role allocation, group outdoor challenge task division, small-group movement sequence design. Different contexts create different negotiation pressures and build transferable skill.

nodes.label: Contributing positively across the full group experience
criteria: Demonstrates all three elements — contribution, encouragement, negotiation — within the same group activity
Participation is sustained across the activity, not only at the beginning or end

width.minimum: Participate in a group activity and demonstrate contribution, encouragement and negotiation across different phases of the activity.

modes.reason: Full group activity requiring all three participation elements. This is the complete descriptor demand — positive participation is integrated, not compartmentalised.

descriptors.title: Identities influenced by people and places
descriptors.description: explain how identities can be influenced by people and places, and how we can create positive self-identities
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students described how choices and actions can be influenced by stereotypes (AC9HP4P03). They understand that external forces can shape behaviour and choices. They have not yet explicitly analysed how identities are formed through relationships with specific people and connections to place, or how to actively create positive self-identities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how identities are influenced by people and places, and describe strategies for creating positive self-identities.

nodes.label: Understanding identity as shaped by relationships
criteria: Identifies specific types of relational influence (role model, peer, family, cultural figure) rather than just 'other people'
Can explain the mechanism of influence — how the relationship shapes identity, not just that it does
nodes.hinge_reason: The 'create positive self-identities' part of the descriptor requires students to understand what they are acting on. Students who have only a surface understanding of relational influence will propose generic identity-building strategies without understanding the mechanisms they are working with.

width.minimum: Name at least two types of people or relationships that influence identity and explain how each contributes to the way individuals see themselves.

modes.reason: Map relational influences explicitly: who are the key people, what do they model or communicate, how does that shape the individual's sense of self? The mechanism of influence (modelling, messaging, belonging) is the conceptual content.

Examine identity influence across diverse cultural and community contexts: First Nations connections to Country/Place; family and cultural practices for Australians of Asian heritage; sporting role models; social media influencers. Each reveals different mechanisms and prevents convergence on a single cultural norm of identity formation.

nodes.label: Understanding identity as shaped by place
criteria: Identifies a specific place relationship (not 'where you live' generically)
Can explain how the place connection contributes to identity — belonging, cultural meaning, history, or relationship with the natural environment

width.minimum: Describe at least one way that connection to a place (community, Country, special location) can influence a person's identity.

modes.reason: Investigate place-based identity across contexts: First Nations Australian connections to Country/Place (including cultural group, clan, Country); students' own community place connections; how place connections change during transitions like moving school or neighbourhood.

nodes.label: Creating positive self-identities
criteria: Strategy is specific and actionable — not 'believe in yourself'
Links back to the relational or place mechanisms identified in N1 or N2

width.minimum: Describe at least one strategy for creating or maintaining a positive self-identity and explain how it engages with the relational or place influences on identity.

modes.reason: Integrates understanding of people-influence, place-influence, and cultural diversity in identity formation into a personal strategy framework. The full descriptor demand: explain influence and how to create positive self-identities.

descriptors.title: Managing changes and transitions including puberty
descriptors.description: investigate resources and strategies to manage changes and transitions, including changes associated with puberty
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students planned, rehearsed and reflected on strategies to cope with different changes and transitions they experience (AC9HP4P02). They have experience with strategies for change at a general level. This descriptor specifically includes puberty as a named change type, representing a significant new content area.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate a range of resources and strategies to manage changes and transitions, including the physical and social changes associated with puberty.

nodes.label: Understanding puberty as a change and transition
criteria: Describes changes accurately and without unnecessary value judgement
Acknowledges that timing, experience and expression of puberty varies between individuals
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who lack accurate, non-stigmatising understanding of puberty cannot engage with strategies to manage it or with the resources available. Misconceptions or shame-laden framings at this node will undermine every subsequent node in this descriptor and adjacent descriptors about consent and relationships.

width.minimum: Describe at least three physical changes associated with puberty and explain that puberty experiences differ between individuals.

modes.reason: Accurate, calm, normalising presentation of puberty information. Students need to develop fluency with the vocabulary and concepts in a low-stakes environment before engaging with management strategies. Misconceptions should be addressed here, not later.

Examine puberty in diverse cultural contexts: First Nations Australian rites of passage connected to puberty; how different families acknowledge developmental stages; the range of products and resources available for managing physical changes. Cultural breadth normalises diversity of experience.

nodes.label: Identifying resources and strategies
criteria: Identifies resources across more than one type (physical products AND social/support resources)
Can explain the purpose of each resource in terms of what aspect of the change it addresses

width.minimum: Identify at least two types of resources or strategies available for managing puberty changes, and explain the purpose of each.

modes.reason: Survey resource types: physical products for managing menstruation and other changes; trusted support people; reliable information sources; strategies for managing changing social roles and responsibilities. Breadth across resource types ensures students aren't left with only one type of management strategy.

nodes.label: Personalising strategies for managing transitions
criteria: Acknowledges personal choice and individual difference without prescribing a single approach
Can identify at least one factor that might influence which resources or strategies a person chooses

width.minimum: Describe how a person might make choices about resources and strategies for managing puberty changes, acknowledging that these choices are personal and may differ between individuals.

modes.reason: Connects understanding of puberty changes, available resources, and the principle of personal agency into a coherent framework for managing transitions. Integrates the physical, social and cultural dimensions addressed across the nodes.

descriptors.title: Gender stereotypes and societal roles
descriptors.description: investigate how the portrayal of societal roles and responsibilities can be influenced by gender stereotypes
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students described how choices and actions can be influenced by stereotypes (AC9HP4P03). They understand that stereotypes exist and can shape behaviour. This descriptor extends that understanding specifically to gender stereotypes and their influence on societal roles and responsibilities — a more specific and politically situated application.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how gender stereotypes influence the portrayal of societal roles and responsibilities, identifying limiting effects and proposing strategies for gender equality.

nodes.label: Identifying gender stereotypes in societal portrayals
criteria: Identifies a specific portrayal (not a general claim that stereotypes exist)
Explains the connection between the portrayal and the expectation of roles or responsibilities — not just that the portrayal is stereotyped
nodes.hinge_reason: The critical analysis in N2 depends on students being able to identify the specific mechanism by which a portrayal influences expectations. Without this, students' critiques of stereotypes are abstract, and their proposals for change (N3) lack specificity.

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of a gender stereotype in a text or media example and explain how it influences the expected roles or responsibilities of a person in that portrayal.

modes.reason: Analyse specific examples: 'What is being shown? What does this imply about expected roles? What choices or opportunities does this open or close?' Concrete examples prevent the discussion from remaining abstract.

Analyse portrayals across different contexts: fictional characters who challenge stereotypes; social and cultural norms in family roles; sport and physical activity contexts. Cross-context analysis builds a richer understanding of how stereotypes operate.

nodes.label: Analysing limiting and harmful effects
criteria: Effect is described specifically — a named constraint on choices or opportunities, not just 'it's unfair'
Can connect the effect to the individual's human rights or wellbeing — not just social preference

width.minimum: Describe at least one limiting or harmful effect of a gender stereotype on an individual's choices or opportunities.

modes.reason: From portrayal to mechanism to effect: 'What does this stereotype expect? Who is constrained by this expectation? What choices or opportunities are limited or removed?' Analytical chain keeps the reasoning grounded rather than rhetorical.

nodes.label: Proposing strategies for gender equality
criteria: Strategy is specific to the identified stereotype or practice — not a generic 'treat everyone equally'
Connects the strategy to the limiting effect identified in N2

width.minimum: Propose at least one strategy to challenge a specific gender stereotype or promote gender equality, and explain how it addresses the identified limiting effect.

modes.reason: Integrates identification of stereotypes, analysis of their effects, and construction of equity strategies — the full descriptor demand of investigating how portrayals are influenced by gender stereotypes and working toward gender equality.

descriptors.title: Respect and empathy in relationships
descriptors.description: describe and demonstrate how respect and empathy can be expressed to positively influence relationships
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students selected, used and refined personal and social skills to establish, manage and strengthen relationships (AC9HP4P04). They have a repertoire of relationship skills. This descriptor requires specifically demonstrating respect and empathy as relationship-influencing mechanisms, and understanding how language and behaviour directed at others (including First Nations Australians) can affect relationships.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe and demonstrate how respect and empathy can be expressed to positively influence relationships in a range of contexts.

nodes.label: Understanding respect and empathy as distinct capacities
criteria: Can describe both concepts specifically — empathy is not just 'being nice', respect is not just 'being polite'
Examples demonstrate the distinction, not the same behaviour labelled differently
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate respect and empathy (treating them as synonyms for 'being nice') will not be able to deliberately demonstrate either in a focused way, undermining both the 'describe' and 'demonstrate' demands of the descriptor.

width.minimum: Describe the difference between respect and empathy as relationship behaviours, with a concrete example of each.
