modes.reason: Contrast the two: when is empathy the right response? when is respect? Scenario-based discussion that surfaces the distinction through cases rather than definition-recitation.

nodes.label: Demonstrating expression of respect and empathy
criteria: Expression is behavioural — something visible and specific, not just an internal feeling
Can describe the effect on the relationship, not just report that the expression was made

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least one expression of respect and one of empathy in a role-play or live scenario, and describe the effect on the relationship.

modes.reason: Practise expressions of respect and empathy across contexts: relationship changes; dealing with bullying; building cross-cultural connections including awareness of language that can cause offence to First Nations Australians. Each context demands different relational behaviour.

nodes.label: Connecting expressions to relationship outcomes
criteria: Relationship outcome is described specifically (not just 'things got better')
The connection between the expression and the outcome is explained, not asserted

width.minimum: Describe a situation in which expressing respect or empathy changed or positively influenced a relationship, and explain the connection between the expression and the outcome.

modes.reason: Connects the description and demonstration of respect and empathy to their relationship-influencing effect — the full descriptor demand of 'positively influence relationships'.

descriptors.title: Strategies to value diversity
descriptors.description: describe and implement strategies to value diversity in their communities
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students described how valuing diversity influences wellbeing and identified actions that promote inclusion (AC9HP4P05). They understand that diversity has wellbeing value and can identify inclusive actions. This descriptor moves to implementing strategies and addressing specific forms of discrimination including sexism, racism and homophobia.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe and implement strategies to value diversity in their communities, including addressing discrimination and supporting belonging for diverse groups.

nodes.label: Identifying discrimination and its effects on belonging
criteria: Names specific forms (not just 'discrimination generally')
Connects each form to a specific effect on belonging or wellbeing — not just 'it's wrong'
nodes.hinge_reason: Strategies for valuing diversity that do not address specific forms of discrimination will be generic. Implementation (the descriptor's demand) requires knowing what specific practices to challenge. Students who remain at a general level will not be able to propose targeted strategies.

width.minimum: Name at least two specific forms of discrimination and describe how each affects a person's sense of belonging or wellbeing.

modes.reason: Case analysis: examine specific discrimination examples and trace the effect on belonging and wellbeing. Concrete examples prevent the discussion from remaining abstract and ensure students understand the mechanism, not just the label.

Examine discrimination and belonging across community contexts: sport and cultural groups that counter discrimination; First Nations Australian cultural expression and connection to Country as a source of belonging and wellbeing; multicultural community examples. Cultural breadth prevents a single-community framing.

nodes.label: The bystander role
criteria: Describes a specific bystander action (not just 'say something')
Explains why bystander action matters — the mechanism by which it affects the discriminatory behaviour or the affected person

width.minimum: Describe at least one way a bystander can promote respectful interaction and explain why bystander action matters.

modes.reason: Bystander skills require rehearsal. Role-play bystander scenarios that vary in difficulty — ranging from lower-stakes to more challenging interventions. Precision matters: the difference between an effective and ineffective bystander response is often small.

nodes.label: Implementing community strategies
criteria: Strategy is specific to a named community context
Includes implementation steps — not just 'promote inclusion'

width.minimum: Describe at least one strategy for promoting diversity in a specific community context and explain the steps involved in implementing it.

modes.reason: Implements the full descriptor demand: describe and implement strategies to value diversity. Brings together understanding of discrimination, belonging, and bystander action into a concrete community strategy.

descriptors.title: Emotions and interactions
descriptors.description: apply strategies to manage emotions and analyse how emotional responses influence interactions
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students explained how and why emotional responses can vary and practised strategies to manage their emotions (AC9HP4P06). They have strategies for emotion management and understand that responses vary. This descriptor adds analysis: how emotional responses influence the quality of interactions — not just managing emotions internally but understanding their relational consequences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply strategies to manage emotions and analyse how emotional responses influence interactions in a range of situations.

nodes.label: Recognising emotions in interaction contexts
criteria: Contexts are distinct — not just the same emotion in slight variations
Can describe the interaction effect specifically — not just that the emotion was present
nodes.hinge_reason: The analysis demand ('analyse how emotional responses influence interactions') requires students to make the emotion-to-interaction connection explicit. Students who only identify emotions without connecting them to interaction outcomes cannot satisfy the descriptor's analytical demand.

width.minimum: Identify at least two emotional responses in different interaction contexts and describe how each affects the quality of the interaction.

modes.reason: Scenario analysis: 'In this situation, what emotion is present? How is that emotion showing up in the interaction? What effect is it having?' Builds the emotion-to-interaction chain explicitly.

nodes.label: Applying strategies for intense and complex emotions
criteria: Strategy is specific and action-oriented (not just 'take a deep breath' as a universal response)
Student can explain how the strategy addresses the emotion in that specific context

width.minimum: Describe and apply at least one strategy for managing a strong or intense emotion in an interaction context.

modes.reason: Apply management strategies across distinct emotional contexts: peer-group situations where emotions influence decisions; feelings of grief associated with loss; emotions associated with feeling unsafe or uncomfortable. Each context introduces different regulation demands.

nodes.label: Analysis and deliberate application
criteria: Analytical chain is complete: emotion → influence on interaction → strategy → outcome
Strategy choice is justified in terms of the specific emotional context, not just 'it works'

width.minimum: Analyse a situation in which an emotional response influenced an interaction, identify the strategy that was or could be applied, and describe the effect on the interaction outcome.

modes.reason: The full descriptor: applying strategies and analysing how emotional responses influence interactions. The integration moves from internal management to relational consequence.

descriptors.title: Consent strategies
descriptors.description: describe strategies for seeking, giving or denying consent and rehearse how to communicate their intentions effectively and respectfully
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students rehearsed and refined strategies for seeking, giving and denying permission respectfully and described situations when permission is required (AC9HP4P07). They have language for permission in concrete situations. This descriptor introduces consent explicitly (not just permission), adds the step of communicating intentions effectively, and addresses the emotional responses when consent is denied.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe strategies for seeking, giving or denying consent and rehearse how to communicate intentions effectively and respectfully across a range of situations.

nodes.label: Understanding consent and its steps
criteria: Can name and describe all four steps (asking, responding, listening, reacting)
Understands that each step places demands on both parties — not just the person asking or the person responding
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who reduce consent to a simple yes/no exchange cannot rehearse the full complexity of consent communication — the verbal and non-verbal cues in the listening step, and the emotional management in the reacting step (N2 and N3) both depend on this four-step framework.

width.minimum: Describe the four steps of consent communication and explain what each step requires of the person in that role.

modes.reason: Explicit step-by-step analysis of consent scenarios. Walk through each step and identify what is happening and what is required. The four-step framework is the scaffold for all subsequent rehearsal.

nodes.label: Verbal and non-verbal communication of consent
criteria: Can identify non-verbal cues specifically (not just 'body language' generically)
Rehearsal demonstrates intentional use of both verbal and non-verbal communication — not just verbal rehearsal

width.minimum: Identify at least one verbal and one non-verbal cue related to seeking or denying consent, and rehearse communicating intentions using both types of cue.

modes.reason: Repeated rehearsal of specific communication scenarios. Precision in the listening step (reading non-verbal cues accurately) requires practice across multiple scenario types.

Rehearse consent communication across different contexts: personal space and possessions, physical activity situations, online and social interactions. Each context has different cue types and communication challenges.

nodes.label: Managing reactions when consent is denied
criteria: Names a specific emotional response (not just 'feeling bad')
Rehearsal demonstrates a specific respectful response strategy — not just 'accept it'

width.minimum: Describe at least one emotional response that can arise when consent is denied, and rehearse at least one strategy for managing that response respectfully.

modes.reason: Integrates consent communication steps, verbal/non-verbal cue reading, and emotional regulation into the full consent framework. The reacting step is where consent understanding connects to emotional management — the complete descriptor demand.

descriptors.title: Protective behaviours online and offline
descriptors.description: analyse and rehearse protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies that can be used in a range of online and offline situations
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students described and applied protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies in a range of online and offline situations (AC9HP4P08). They can apply known strategies. This descriptor adds analysis — students evaluate the efficacy of strategies, not just apply them — and extends to bystander situations and reducing stigma around help-seeking.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and rehearse protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies for online and offline situations, including acting as bystanders and normalising help-seeking.

nodes.label: Analysing the efficacy of protective strategies
criteria: Analysis names a specific feature of the strategy that contributed to its effectiveness or failure
Goes beyond 'they did the right thing' — explains the mechanism
nodes.hinge_reason: The analysis demand differentiates this descriptor from the Y3-4 version. Students who can only apply strategies but not analyse them cannot engage with the efficacy questions, the stigma discussion, or the bystander situations — all of which require evaluative judgement.

width.minimum: Analyse at least one scenario (real or media-based) in which protective behaviour or help-seeking was or wasn't effective, and explain what made it effective or ineffective.

modes.reason: Media or scenario analysis: evaluate the responses of characters in TV shows or movies when in unsafe situations. What did they do? Why did it work or not? This externalises the analysis before students apply it to their own strategies.

nodes.label: Online safety strategies and reporting
criteria: Strategies are specific to online contexts — not generic safety advice applied to online
Can describe a reporting pathway — not just 'tell someone'

width.minimum: Describe at least two online safety strategies and explain the process for reporting harmful online behaviour to a trusted person or platform.

modes.reason: Rehearse online safety strategies across distinct online contexts: social media, gaming, image sharing, contact from unknown people. Each has different risks, different strategies and different reporting mechanisms.

nodes.label: Normalising help-seeking and bystander action
criteria: Stigma-reduction strategy addresses the stigma mechanism specifically — not just 'encourage help-seeking'
Bystander strategy is specific and rehearsed — not just stated

width.minimum: Describe at least one strategy for reducing help-seeking stigma and at least one strategy for acting as a bystander when others are in unsafe situations.

modes.reason: Integrates analysis of effective strategies, online and offline safety knowledge, and the social dimensions of help-seeking (stigma, bystander action) into the full descriptor demand.

descriptors.title: Health information sources and application
descriptors.description: investigate different sources and types of health information and how these apply to their own and others' health choices
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students interpreted the nature and intention of health information and messages and reflected on how they influence personal decisions (AC9HP4P09). They can interpret individual health messages. This descriptor adds investigation across source types, reliability evaluation, and application to real health choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate different sources and types of health information, evaluate their reliability, and apply them to their own and others' health choices.

nodes.label: Mapping health information sources
criteria: Sources are genuinely distinct types (not three social media platforms as three sources)
Can describe the influence mechanism — not just that the source exists
nodes.hinge_reason: Reliability evaluation (N2) depends on understanding the landscape of sources. Students who only have one or two types of sources cannot meaningfully evaluate relative reliability or make informed choices about which sources to apply to health decisions.

width.minimum: Identify at least three distinct types of health information sources and describe how each influences health choices.

modes.reason: Source mapping activity: for a specific health topic, identify all the places students could find information. Categorise them by type and discuss how each type influences choices. Builds the source landscape before reliability judgements are introduced.

nodes.label: Evaluating reliability and accuracy
criteria: Reliability judgement is based on specific criteria (evidence base, purpose, expertise) — not just preference or familiarity
Can identify one feature of a source that makes it more or less reliable

width.minimum: Compare health information from at least two different source types on the same topic and explain which is more reliable and why.

modes.reason: Evaluate reliability across different health domains: nutritional information and labelling; physical activity recommendations (e.g. Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines); mental health and wellbeing advice. Different domains have different types of misinformation and different reliability markers.

nodes.label: Applying health information to choices
criteria: Application is specific — a named health choice informed by a named source
Communication of health concern is to a specific type of trusted person for a specific purpose

width.minimum: Use health information from a reliable source to inform a specific health choice or strategy, and describe how they would communicate a health concern to a trusted person.

modes.reason: Integrates source investigation, reliability evaluation, and application to health choices — the full descriptor demand of investigating sources and applying them to health choices.

descriptors.title: Behaviours and community health and wellbeing
descriptors.description: analyse how behaviours influence the health, safety, relationships and wellbeing of individuals and communities
descriptors.knowledge: At Years 3-4, students investigated and applied behaviours that contribute to their own and others' health, safety, relationships and wellbeing (AC9HP4P10). They can apply health-promoting behaviours. This descriptor moves to analysis — examining how behaviours operate at individual and community scales, including online environments, food systems, and First Nations community wellbeing structures.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how individual and community behaviours influence health, safety, relationships and wellbeing, and propose strategies to promote positive community wellbeing.

nodes.label: Analysing behaviour-health connections at scale
criteria: Distinguishes individual-scale from community-scale effect (not the same point restated)
Analysis is specific to the behaviour — not generic 'healthy behaviour is good'
nodes.hinge_reason: The community-scale analysis is the new demand at this year band. Students who can only analyse at individual level cannot engage with community strategies, First Nations wellbeing structures, or online community behaviour — all of which require thinking across scales.

width.minimum: Analyse at least one behaviour and explain its effects on health or wellbeing at both an individual level and a community level.

modes.reason: Individual-to-community scale shift: 'If one person does X, what happens? If many people in a community do X, what happens?' Builds the community-scale thinking from familiar individual-scale analysis.

Analyse behaviour effects across community contexts: physical activity in communities; food practices including sustainable food systems; First Nations kinship structures and community health and wellbeing support; online community behaviours. Each context reveals different community-scale mechanisms.

nodes.label: Community safety and contamination prevention
criteria: Both individual-protection and community-protection mechanisms are explained for each behaviour
At least one behaviour is specific to community safety (not just personal safety)

width.minimum: Describe at least two community safety behaviours and explain how each protects both individuals and the community.

modes.reason: These are precision-dependent behaviours (infection control, anaphylaxis awareness) where errors in understanding have direct safety consequences. Consolidation ensures accuracy before students incorporate these into community strategy proposals.

nodes.label: Proposing community wellbeing strategies
criteria: Strategy targets community-level change (not just individual behaviour change in isolation)
Identifies the community-scale mechanism — how individual behaviour change aggregates to community effect

width.minimum: Propose at least one strategy to promote health or wellbeing at a community level, explaining the behaviours involved and the community-scale effect expected.

modes.reason: Integrates analysis of behaviour-health connections across scales, safety knowledge, and the principles of community wellbeing promotion into a proposal. The full descriptor demand: analyse and act at community scale.

descriptors.title: Analyse and transfer movement skills
descriptors.description: analyse, refine and transfer movement skills in a variety of movement situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students have adapted and modified movement skills across a variety of situations and transferred familiar movement strategies to different movement contexts (Y5-6). They can identify and describe movement adjustments in response to changing conditions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse, refine and transfer movement skills across varied movement situations using feedback from multiple sources.

nodes.label: Receiving and interpreting feedback
nodes.checkpoint: Students can receive specific movement feedback, identify what it is asking them to change, and explain the intended effect on their movement.
criteria: Identifies at least one specific movement change implied by feedback received
Explains what improvement to the movement outcome the change is intended to produce
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot interpret and act on movement feedback cannot meaningfully engage with the refinement cycle — skill analysis and transfer depend on students being able to identify what specifically needs to change and why. Without this, subsequent nodes become disconnected self-assessment.

width.minimum: Receive feedback from one source (teacher or peer) about a specific movement in a game or activity and identify what change is being requested.
width.typical: Receive and interpret feedback from multiple sources (teacher, peer, self-review) across at least two movement contexts; distinguish between feedback that identifies a problem and feedback that prescribes a specific fix.
wider: Compare how feedback is structured and delivered differently across movement forms (e.g. teacher demonstration vs peer verbal cue vs video review) and evaluate which source was most effective for their own refinement
Explore how elite athletes in different sports structure feedback loops with coaches and reflect on how a simplified version could improve their own skill refinement process

modes.reason: Invest in explicitly modelling how to decode feedback — distinguish between what is described (the current movement), what is prescribed (the change), and what outcome is intended. Students need a framework for interpreting feedback, not just practice receiving it.
Encountering feedback in multiple movement forms (game-based, aquatic, dance, outdoor) builds the ability to transfer feedback interpretation across varied contexts.

nodes.label: Refining movement in response to feedback
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make a deliberate adjustment to a movement skill in response to feedback and observe whether the adjustment produced the intended change.
criteria: Makes at least one deliberate movement adjustment in response to feedback
Describes whether the adjustment produced the intended change and gives a reason

width.minimum: Attempt at least one movement adjustment in response to feedback and comment on whether it changed the outcome as expected.
width.typical: Make targeted adjustments across multiple refinement cycles in at least one movement context; distinguish between adjustments that improved the outcome and those that did not; explain what was different in successful refinement attempts.
wider: Refine a range of swimming strokes using feedback from teacher, peers or video resources, comparing refinement patterns across different stroke techniques
Use feedback from others to refine the composition of a group dance sequence, evaluating how individual movement refinements affected the group performance as a whole

modes.reason: Students need repeated refinement cycles — the skill of making deliberate adjustments and evaluating their effect improves with iteration. A single refinement attempt is not enough to build reliable self-correction habits.

nodes.label: Analysing movement skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe a movement situation and identify specific aspects of a movement skill that could be refined, with reference to what an effective version of the skill looks like.
criteria: Identifies at least one specific aspect of a movement skill that affects its effectiveness
References a criterion or benchmark for effective movement when explaining the identified area
nodes.hinge_reason: Analysis is prerequisite to transfer — students who cannot articulate what makes a movement effective cannot strategically apply it in a new context. Transfer without analysis is pattern-matching, not the capability the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Observe a movement (own or peer) and identify at least one specific aspect that affects its effectiveness, with reference to a criterion for what good execution looks like.
width.typical: Analyse movement across multiple situations and skill types; identify strengths and areas for refinement using movement criteria; link observations to specific feedback that could drive improvement.
wider: Analyse movement in peer coach scenarios — e.g. using video or live observation to diagnose movement in invasion games, swimming or gymnastics contexts, and provide targeted feedback
Compare movement analysis across game forms (net/court, invasion, striking/fielding, target) and identify how effective movement criteria differ across these forms

modes.reason: Explicitly scaffold movement analysis using frameworks — e.g. task-conditions-performance criteria. Students benefit from structured observation tools before attempting unguided analysis.

nodes.label: Transferring movement skills to new situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply a refined movement skill to a new or varied movement situation, adapting execution appropriately to the new context.
criteria: Applies a movement skill from a practised context to a new movement situation
Identifies at least one adaptation made to execution to suit the new context
Uses feedback (from self or others) to evaluate whether the transfer was effective

width.minimum: Apply a movement skill practised in one context to a different movement situation and describe one adaptation made to suit the new context.
width.typical: Transfer movement skills and strategies across a range of movement situations — including different game categories, performance contexts and outdoor/obstacle settings — explaining what was adapted and why.
wider: Use feedback from others to safely and efficiently travel around, over, up, under and through natural or built obstacles — applying movement skills learned in structured game contexts to unpredictable outdoor environments
Investigate how movement skills in one game category (e.g. invasion) transfer to a different category (e.g. net/court or target), identifying shared and divergent requirements

modes.reason: Transfer is the evidence of capability — students who have only practised in one context cannot demonstrate transfer. Breadth of movement contexts is not enrichment; it is the mechanism by which transfer capability is built and assessed.

This node integrates the feedback interpretation, refinement, and analysis capabilities from earlier nodes into coordinated performance across new contexts. Instruction should explicitly support students in drawing on all three in the transfer situation.

descriptors.title: Design movement strategies
descriptors.description: design and demonstrate how movement strategies can be manipulated to improve movement outcomes
descriptors.knowledge: Students have transferred familiar movement strategies to different movement situations and can identify when strategies are or are not working (Y5-6). They can describe how strategies affect movement outcomes in broad terms.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design and demonstrate how movement strategies can be manipulated to improve movement outcomes across a range of movement situations.

nodes.label: Understanding movement strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and name movement strategies relevant to at least one movement context and describe what each strategy is intended to achieve.
criteria: Names at least two movement strategies for a given context
Explains the intended movement outcome of each strategy
nodes.hinge_reason: Design requires a repertoire of strategies to draw from — students who cannot name and explain existing strategies cannot make purposeful design decisions. Without this conceptual base, design becomes guessing rather than deliberate manipulation.

width.minimum: Identify at least two movement strategies applicable to one movement scenario and explain what each is trying to achieve.
width.typical: Identify and describe movement strategies across game categories and movement forms; explain the intended outcome of each strategy in terms of space, possession, scoring or performance quality.
wider: Compare movement strategies across different game categories (invasion, net/court, target) and identify shared principles that apply across all three
Investigate how static and dynamic balance underpin movement strategies in both game-based and performance contexts, identifying the common biomechanical basis

modes.reason: Build a working vocabulary of movement strategies through exposure across contexts. Students need multiple strategy types on which to draw before they can make design choices.

nodes.label: Selecting and adapting strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select a movement strategy appropriate to a specific scenario, justifying the selection, and adapt previously successful strategies to new movement challenges.
criteria: Selects a movement strategy appropriate to a specific scenario
Gives at least one reason why the strategy suits the context or challenge

width.minimum: Select one movement strategy for a given scenario and give at least one reason why it is appropriate for that context.
width.typical: Select and apply strategies across several movement scenarios; draw on previously successful strategies and adapt them to new challenges; explain adaptations made and predicted outcomes.
wider: Predict the effectiveness of changes in tactics or strategies on scoring opportunities in a game and suggest reasons for unexpected results — applying this cycle across multiple game forms
Explore similarities between bases of support and flow of movements across different movement sequences requiring static and dynamic balance, selecting strategies that exploit these shared principles

modes.reason: Strategy selection becomes meaningful only when students encounter varied scenarios that require different selections. Multiple contexts prevent strategy fixation on one default approach.

nodes.label: Designing and demonstrating movement strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a movement strategy for a specific scenario, implement it, and evaluate whether the design achieved the intended improvement in the movement outcome.
criteria: Designs a movement strategy for a specified scenario with at least one explicit design rationale
Demonstrates the strategy in practice
Evaluates whether the strategy achieved the intended movement outcome improvement

width.minimum: Design one movement strategy for a specific scenario, implement it, and comment on whether it produced the intended improvement.
width.typical: Design and implement movement strategies across a range of scenarios; predict outcomes before implementation; evaluate actual outcomes against predictions; explain how design choices related to space, balance, flow or tactics influenced the result.
wider: Design movement strategies for non-traditional or student-invented game scenarios, evaluating how strategic principles generalise to unfamiliar contexts

Develop and implement a strategy for a complex movement challenge involving multiple variables (e.g. changing teams, modified rules) and document how the strategy was adjusted in response to unexpected outcomes

modes.reason: Design integrates strategy knowledge, selection judgement and implementation — instruction should scaffold the full design-implement-evaluate cycle, not just the planning phase.

descriptors.title: Manipulate movement concepts
descriptors.description: demonstrate and explain how movement concepts related to effort, space, time, objects and people can be manipulated to improve movement outcomes
descriptors.knowledge: Students have investigated how movement concepts (effort, space, time, objects, people) can be applied to improve movement outcomes (Y5-6). They can apply these concepts to specific situations but have not yet been asked to explain manipulations systematically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students demonstrate and explain how movement concepts related to effort, space, time, objects and people can be manipulated to improve movement outcomes.

nodes.label: Identifying movement concepts in action
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe a movement situation and identify which movement concepts (effort, space, time, objects, people) are at work and how they are affecting the movement outcome.
criteria: Identifies at least two movement concepts operating in an observed movement situation
Describes what each identified concept is contributing to the movement outcome
nodes.hinge_reason: Explanation and deliberate manipulation both require students to have a working conceptual map of movement concepts. Students who cannot identify which concepts are operating cannot explain how to manipulate them intentionally.

width.minimum: Observe one movement situation and identify at least two movement concepts at work, describing what each is contributing to the outcome.
width.typical: Identify all five movement concept categories across a range of movement forms; describe how each concept is operating in specific situations and contributing to movement quality or outcome.
wider: Perform a range of movements and analyse technique based on understanding of effort in relation to take-off, body position and landing, identifying how multiple concepts interact
Create and appraise rhythmic movement sequences, identifying how flow, space and relationships to other performers are operating simultaneously

modes.reason: Use explicit observation frameworks that direct students to look for each concept category in sequence. Build the habit of systematic concept identification before expecting integrated explanation.

nodes.label: Explaining how manipulation changes outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how deliberately changing one or more movement concepts (effort, space, time, objects, people) will produce a different movement outcome, with reference to a specific movement context.
criteria: Explains how changing a named movement concept will alter the movement outcome
Provides a specific causal reason linking the concept change to the outcome change

width.minimum: Explain how changing one movement concept in a given situation would change the movement outcome, with a specific reason.
width.typical: Explain how manipulating each of the five concept categories in different movement situations changes outcomes; make predictions about outcome changes before trying them; link biomechanical concepts (angle, trajectory, effort) to specific outcome changes.
wider: Demonstrate understanding of how to adjust the angle of release of an object and explain how this affects the height and distance of flight across different throwing or striking implements
Design a movement performance that deliberately manipulates space and relationships between performers to achieve a specific communicative or tactical outcome

modes.reason: Explanation requires causal reasoning — help students build if-then reasoning habits: 'If I change X, then Y changes because...' This structure prevents description from being mistaken for explanation.

nodes.label: Demonstrating deliberate manipulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate deliberate manipulation of movement concepts in a variety of movement forms, showing that the manipulation produces an improved or intended outcome.
criteria: Demonstrates deliberate manipulation of at least one movement concept in a physical activity
Explains what manipulation was made and why it was expected to improve the movement outcome
Evaluates whether the demonstration achieved the intended outcome change

width.minimum: Demonstrate manipulation of at least one movement concept in one activity, showing that the change produced the intended improvement.
width.typical: Demonstrate manipulation of movement concepts across multiple forms (game-based performance, rhythmic sequences, outdoor movement); connect biomechanical principles (effort, angle, spatial relationships) to performance design and execution.
wider: Create, perform and appraise rhythmic movement sequences that demonstrate intentional variations in flow, space and relationships — evaluating whether each manipulation achieved its intended effect
Design and refine performances demonstrating how to manipulate space and relationships between players to achieve successful movement outcomes in a tactical game context

modes.reason: Demonstration integrates conceptual understanding with physical execution and reflective evaluation. The full demand requires students to know what they are doing and why — instruction should keep all three layers visible simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Fitness and health participation
descriptors.description: participate in physical activities designed to improve fitness and wellbeing to investigate the impact of regular participation on health, fitness and wellbeing
descriptors.knowledge: Students have participated in physical activities and investigated the body's reaction to different levels of intensity (Y5-6). They can describe physical changes during exercise but have not yet systematically investigated the relationship between regular participation and health outcomes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in physical activities designed to improve fitness and wellbeing and investigate the impact of regular participation on health, fitness and wellbeing.

nodes.label: Understanding fitness components and wellbeing dimensions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the main fitness components (e.g. cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility) and wellbeing dimensions and explain what types of physical activities target each.
criteria: Names at least two fitness components or wellbeing dimensions
Identifies at least one activity type designed to improve each named component or dimension
nodes.hinge_reason: The investigation requirement in the descriptor depends on students having a conceptual framework for what aspects of health and fitness can vary. Without this, participation becomes physically purposeful but analytically empty — students cannot investigate impact without knowing what to measure.

width.minimum: Identify at least two fitness components or wellbeing dimensions and describe one activity type that targets each.
width.typical: Identify the range of fitness components and wellbeing dimensions (physical, social, emotional, mental); explain which activity types address which components; connect these to the elaboration contexts (circuit training, yoga, mindfulness, HIIT).
wider: Research unfamiliar activity forms (yoga, mindfulness meditation, gym classes, HIIT) and compare how each targets different components and dimensions of health and wellbeing
Investigate how different cultures define and pursue health and wellbeing through physical practice, examining examples relevant to the class community

modes.reason: Build a shared framework for fitness components and wellbeing dimensions before launching investigation. Use it as an analytical lens that students apply consistently across different activity types.

nodes.label: Participating with investigative intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in physical activities designed to improve fitness or wellbeing while noticing and recording specific evidence of impact on their health, fitness or wellbeing.
criteria: Participates in a physical activity designed to improve fitness or wellbeing
Records at least one specific piece of evidence of impact on their health, fitness or wellbeing

width.minimum: Participate in one physical activity and record at least one piece of evidence about its impact on health, fitness or wellbeing.
width.typical: Participate in activities targeting different fitness components and wellbeing dimensions; collect evidence of impact using observation, self-report or digital tools; compare effects across different activity types or durations.
wider: Use digital tools to track participation data over multiple sessions and identify patterns in health, fitness or wellbeing indicators
Design and perform a fitness circuit that could be implemented at home with minimal equipment and monitor its impact on at least one fitness component over time

modes.reason: Investigative participation requires repeated practice — a single session of noticing and recording does not establish the pattern recognition that 'regular participation' implies. Students need multiple cycles of participation plus evidence collection.

nodes.label: Investigating the impact of regular participation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the relationship between regular physical activity participation and outcomes for health, fitness and wellbeing, drawing on their participation data and research evidence.
criteria: States at least one finding about the impact of regular participation on health, fitness or wellbeing
Connects the finding to either personal participation evidence or an external source
Links the finding to a design decision in a personal or class activity program

width.minimum: Describe at least one finding from their own participation or from a research source about the impact of regular physical activity on health, fitness or wellbeing.
width.typical: Investigate the impact of regular participation using a combination of personal participation data and external sources; compare effects on different health and wellbeing outcomes; design a personal activity program responsive to individual goals and the investigation findings.
wider: Design and monitor a personal physical activity program using digital tools, evaluating its effectiveness against individual health, wellbeing and fitness goals over multiple weeks
Research how access to fitness and wellbeing activities differs across community contexts and examine the implications for health equity

modes.reason: Investigation integrates participation experience with research evidence and personal data analysis. Instruction should support students in drawing these together rather than treating participation and investigation as separate tasks.

descriptors.title: Community spaces and outdoor settings
descriptors.description: participate in physical activities that utilise community spaces and outdoor settings, and evaluate strategies to support increased use of these spaces
descriptors.knowledge: Students have participated in physical activities in natural and outdoor settings and analysed the steps and resources needed to promote participation (Y5-6). They can identify what supports participation but have not yet evaluated management strategies at a community level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in physical activities using community spaces and outdoor settings, and evaluate strategies to support increased use of these spaces.

nodes.label: Understanding community and outdoor spaces for physical activity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the range of community and outdoor settings used for physical activity in their local area and describe key features that make them suitable or unsuitable for different activity types.
criteria: Identifies at least two community or outdoor settings available for physical activity
Describes at least one feature that supports or limits use of each setting

width.minimum: Identify at least two community or outdoor settings available locally for physical activity and describe one feature that supports or limits use of each.
width.typical: Map a range of local community and outdoor settings; describe what makes each suitable for different activity types; identify barriers to and enablers of participation in these settings.
wider: Investigate how urban planning and design decisions have shaped access to outdoor and community physical activity spaces in the local area, considering equity of access across different groups
Explore how different community groups use the same outdoor spaces and what this means for managing competing needs

modes.reason: Familiarity with a range of community settings is foundational for evaluating strategies — students who only know one space type have a limited basis for evaluation.

nodes.label: Participating in community and outdoor settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in physical activities in at least one community or outdoor setting, demonstrating safe and appropriate use of the environment.
criteria: Participates in a physical activity in a community or outdoor setting
Demonstrates at least one practice appropriate to the safe and sustainable use of that setting

width.minimum: Participate in one physical activity in a community or outdoor setting, following safe and appropriate practices for that environment.
width.typical: Participate in activities across at least two different community or outdoor setting types; demonstrate awareness of environmental safety, minimal-impact practices, and appropriate behaviour for each setting.
wider: Participate in outdoor or nature-based activities such as bushwalking, orienteering or minimal-impact recreation, demonstrating understanding of environmental stewardship practices
Investigate First Nations Australian custodial approaches to Country/Place and apply principles from this understanding to participation in local outdoor settings

modes.reason: Participation with environmental awareness is a practiced disposition — students need repeated encounters in actual settings rather than simulated ones.

nodes.label: Evaluating strategies for increased use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate strategies designed to support increased or sustainable use of community and outdoor physical activity spaces, weighing their benefits against potential drawbacks.
criteria: Identifies at least one strategy for supporting increased use of a community or outdoor physical activity space
Evaluates the strategy using at least one clear criterion (e.g. effectiveness, equity, environmental impact)
Weighs at least one benefit and one limitation of the strategy

width.minimum: Identify one strategy for increasing use of a community or outdoor space and give at least one reason why it would or would not be effective.
width.typical: Evaluate a range of strategies for managing, protecting and increasing use of community and outdoor spaces; consider environmental impact, community equity, and sustainability; design physical activity options that reimagine or better utilise community spaces.
wider: Investigate different approaches to custodial responsibility for Country/Place used by First Nations Australian communities, and evaluate how these principles could inform management of local physical activity spaces

Evaluate strategies used to manage and protect environments where physical activities take place (bushwalking trails, surf beaches, skate parks, sporting fields), identifying trade-offs between access and environmental protection

modes.reason: Evaluation requires students to apply criteria and weigh trade-offs — scaffold this with explicit criteria (e.g. effectiveness, equity, environmental impact, sustainability) before expecting independent evaluation.

descriptors.title: Design physical activity strategies
descriptors.description: design and justify strategies to increase physical activity levels to achieve health and wellbeing outcomes
descriptors.knowledge: Students have proposed and explained strategies to increase physical activity and reduce sedentary behaviour (Y5-6). They can describe what strategies might work but have not yet been expected to design and justify strategies against specific health and wellbeing outcome targets.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design and justify strategies to increase physical activity levels to achieve health and wellbeing outcomes.

nodes.label: Identifying physical activity barriers and enablers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify factors that support or limit physical activity participation for themselves and their peer group, including personal, social and environmental factors.
criteria: Identifies at least two factors that influence their own physical activity participation
Categorises factors as personal, social or environmental
nodes.hinge_reason: Design decisions require a clear understanding of what is being designed against — students who cannot identify the specific barriers and enablers in their own context will produce generic strategies with no real justification grounded in evidence.

width.minimum: Identify at least two factors (personal, social or environmental) that influence their own physical activity levels.
width.typical: Identify and categorise factors that support and limit physical activity participation across personal, social and environmental domains; compare their current activity levels with Australia's 24-Hour Movement Guidelines; identify specific gaps.
wider: Compare physical activity levels, sleep and sedentary time against the 24-Hour Movement Guidelines and map personal and social factors contributing to any identified gaps
Investigate which physical activities different peer groups engage in for social and emotional wellbeing, identifying patterns in motivation and participation

modes.reason: Use a structured analysis framework (personal/social/environmental) to ensure students map their own context systematically before designing. Strategies should be explicitly linked to identified barriers.

nodes.label: Understanding health and wellbeing outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the health and wellbeing outcomes that increased physical activity is intended to achieve, with reference to specific outcome areas (physical, social, emotional, mental).
criteria: Names at least one health or wellbeing outcome that increased physical activity supports
Explains the link between a specific activity type and the outcome named

width.minimum: Identify at least one health or wellbeing outcome that increased physical activity can support and explain the link.
width.typical: Explain how increased physical activity contributes to outcomes across physical, social, emotional and mental wellbeing dimensions; connect activity types to specific outcomes; use the 24-Hour Movement Guidelines as a reference point.
wider: Investigate how physical activity supports emotional and social wellbeing specifically — examining the evidence for social connection and mood benefits beyond physical fitness outcomes
Research how sedentary behaviour alongside insufficient activity creates compounding health risks, and use this understanding to justify targeting both in a strategy

modes.reason: Justification requires specific outcome understanding — width here means connecting a range of outcome types to different activity strategies rather than knowing one outcome type deeply.

nodes.label: Designing and justifying strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a strategy to increase physical activity levels for themselves or others, with explicit justification linking design decisions to identified barriers and targeted health or wellbeing outcomes.
criteria: Designs a strategy to increase physical activity levels for themselves or others
Justifies at least one design decision by linking it to an identified barrier or a specific health/wellbeing outcome
Identifies a realistic way to monitor or evaluate the strategy's effectiveness

width.minimum: Design one strategy to increase physical activity and justify at least one design decision by linking it to an identified barrier or health/wellbeing outcome.
width.typical: Design a realistic personal or peer-targeted physical activity strategy addressing multiple barriers and targeting specific health and wellbeing outcomes; justify each key design decision with reference to evidence; include monitoring or evaluation mechanisms.
wider: Design and monitor a personal physical activity plan over multiple weeks, evaluating whether the strategy achieved the intended wellbeing outcomes and revising it accordingly

Design an activity program for a specific peer group (e.g. students who prefer non-competitive activities) with explicit justification for design decisions tailored to that group's barriers and preferences

modes.reason: Design and justify integrates barrier analysis, outcome understanding, and strategic planning into one coherent artefact. Instruction should scaffold the full design-justify cycle rather than treating design as the endpoint.
Justification quality increases when students have a range of health/wellbeing outcome types to draw on. Width in outcome knowledge directly improves justification depth.

descriptors.title: Evaluate movement strategies
descriptors.description: propose and evaluate movement strategies and skills that would be most effective in different movement situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students have predicted and tested the effectiveness of different skills and strategies in a range of movement situations (Y5-6). They can make predictions and test them but have not yet been expected to systematically propose and evaluate across a range of situation types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students propose and evaluate movement strategies and skills that would be most effective in different movement situations.

nodes.label: Proposing movement strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the key features of a movement situation and propose a strategy or skill selection that responds to those features with a stated rationale.
criteria: Identifies at least one key feature of a movement situation that informs strategy selection
Proposes a movement strategy or skill appropriate to that situation with a stated rationale
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluation requires a proposal to evaluate — students who cannot make reasoned proposals have no object for their evaluation. The quality of proposal reasoning determines whether evaluation is substantive or superficial.

width.minimum: Identify the key features of one movement situation and propose a strategy or skill most likely to be effective, giving one reason.
width.typical: Identify relevant contextual features across a range of movement situations; propose strategies and skills that respond to each; articulate the rationale for each proposal in terms of what the situation demands.
wider: Explain and justify the movement strategies selected in response to outdoor or nature-based activity challenges (rope courses, bushwalking, orienteering, canoeing) where environmental unpredictability is a key contextual feature
Investigate how movement strategy selection differs between competitive and cooperative movement contexts and what contextual features drive the differences

modes.reason: Scaffold proposal reasoning by explicitly modelling situation analysis: what are the demands of this situation, what skills or strategies address those demands, and why? Build this as a consistent thinking routine before evaluation is introduced.

nodes.label: Testing and acting on proposals
nodes.checkpoint: Students can put proposed movement solutions into action, predicting outcomes in advance and observing whether actual outcomes match predictions.
criteria: Implements a proposed movement strategy in a physical activity
States a prediction about the outcome before implementation
Describes whether the actual outcome matched the prediction

width.minimum: Implement a proposed movement strategy and describe whether the outcome matched what was predicted.
width.typical: Implement proposals across multiple movement situations; predict outcomes before each attempt; compare actual and predicted outcomes; identify what caused divergence where it occurred.
wider: Put movement solutions into action in outdoor or nature-based activity contexts where the environment introduces unexpected variables, and reflect on how predictions needed to be revised
Design a movement challenge that requires peers to propose a strategy before participating, then evaluate their proposals against actual outcomes

modes.reason: The propose-predict-test cycle builds through iteration — students need multiple rounds of testing proposals against outcomes to develop reliable prediction judgement.

nodes.label: Evaluating effectiveness and transfer potential
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of movement strategies across situations, identifying factors that enabled success and considering how successful approaches might transfer to other contexts.
criteria: Evaluates whether a proposed movement strategy was effective, with at least one reason
Identifies a factor that contributed to the outcome (positive or negative)
Makes a reasoned judgement about whether the strategy or skill could be transferred to a different movement context

width.minimum: Evaluate whether a proposed strategy was effective and identify one factor that influenced the outcome.
width.typical: Evaluate strategy effectiveness across a range of situations; identify enabling and limiting factors; justify why certain strategies would transfer to other contexts and which would not; connect evaluation findings to future strategy selection.
wider: Evaluate factors that enabled success in movement activities and justify how these factors can be transferred to other learning contexts beyond HPE
Compare evaluate-and-transfer cycles across indoor game contexts and outdoor/nature activity contexts, examining which strategies proved most generalisable

modes.reason: Evaluation integrates proposal reasoning, testing experience and transfer judgement into one reflective capability. Instruction should keep the full cycle visible — evaluation is not a standalone final step but a return to proposal reasoning.
Transfer potential is only visible when students have evaluated across multiple situation types. Width in movement situation types is what makes transfer claims substantive rather than speculative.

descriptors.title: Modifications for inclusion
descriptors.description: investigate modifications to equipment, rules and scoring systems that support fair play and inclusive participation
descriptors.knowledge: Students have devised and tested alternative rules and game modifications to support fair play and inclusive participation (Y5-6). They have tested modifications but have not yet systematically investigated how and why modifications work.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate modifications to equipment, rules and scoring systems that support fair play and inclusive participation.

nodes.label: Understanding fair play and inclusion as design criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what fair play and inclusive participation mean in a physical activity context and identify specific conditions that threaten or support them.
criteria: Explains what fair play means in a physical activity context
Explains what inclusive participation means and gives one example of a condition that limits it
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding fair play and inclusion as criteria, modification investigations become arbitrary rather than purposeful. Students need to know what they are designing for before they can evaluate whether modifications achieve it.

width.minimum: Explain what fair play and inclusive participation mean and identify one condition in a physical activity that threatens either.
width.typical: Explain fair play and inclusion as design criteria; identify a range of conditions (equipment, skill gaps, rule complexity, physical ability) that can threaten or support each; explain how scoring systems can be structured to advantage or disadvantage different participant groups.
wider: Analyse the benefits and potential drawbacks of player-officiated games where players rather than an independent official are responsible for officiating, examining how this affects fair play
Explore how traditional games of First Nations Australians are structured to support fair play and inclusive participation, identifying the design principles underlying these structures

modes.reason: Explicitly establish fair play and inclusion as design criteria with concrete indicators before investigation begins. Ask students to identify who is disadvantaged in a given game and what the modification is trying to fix.

nodes.label: Investigating modification types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate specific modifications to equipment, rules or scoring systems and explain how each modification is intended to support fair play or inclusive participation.
criteria: Investigates at least one modification and explains how it is intended to support fair play or inclusive participation
Identifies which modification type (equipment, rules, or scoring) the modification belongs to

width.minimum: Investigate one modification (equipment, rules or scoring) and explain how it is intended to support fair play or inclusive participation.
width.typical: Investigate a range of modifications across all three types (equipment, rules, scoring); apply and adapt scoring systems to assess movement performances consistently and fairly; examine how modifications interact and whether they create new inequities.
wider: Explore rules, equipment and scoring systems of traditional games of First Nations Australians, investigating how they support skill development and fair and inclusive play

Research how modified sport programs (e.g. sitting volleyball, bocce, Auslan volleyball) have been designed to extend participation, comparing the design principles to those used in class game modifications

modes.reason: Investigation across all three modification types (equipment, rules, scoring) builds a complete toolkit — students who have only investigated one type have an incomplete picture of how game design supports inclusion.

nodes.label: Applying and evaluating modifications
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply modifications in practice and evaluate their effectiveness at supporting fair play and inclusive participation, identifying strengths and limitations.
criteria: Applies at least one modification in a physical activity
Evaluates whether the modification achieved its intended purpose (fair play or inclusive participation)
Identifies at least one strength and one limitation of the modification

width.minimum: Apply one modification in a physical activity and evaluate whether it achieved its intended purpose, giving one reason.
width.typical: Apply and evaluate modifications across multiple activity contexts; assess whether modifications enable all participants to experience success; identify unintended consequences; propose refinements based on evaluation findings.
wider: Modify rules, equipment or scoring systems from scratch for a specific group with particular participation needs, testing and evaluating the design against inclusion criteria through multiple iterations
Analyse a player-officiated game context and evaluate how the absence of an independent official affects both fair play and inclusive participation dynamics

modes.reason: Applying and evaluating modifications integrates design criteria understanding, modification knowledge and reflective evaluation. The evaluation must circle back to the original design criteria — fair play and inclusive participation — not just satisfaction or enjoyment.

descriptors.title: Leadership and collaboration
descriptors.description: practise and apply leadership, collaboration and group decision-making processes when participating in a range of physical activities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have participated positively in groups and teams by contributing to group activities, encouraging others and negotiating roles and responsibilities (Y5-6). They can participate constructively but have not yet been expected to undertake explicit leadership roles or apply group decision-making processes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students practise and apply leadership, collaboration and group decision-making processes when participating in a range of physical activities.

nodes.label: Understanding leadership and collaboration roles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different leadership and collaboration roles, describe what each involves, and explain how the roles contribute to team and group outcomes.
criteria: Identifies at least two roles in a team or group physical activity context (including one leadership role)
Explains what each role contributes to the team or group outcome

width.minimum: Identify at least two distinct roles (one leadership, one collaboration) and explain what each contributes to a team or group outcome.
width.typical: Identify a range of leadership and collaboration roles across different physical activity contexts; explain how roles distribute responsibility and contribute to cohesion and success; distinguish between formal and informal leadership.
wider: Investigate how leadership styles differ across competitive team sport and cooperative outdoor activities, examining what makes each style effective in its context
Explore how cultural understandings of leadership and collective decision-making influence group dynamics in physical activity contexts from different communities

modes.reason: Encountering diverse role types prevents students from developing a single fixed model of leadership. Breadth here builds adaptability.

nodes.label: Reading group dynamics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret verbal, physical and situational cues from others in a team or group and respond appropriately to support positive group functioning.
criteria: Identifies at least one verbal or non-verbal cue from a team or group member
Describes an appropriate response to the cue that supports positive group functioning
nodes.hinge_reason: Effective leadership and collaboration depend on situational awareness — students who cannot read group dynamics will apply generic responses that may undermine rather than support the group. Decision-making quality directly depends on cue interpretation.

width.minimum: Identify at least one verbal or non-verbal cue from a teammate or group member during a physical activity and describe an appropriate response.
width.typical: Interpret verbal, physical and situational cues across different group contexts; respond adaptively to the feelings and motives of others; recognise when group cohesion is being helped or hindered and adjust responses accordingly.
wider: Reflect on how verbal, physical and situational cues are interpreted differently in competitive vs cooperative physical activity contexts, and what this means for leadership and collaboration responses
Investigate how awareness of group dynamics in physical activity contexts connects to leadership and collaboration in other areas of school and community life

modes.reason: Explicitly teach cue interpretation as a skill — what cues are available (verbal, physical, situational), what do they signal, and what response options are available? Use real physical activity scenarios as the teaching context.

nodes.label: Practising leadership and collaboration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adopt varied leadership and collaboration roles across physical activities, contributing actively to group decision-making and reflecting on how their actions affected outcomes.
criteria: Adopts at least one leadership or collaboration role in a physical activity
Describes at least one specific action taken in that role
Reflects on how that action contributed to the team or group outcome

width.minimum: Adopt at least one leadership or collaboration role in a physical activity and describe one way your actions in that role contributed to the group or team outcome.
width.typical: Adopt varied roles (leader, collaborator, planner) across multiple physical activities; apply group decision-making processes; reflect on how specific actions initiated in each role led to outcomes; support peers in planning and executing physical activities.
wider: Plan and lead a physical activity for a peer group from design through to facilitation, evaluating the leadership decisions made at each stage
Undertake the role of activity planner for a team, developing a collaborative decision-making process and reflecting on how group input shaped the final plan

modes.reason: Leadership and collaboration are dispositional capabilities that develop through repetition across varied contexts — students need multiple role experiences, not a single leadership task.

Planning and leading physical activities integrates role awareness, cue-reading and decision-making into coordinated action. Structured reflection after each role experience is essential to consolidate the learning.

descriptors.title: Values, beliefs and identities
descriptors.description: analyse and reflect on the influence of values and beliefs on the development of identities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explained how identities can be influenced by people and places, and how positive self-identities can be created (Y5-6). They can identify external influences on identity but have not yet been expected to analyse how values and beliefs specifically operate as mechanisms of influence.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and reflect on the influence of values and beliefs on the development of identities.

nodes.label: Understanding values and beliefs as identity influences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what values and beliefs are and describe how they can shape how a person sees themselves.
criteria: Explains what values and beliefs are
Gives at least one example of how a value or belief influences how a person sees themselves
nodes.hinge_reason: Analysis requires a conceptual framework for what values and beliefs are and how they function — students who cannot distinguish values and beliefs from other identity influences cannot meaningfully analyse their specific role. Reflection on personal identity is equally dependent on this foundation.

width.minimum: Define values and beliefs and give at least one example of how a personal or family value influences how a person sees themselves.
width.typical: Explain how values and beliefs from different sources (personal, family, peer, cultural) operate as influences on identity; describe specific mechanisms by which values and beliefs shape self-perception.
wider: Examine how cultural values and beliefs from diverse communities in Australia — including young Australians of Asian heritage — influence self-perception and identity in distinctive ways
Explore how digital culture and social media create new sites where values and beliefs about identity are negotiated and contested for young people

modes.reason: Distinguish between values (what one believes is important) and beliefs (what one holds to be true) and model how each type of influence operates through specific examples before students attempt their own analysis.

nodes.label: Analysing influence on identity development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how specific values and beliefs — from personal, family, peer or cultural sources — influence identity development, identifying the mechanism of influence.
criteria: Identifies at least one source of values or beliefs and names the source (personal, family, peer or cultural)
Analyses at least one specific way that source influences identity development

width.minimum: Identify one source of values or beliefs (personal, family or cultural) and analyse how it influences identity development in at least one specific way.
width.typical: Analyse how values and beliefs from multiple sources influence identity development across a range of contexts; examine how cultural beliefs about puberty, gender, and physical change specifically affect the development of gender, cultural and sexual identities.
wider: Analyse how naming of deceased protocols (such as kumanjayi) in First Nations Australian communities reflect community values and impact the identities of community members
Examine how cultural beliefs about puberty and physical change create different pathways to gender, cultural and sexual identity across different cultural communities

modes.reason: Analysis of identity influence deepens when students encounter culturally diverse examples — encountering how the same mechanism (values → identity) operates differently across cultural contexts builds genuine analytical capacity rather than culturally narrow conclusions.

nodes.label: Reflecting on personal identity development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on how their own values and beliefs — and those of the people and communities around them — have contributed to their developing sense of identity.
criteria: Identifies at least one personal, family or cultural value or belief that has influenced their own identity
Reflects on at least one specific way that value or belief has shaped their sense of self

width.minimum: Identify at least one personal or family value or belief and reflect on one way it has shaped their own sense of identity.
width.typical: Reflect on how values and beliefs from multiple sources (personal, family, friends, cultural community) have influenced their own identity development; connect this reflection to the broader analysis completed in prior nodes.
wider: Reflect on how navigating between different cultural value systems (e.g. for students with bicultural or multicultural backgrounds) has shaped their developing identity in distinctive ways
Investigate how their own values about identity compare to and differ from those of their family, peer group and cultural community, reflecting on what this reveals about identity negotiation

modes.reason: Reflection integrates the conceptual analysis of values/beliefs/identity with personal experience — instruction should position reflection as an application of the analytical framework, not as separate personal disclosure.

descriptors.title: Changes, transitions and support
descriptors.description: analyse the impact of changes and transitions, and devise strategies to support themselves and others through these changes
descriptors.knowledge: Students have investigated resources and strategies to manage changes and transitions, including puberty (Y5-6). They can identify strategies and resources but have not yet been expected to analyse the impact of transitions systematically or devise strategies for supporting others.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse the impact of changes and transitions, and devise strategies to support themselves and others through these changes.

nodes.label: Understanding types of changes and transitions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the range of significant changes and transitions relevant to their age group and describe the types of impact — social, emotional, physical — each can have.
criteria: Identifies at least two changes or transitions relevant to their age group
Describes at least one type of impact (social, emotional or physical) for each identified transition

width.minimum: Identify at least two changes or transitions relevant to their age group and describe one type of impact each can have.
width.typical: Identify a range of significant transitions (puberty, changing peer/family relationships, social transitions, cultural transitions) and describe their social, emotional and physical impacts; distinguish between predictable and unexpected transitions.
wider: Examine how ceremonies of First Nations Australians involve sharing of cultural knowledge and mark changes in social standing and responsibilities, comparing these transition structures to those in students' own communities
Explore the concept of 'border crossing' — how First Nations Australians navigate multiple cultural contexts — and how this type of ongoing transition can impact sense of belonging

modes.reason: A broad repertoire of transition types prevents students from treating only visible physical changes as significant — emotional, social and cultural transitions are equally important in this descriptor.

nodes.label: Analysing the impact of changes and transitions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse the specific impact of one or more transitions on individuals — including emotional, relational and identity effects — and explain what factors influence how significant the impact is.
criteria: Analyses at least two specific effects of a named transition on an individual
Identifies at least one factor that influences how significant the impact is
nodes.hinge_reason: Devising strategies requires understanding what the strategies are responding to — students who cannot analyse the impact of transitions will devise generic coping strategies unconnected to the specific experience being managed.

width.minimum: Analyse the impact of one transition on an individual, identifying at least two specific effects and one factor that influences how significant the impact is.
width.typical: Analyse the impact of transitions across multiple types; identify factors that mediate impact (social support, coping skills, cultural resources, individual disposition); examine how puberty-related changes affect emotional responses and relationships.
wider: Investigate how accessing and assessing health and sexual health information supports young people through puberty-related transitions, evaluating the quality and relevance of available sources

Examine the emotional and relational impacts of 'border crossing' for First Nations young people navigating multiple cultural contexts, considering how this ongoing transition intersects with other developmental changes

modes.reason: Scaffold impact analysis by explicitly modelling the analysis of a specific transition: what changes, for whom, in what ways, and what makes the impact greater or lesser for different people? This builds the analytical structure students need before devising strategies.

nodes.label: Devising strategies for support
nodes.checkpoint: Students can devise practical strategies to support themselves and others through specific transitions, including accessing relevant health information and services.
criteria: Devises at least one strategy for supporting themselves or another person through a specific transition
Explains why the strategy would be effective for that transition
Identifies at least one health information source or service relevant to the transition

width.minimum: Devise at least one strategy for supporting themselves or another person through a specific transition, giving a reason why it would be effective.
width.typical: Devise a range of strategies — including coping, communication and problem-solving strategies — for supporting themselves and others through multiple transition types; access and assess health information and services relevant to managing specific transitions; evaluate and practise strategies.
wider: Evaluate and practise coping, communication and problem-solving skills for managing emotions and changes associated with puberty and getting older, comparing the effectiveness of different strategy types
Research transition support resources available to young people in their community and evaluate their accessibility and relevance for different transition scenarios
